How do we assign several variables?

            

                You already know how to give one variable a value. But science,
                research, and everyday programs often need several values, such as
                temperature, pressure, and density.
            

        

    


    

        

        

            A common beginner question
            

                Should we use commas, semicolons, spaces, or separate lines when
                assigning several values?
            

        

    


    


        

            
                 Best for beginners
            

            
Write one assignment on each line


            
temperature = 25.0
pressure = 101.3
density = 1.18


            

                This is the clearest and most common style. Press
                Enter after each assignment and write the next one
                on a new line.
            

        


        

            
                 Avoid this style
            

            
Using semicolons on one line


            
temperature = 25.0; pressure = 101.3; density = 1.18


            

                Python allows semicolons, but this style becomes difficult to read.
                Write clean programs on separate lines instead.
            

        


    


    


        

            
            When do we use commas?
        


        

            Use commas when you want to assign several matching values in a single
            line. Python connects values from left to right.
        


        


            
temperature, pressure, density = 25.0, 101.3, 1.18


            

                

                    temperature
                    
                    25.0
                


                

                    pressure
                    
                    101.3
                


                

                    density
                    
                    1.18
                

            


        


        

            
            

                The first variable receives the first value, the second variable
                receives the second value, and so on. This is called
                multiple assignment.
            

        


    

    


    

        
        Be careful: a comma can change the data type
    


    

        Look carefully at the comma after 3. It does not produce an
        error immediately, but it changes a from a number into a
        one-item tuple.
    


    
a = 3,
b = 5

print(a)        # (3,)
print(type(a))  # <class 'tuple'>
print(b)        # 5


    


        

            What Python understands
            a = (3,)
            

                A comma after one value creates a tuple. Parentheses are optional
                in Python, but the comma is important.
            

        


        

            What you probably wanted
            a = 3
            

                Remove the comma when you want a to store one normal
                number.
            

        


    


    


        
            
            The error appears when we try to calculate:
        

        
a = 3,
b = 5

print(a + b)


        

            Python cannot add a tuple (3,) and an integer
            5.
        


        
            TypeError: can only concatenate tuple (not "int") to tuple
        

    


    


        
 Correct use of commas for multiple assignment


        
a, b = 3, 5

print(a)  # 3
print(b)  # 5


        

            Here, Python matches the first variable with the first value and the
            second variable with the second value.
        


    




    


        

            
            Which symbol should I use?
        


        

            
                

                    Situation
                    Use
                    Example
                

            

            
                

                    Assign one variable
                    =
                    temperature = 25.0
                


                

                    Assign several matching variables on one line
                    , and =
                    x, y = 10, 20
                


                

                    Write assignments separately
                    Press Enter
                    x = 10
y = 20		
                


                

                    Separate normal Python statements
                    Do not use a semicolon
                    x = 10
y = 20		
                

            
        


    


    

        

        

            What if I have hundreds of values from Excel?
            

                You do not need to type every value one by one. Later, you will
                learn how Python reads tables efficiently using lists, CSV files,
                Pandas, and NumPy.
            

        

    





    
    
    


        

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Does a variable permanently store a value?
            

            

                 No. A variable can be assigned another value later in the
                program.
            

        


        

            
                Is the assignment symbol the same as mathematical equality?
            

            

                No. In Python, = assigns a value. Python uses
                == when it needs to compare two values. We will
                learn comparisons in a later lesson.
            

        


        

            
                Can I use capital letters in a variable name?
            

            

                Yes, but ordinary variable names are normally written in
                lowercase. Names written completely in capital letters are
                commonly used for values that should remain constant.
            

        

        

            
                Can a variable contain different types of values?
            

            

                Yes. Python allows the same variable name to be assigned values
                of different types, although repeatedly changing its meaning
                can make a program difficult to understand.
            

        

        

            
                Can I use a very short name such as x?
            

            

                Yes. Short names are sometimes useful in formulas or small
                examples. For most programs, descriptive names such as
                total_price are easier to understand.
            

        


    

    
    

        

        
    




12. Numbers and Arithmetic Operators
Stage II · Core PythonPlanned


        

            Python can act as a simple calculator, but its real power
            begins when calculations become part of a larger program. In
            this lesson, we will work with numbers and learn the symbols
            Python uses for arithmetic.
        



    
    


        


            

                17 % 5 = 2
            


            

                7
                8
                9
                4
                5
                6
                1
                2
                3
            


        


        


            
Python is more than a calculator


            

                Researchers calculate averages, engineers calculate
                forces, businesses calculate profit, and students
                calculate grades. Python uses familiar mathematical
                ideas but represents some operations with special
                symbols.
            


            

                For example, Python uses ** for powers and
                % for the remainder after division.
            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            Python's main number types
        


        

            Python has three main built-in numeric types: integers,
            floating-point numbers, and complex numbers.
        


        


            
            


                


                    int

                    Integer

                


                


                    

                        A whole number without a decimal point. It may be
                        positive, negative, or zero.
                    


                    25
                    -7
                    0

                


            



            
            


                


                    float

                    Floating-point number

                


                


                    

                        A number containing a decimal point or written
                        using scientific notation.
                    


                    27.5
                    -0.03
                    1.2e3

                


            



            
            


                


                    complex

                    Complex number

                


                


                    

                        A number containing a real and an imaginary part.
                        Python uses j for the imaginary unit.
                    


                    3 + 5j
                    -2j
                    4 - 1.5j

                


            


        


        


            

            

                You do not need complex numbers for ordinary beginner
                programs. They are included here so you know that Python
                supports them when scientific or engineering work
                requires them.
            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            How can we check a number's type?
        


        

            Python's built-in type() function tells us the
            type of a value.
        


        


            


                
Integer


                
print(type(25))

# Output:
<class 'int'>


            


            


                
Floating-point number


                
print(type(25.0))

# Output:
<class 'float'>


            

            

            


                
Tuplet


                
a=(3,)
print(type(a))

# Output:
<class 'tuple'>


            

            

            


                
string


                
print(type("hello"))

# Output:
<class 'str'>


            


        


        


            

            

                Although 25 and 25.0 represent
                the same mathematical quantity, Python stores them as
                different numeric types.
            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            Arithmetic operators
        


        

            An operator is a symbol that tells Python to perform an
            operation on one or more values.
        


        


            


                +

                

                    Addition
                    Adds two numbers.
                


                
                    8 + 3 → 11
                

            


            


                −

                

                    Subtraction
                    Subtracts the second number.
                


                
                    8 - 3 → 5
                

            


            


                *

                

                    Multiplication
                    Multiplies two numbers.
                


                
                    8 * 3 → 24
                

            


            


                /

                

                    Division
                    Returns the division result as a float.
                


                
                    8 / 3 → 2.666...
                

            


            


                //

                

                    Floor division
                    
                        Divides and rounds the result downward.
                    
                


                
                    8 // 3 → 2
                

            


            


                %

                

                    Modulo
                    Returns the remainder after division.
                


                
                    8 % 3 → 2
                

            


            


                **

                

                    Exponentiation
                    Raises one number to a power.
                


                
                    2 ** 3 → 8
                

            


        


        


            

            

                Python uses * for multiplication and it does not use the
                handwritten symbol ×. It uses
                ** for exponentiation instead of mathematical notation
                ^.
            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            Three questions hidden inside division
        


        

            Suppose 17 samples must be placed equally into groups of 5.
            Python can answer three different questions.
        


        


            


                
Exact division


                17 / 5

                
                    3.4
                

                

                    How many groups exactly?
                


            


            


                
Complete groups


                17 // 5

                
                    3
                

                

                    How many complete groups fit?
                


            


            


                
Remaining samples


                17 % 5

                
                    2
                

                

                    How many samples remain?
                


            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            Python Arithmetic Calculator
        


        

            Enter two numbers and choose a Python arithmetic operator.
            This calculator reproduces the basic behavior of the selected
            operator.
        


        


            


                


                    

                    

                


                


                    

                    

                


                


                    

                    

                


                

            


            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            Operator precedence
        


        

            When one expression contains several operators, Python
            follows an order of operations "BADMAS(brackets, orders, division,multiplication, addition,subtraction)". Parentheses can be used to
            make your intended order clear.
        


        


            


                1

                ( )

                Expressions inside parentheses.

            


            


                2

                **

                Exponentiation.

            


            


                4

                *, /, //, %

                
                    Multiplication, division, floor division, and modulo.
                

            


            


                5

                +, -

                Addition and subtraction.

            


        


        


            


                
Without parentheses


                
result = 2 + 3 * 4
print(result)

# Output: 14


                

                    Multiplication happens before addition.
                


            


            


                
With parentheses


                
result = (2 + 3) * 4
print(result)

# Output: 20


                

                    The expression inside parentheses happens first.
                


            


        


        


            

            

                Even when parentheses are not required, using them can
                make a complicated expression easier for humans to read.
            


        


    

    


    

        
        Plus, Minus, and Updating a Value
    


    

        The symbols + and - can work between two
        numbers, or they can work on one number.
    


    


        

            +x
            
Unary plus

            
Keeps the numerical value unchanged.


            
x = 5

print(+x)  # 5

        


        

            -x
            
Unary minus

            
Changes the sign of a number.


            
x = 5

print(-x)  # -5

        


    


    


        

            
            Python does not use x++ or x--
        


        


            

                Do not write this

                
x++
x--


                

                    These produce a syntax error when written as complete Python
                    statements.
                

            


            

                Write this in Python

                
x += 1  # Increase x by 1
x -= 1  # Decrease x by 1


                

                    These are called augmented assignment operators.
                

            


        

    


    


        
 Small example


        
x = 10

x += 1
print(x)  # 11

x -= 3
print(x)  # 8

x *= 2
print(x)  # 16

x /= 4
print(x)  # 4.0


    


    


        
 A strange Python detail


        
x = 5

print(++x)  # 5
print(--x)  # 5


        

            These do not change x. Python reads ++x as
            +(+x) and --x as -(-x).
            Avoid using them—they are confusing.
        

    



    
    


        

            
            Arithmetic in practical programs
        


        


            


                
Calculate an average


                
total = 85 + 92 + 78
average = total / 3

print(average)


                

                    Output: 85.0
                


            


            


                
Calculate a rectangle's area


                
length = 12
width = 5

area = length * width
print(area)


                

                    Output: 60
                


            


            


                
Check even or odd


                
number = 17
remainder = number % 2

print(remainder)


                

                    A remainder of 0 means even; 1 means odd.
                


            


            


                
Calculate a square


                
side = 6
area = side ** 2

print(area)


                

                    Output: 36
                


            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            A small surprise with decimal numbers
        


        

            Computers store most floating-point values using binary
            approximations. As a result, some decimal calculations may
            display a tiny representation difference.
        


        


            
                >>>
            

            0.1 + 0.2

            


            
                0.30000000000000004
            

        


        


            

            

                This does not mean that Python is randomly calculating
                the wrong answer. It comes from how decimal fractions are
                represented in binary floating-point hardware. We will
                learn appropriate rounding and precision tools later.
            


        


    



    
    


        

            
            Division by zero
        


        

            Division by zero is undefined. Python stops the calculation
            and reports a ZeroDivisionError.
        


        


            
                >>>
            

            10 / 0

            


            
                ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
            

        


        


            

            

                The operators /, //, and
                % all require a nonzero divisor.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                What is the difference between / and
                //?
            

            

                / performs ordinary division and returns a
                floating-point result. // performs floor
                division and rounds the mathematical result downward.
            

        


        

            
                Why is 7 / 2 equal to 3.5 but
                7 // 2 equal to 3?
            

            

                Ordinary division keeps the fractional part. Floor
                division returns the greatest whole-number value that is
                less than or equal to the exact result.
            

        


        

            
                What does the modulo operator do?
            

            

                The % operator returns the remainder after
                division. For example, 17 % 5 returns
                2.
            

        

        

            
                Does ^ calculate a power in Python?
            

            

                No. Python uses ** for exponentiation.
                The ^ symbol performs a different bitwise
                operation that we will not study in this lesson.
            

        

        

            
                Why does ordinary division return a float?
            

            

                In Python 3, the / operator returns a
                floating-point result even when the mathematical answer
                is a whole number. For example, 8 / 4
                returns 2.0.
            

        

        

            
                Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not displayed as exactly
                0.3?
            

            

                Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly
                using finite binary floating-point values. Python stores
                the closest available approximation.
            

        


    

    
    
    


        

        

    







    
13. Strings and Text Processing


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Python can work with words too!

            

                Until now, we have worked mainly with numbers. But programs also
                need to handle names, messages, file names, emails, passwords,
                answers from users, and much more. In Python, text is called a
                string.
            

        

    


    

        
 What is a string?


        

            A string is a collection of characters written inside quotation marks.
            Letters, spaces, symbols, and even numbers can be part of a string.
        


        

            
name = "Haripriya"
message = 'Welcome to Python!'
year_as_text = "2026"

print(name)
print(message)

        


        

            
            

                "2026" is text because it is inside quotation marks.
                But 2026 without quotation marks is a number.
            

        

    


    


        

            
 Single or double quotes?


            
Both single and double quotation marks can create strings.


            
course = "Python"
teacher = 'Guido van Rossum'


            

                Use the other type of quotation mark when your text already
                contains a quote.
            


            
sentence = "She said, 'Hello!'"

        


        

            
 String length


            

                Python can count how many characters are in a string using
                len().
            


            
word = "Python"

print(len(word))  # 6


            

                Spaces and punctuation marks are also counted as characters.
            

        


    


    


        
 Joining text together


        

            Use + to join strings. This is called
            concatenation.
        


        
first_name = "Asha"
last_name = "Das"

full_name = first_name + " " + last_name

print(full_name)


        

            A cleaner way is an f-string. Put the letter
            f before the quotation marks and place variables inside
            curly brackets.
        


        
name = "Asha"
topic = "Python"

print(f"{name} is learning {topic}.")


    


    

    


        
 Useful text methods


        

            Methods are ready-made actions that help us clean, change, and analyse text.
        


        


            

                .upper()
                
Make text uppercase

                
"python".upper() → PYTHON

            


            

                .lower()
                
Make text lowercase

                
"PYTHON".lower() → python

            


            

                .strip()
                
Remove extra spaces

                
" hello ".strip() → hello

            


            

                .replace()
                
Replace a part of text

                
"I like C".replace("C", "Python")

            


            

                .split()
                
Split text into pieces

                
"red,blue".split(",") creates a list.

            


            

                .count()
                
Count text

                
"banana".count("a") → 3

            


        


    


    


        
 Try the Text Studio


        

            Type any sentence, choose an action, and see how Python would process it.
        


        
        

        


            

            

            

            

            

        


        

            

            

            
        


        

            Python result
            HELLO, PYTHON LEARNER!
        


    


    


        
 Strings cannot be changed character by character


        

            Strings are immutable. This means you cannot directly
            replace one character inside an existing string.
        


        
word = "Python"

# word[0] = "J"     ❌ This causes an error

new_word = "J" + word[1:]

print(new_word)    # Jython


        

            Instead, create a new string and store it in a variable.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Should I use single quotes or double quotes for strings?
            

            

                Both work the same: "hello" and 'hello' are identical. Pick one style and stay consistent. Use the other kind when your text contains a quote, for example "It's sunny".
            

        


        

            
                Why can't I change one letter with text[0] = "J"?
            

            

                Strings are immutable, which means they cannot be changed after they are created. Make a new string instead: text = "J" + text[1:] or text = text.replace("h", "J").
            

        


        

            
                Why does "5" + 5 give an error?
            

            

                Python does not mix text and numbers automatically. Convert one of them first: "5" + str(5) gives "55", while int("5") + 5 gives 10.
            

        

        

            
                Does name.upper() change my original string?
            

            

                No. String methods return a new string and leave the original unchanged. Save the result if you want to keep it: name = name.upper().
            

        

        

            
                How do I write a string over several lines?
            

            

                Use triple quotes, """like this""", and press Enter inside them. You can also put \n inside a normal string: print("Line 1\nLine 2").
            

        


    

    

        

        
    







    
14. Booleans, Comparisons, and Logical Operators


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    


        

            
        


        

            
How does Python make decisions?

            

                Every day, we make simple decisions: Is it raining?
                Do I have enough money? Is my assignment finished?
                Python also needs answers to these kinds of questions.
            

        


    


    


        
 What is a Boolean?


        

            A Boolean is a data type that has only two possible
            values:
        


        

            

                
                True
                Yes, correct, or condition satisfied
            


            

                
                False
                No, incorrect, or condition not satisfied
            

        


        
is_python_fun = True
is_exam_today = False

print(is_python_fun)
print(is_exam_today)


        

            
            

                Always write True and False with a capital
                first letter. Python treats true and false
                as different, unknown names.
            

        


    


    


        
 Comparison operators


        

            Comparison operators compare two values and return either
            True or False.
        


        


            

                ==
                Equal to
                
5 == 5 → True

            


            

                !=
                Not equal to
                
5 != 3 → True

            


            

                >
                Greater than
                
10 > 4 → True

            


            

                <
                Less than
                
2 < 1 → False

            


            

                >=
                Greater than or equal to
                
7 >= 7 → True

            


            

                <=
                Less than or equal to
                
4 <= 2 → False

            


        


    


    


        
 Do not confuse = and ==


        


            

                =
                
Assignment

                
Stores a value inside a variable.


                
age = 25

            


            

                ==
                
Comparison

                
Checks whether two values are equal.


                
age == 25

            


        


        

            Read it like this: = means “becomes”, while
            == means “is equal to?”
        


    


    


        
 A real example


        

            Imagine that you want to check whether a student has passed an exam.
        


        
mark = 72

print(mark >= 50)   # True
print(mark < 50)    # False
print(mark == 100)  # False


        

            These Boolean results will later help us write programs that react
            differently in different situations.
        


    


    


        
 Logical operators


        

            Logical operators help us combine more than one condition.
            Python has three important logical operators:
            and, or, and not.
        


        


            

                
and

                

                    Both conditions must be True.
                


                
age = 20
has_ticket = True

print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
# True

            


            

                
or

                

                    At least one condition must be True.
                


                
is_weekend = False
is_holiday = True

print(is_weekend or is_holiday)
# True

            


            

                
not

                

                    Changes True to False, and vice versa.
                


                
is_raining = True

print(not is_raining)
# False

            


        


    


    


        
 Quick truth table


        

            
                

                    Condition A
                    Condition B
                    A and B
                    A or B
                

            

            
                

                    True
                    True
                    True
                    True
                

                

                    True
                    False
                    False
                    True
                

                

                    False
                    True
                    False
                    True
                

                

                    False
                    False
                    False
                    False
                

            
        


    


    


        
 Try it yourself


        

            Predict the output first. Then run the code and check your answer.
        


        
temperature = 30
is_sunny = True

print(temperature > 25)
print(temperature < 20)
print(temperature > 25 and is_sunny)
print(temperature < 20 or is_sunny)
print(not is_sunny)


    


    


        

        

            Coming next:
            

                In the next lesson, we will use these Boolean conditions to make
                Python choose actions using if, elif,
                and else.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                What is the difference between = and ==?
            

            

                = stores a value in a variable: age = 20. == asks a question and answers with True or False: age == 20.
            

        


        

            
                Why must True and False start with a capital letter?
            

            

                They are special Python keywords and must be written exactly like that. Python reads true as an unknown variable name and shows a NameError.
            

        


        

            
                Can numbers and text behave like True or False?
            

            

                Yes. Empty or zero values count as False: 0, 0.0, "", [], and None. Almost everything else counts as True. Try bool(0) and bool("hi").
            

        

        

            
                Can I compare words using < and >?
            

            

                Yes. Python compares strings letter by letter, like a dictionary order, but capital letters come before small letters. "apple" < "banana" is True, but "apple" < "Banana" is False.
            

        

        

            
                If and and or are in the same line, which one runs first?
            

            

                Python checks not first, then and, then or. To avoid confusion, use brackets to show the order you mean: (a or b) and c.
            

        


    

    

        

        
    







    
15. Input, Output, f-Strings, and Type Conversion


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Let your program talk with people

            

                Until now, we have written values directly in our program. But a
                useful program should be able to ask a user for information,
                process it, and show a meaningful result.
            

        

    


    


        
 Output: showing information with print()


        

            We use print() when we want Python to show something on
            the screen.
        


        
print("Hello, Python!")
print(25)
print("My score is", 92)


        

            
            

                Text must be inside quotation marks. Variables and numbers do not
                need quotation marks.
            

        


    


    


        
 Input: asking the user a question


        

            Python uses input() to wait for the user to type an answer.
            The answer is stored in a variable.
        


        
name = input("What is your name? ")

print("Hello", name)


        

            Question shown by Python
            

                What is your name?
                Haripriya
            

            Value stored in the variable name
        


    


    


        
 f-Strings: a clean way to combine text and variables


        

            An f-string lets you place variables directly inside a sentence. Start
            the string with f and write variable names inside
            curly brackets { }.
        


        
name = "Asha"
subject = "Python"

print(f"{name} is learning {subject}.")


        

            
            Asha is learning Python.
        


        

            You can also calculate inside curly brackets.
        


        
apples = 4
price = 15

print(f"Total price: {apples * price} dollars")


    


    


        
 Why do we need type conversion?


        

            Everything entered through input() begins as
            text (a string), even if the user types a number.
        


        
age = input("Enter your age: ")

print(type(age))   # <class 'str'>


        

            To calculate with the value, convert it into the correct type.
        


        


            

                int()
                
Whole numbers

                
age = int(input("Age: "))

            


            

                float()
                
Decimal numbers

                
height = float(input("Height: "))

            


            

                str()
                
Convert to text

                
message = str(2026)

            


        


    


    


        
 Example: calculate the user's age next year


        
name = input("What is your name? ")
age = int(input("How old are you? "))

next_year_age = age + 1

print(f"Hello {name}! Next year, you will be {next_year_age}.")


        

            
            

                Without int(), Python cannot add 1 to
                the age because the age would still be text.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why does input() give me a string even when I type a number?
            

            

                input() always returns text, because the keyboard sends characters. Convert it when you need a number: age = int(input("Age: ")) or float(...) for decimals.
            

        


        

            
                What happens if someone types abc into int(input())?
            

            

                Python cannot turn abc into a whole number, so it stops with a ValueError. In a later lesson you will learn try and except to handle this politely.
            

        


        

            
                What does the f in an f-string do?
            

            

                It tells Python to replace anything inside { } with its value. Without the f, "Hello {name}" prints the braces exactly as written.
            

        

        

            
                How do I show only two decimal places?
            

            

                Add :.2f inside the braces: f"{price:.2f}" turns 3.14159 into 3.14.
            

        

        

            
                How do I print without moving to a new line, or with a different separator?
            

            

                Use end and sep: print("Loading", end="...") keeps the next print on the same line, and print("2026", "05", "14", sep="-") prints 2026-05-14.
            

        


    

    

        

        
    







    
16. Python Indexing: Finding Data by Position


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Every item has an address

            

                Imagine a row of lockers. Each locker has a number, so you can find
                the exact one you need. Python does the same thing: every character
                or item in a collection has a position called an index.
            

        

    


    


        
 Python starts counting from zero


        

            This is one of the first surprising things in programming. The first
            item is at position 0, the second item is at position
            1, and so on.
        


        


            

                012
                345
            


            

                Pyt
                hon
            


            

                -6-5-4
                -3-2-1
            


        


        
word = "Python"

print(word[0])   # P
print(word[1])   # y
print(word[5])   # n


    


    


        
 Negative indexing: count from the end


        

            Python also lets us count backwards. The final item is always at
            index -1.
        


        
word = "Python"

print(word[-1])  # n
print(word[-2])  # o
print(word[-3])  # h


        

            
            

                Positive indexes count from the left. Negative indexes count from
                the right.
            

        


    


    


        
 Indexing works with lists too


        

            Indexing is not only for text. We can use it to select one item from a
            list or tuple.
        


        
fruits = ["apple", "mango", "banana"]

print(fruits[0])   # apple
print(fruits[1])   # mango
print(fruits[-1])  # banana


        

            

                fruits[0]
                apple
            


            

                fruits[1]
                mango
            


            

                fruits[-1]
                banana
            

        


    


    


        
 Slicing: selecting more than one item


        

            A slice selects a range of values using the format
            start:end.
        


        
word = "Python"

print(word[0:2])  # Py
print(word[2:6])  # thon
print(word[:3])   # Pyt
print(word[3:])   # hon


        

            
            

                The ending position is not included. Therefore,
                word[0:2] gives Py, not
                Pyt.
            

        


    


    


        
 What is an IndexError?


        

            An IndexError happens when you ask Python for a position
            that does not exist.
        


        
word = "Python"

print(word[10])  # ❌ IndexError


        

            The word "Python" has six characters, so its valid
            positive indexes are only 0 to 5.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why does Python start counting at 0?
            

            

                An index tells Python how many steps to move from the start. The first item is 0 steps away, so its index is 0. Most programming languages count this way.
            

        


        

            
                What does IndexError: index out of range mean?
            

            

                You asked for a position that does not exist. If something has 5 items, the last valid index is 4, which is len(x) - 1.
            

        


        

            
                How do negative indexes work?
            

            

                They count from the end. [-1] is the last item, [-2] the second last, and so on. This is handy when you do not know the length.
            

        

        

            
                Why does text[1:4] not include position 4?
            

            

                In a slice, the stop position is not included. This makes the count easy: 4 - 1 = 3 items. It also lets text[:4] and text[4:] fit together without overlapping.
            

        

        

            
                Can I use indexing on a number?
            

            

                No. A number such as 2026 is not a sequence. Convert it to a string first: str(2026)[0] gives "2".
            

        


    

    

        

        
    







    
17. Lists, List Operators, Sets, and Unique Values


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Store and organise many values

            

                A list stores many values in order. A
                set stores only unique values, so repeated items
                are automatically removed.
            

        

    


    

        
 What is a list?


        

            A list is an ordered and changeable collection. Use square brackets
            [ ], with commas between items.
        


        
fruits = ["apple", "mango", "banana"]

print(fruits)
print(fruits[0])    # apple
print(fruits[-1])   # banana


        

            
            

                Lists can contain text, numbers, Boolean values, or even other lists.
            

        

    


    

        
 List operators


        


            

                +
                
Join two lists

                
first = [1, 2]
second = [3, 4]

print(first + second)
# [1, 2, 3, 4]

            


            

                *
                
Repeat a list

                
numbers = [1, 2]

print(numbers * 3)
# [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2]

            


            

                in
                
Check whether an item exists

                
fruits = ["apple", "mango"]

print("mango" in fruits)
# True

            


            

                not in
                
Check whether an item is absent

                
fruits = ["apple", "mango"]

print("banana" not in fruits)
# True

            


        

    


    

        
 Useful list methods


        

            
.append()
Add one item at the end.

            
.insert()
Add an item at a chosen position.

            
.remove()
Remove an item by its value.

            
.pop()
Remove the final item.

            
.sort()
Arrange items in order.

            
.reverse()
Reverse the item order.

        


        
tasks = ["Read", "Walk"]

tasks.append("Study")
tasks.insert(1, "Exercise")
tasks.remove("Walk")

print(tasks)
# ['Read', 'Exercise', 'Study']

    


    

        
 Sets: keeping only unique values


        

            A set uses curly brackets { }. It automatically removes
            duplicate values. Sets do not use indexing because they have no fixed order.
        


        
numbers = [2, 4, 2, 5, 4, 7]

unique_numbers = set(numbers)

print(unique_numbers)
# {2, 4, 5, 7}


        

            
            

                Use a set when you need to find unique names, tags, cities, IDs, or answers.
            

        

    


    

        
 Set operations


        


            

                |
                
Union

                
All unique values from both sets.

                
a | b

            


            

                &
                
Intersection

                
Values that appear in both sets.

                
a & b

            


            

                -
                
Difference

                
Values in the first set but not the second.

                
a - b

            


        


        
python_students = {"Asha", "Ravi", "Mina"}
math_students = {"Mina", "Ravi", "Sara"}

print(python_students | math_students)
print(python_students & math_students)
print(python_students - math_students)

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                What is the difference between a list and a set?
            

            

                A list keeps the order, allows duplicates, and lets you use indexes. A set keeps only unique values, has no fixed order, and has no indexes.
            

        


        

            
                Why does my set print items in a different order?
            

            

                Sets do not remember order, so never rely on it. If you need sorted values, use sorted(my_set), which returns a sorted list.
            

        


        

            
                Why does print(my_list.sort()) show None?
            

            

                .sort() changes the list itself and returns nothing. Sort first, then print: my_list.sort() and then print(my_list). Or use sorted(my_list), which returns a new list.
            

        

        

            
                What is the difference between append() and extend()?
            

            

                append() adds one item, even if that item is a whole list. extend() adds each item separately: [1, 2].append([3, 4]) gives [1, 2, [3, 4]], but extend gives [1, 2, 3, 4].
            

        

        

            
                How do I create an empty set?
            

            

                Use set(). Writing {} creates an empty dictionary, not a set.
            

        


    

    

        

        
    







    
18. Tuples and Immutable Data


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
A list that should not change

            

                Sometimes we need to keep related values together but do not want
                anyone to accidentally change them. A tuple is
                perfect for this situation.
            

        

    


    


        
 What is a tuple?


        

            A tuple stores several values in one variable, just like a list.
            However, tuples use parentheses ( ) and cannot be
            changed after they are created.
        


        
location = ("Kaohsiung", 22.6273, 120.3014)

print(location)


        

            
            

                A tuple is immutable. Immutable means
                “cannot be changed after creation.”
            

        


    


    


        
 List vs tuple


        


            

                
 List

                ["apple", "mango"]
                
Uses square brackets.

                
Items can be added, removed, or changed.

                Mutable
            


            

                
 Tuple

                ("apple", "mango")
                
Uses parentheses.

                
Items remain fixed after creation.

                Immutable
            


        


    


    


        
 Accessing tuple items


        

            Tuples use indexes exactly like strings and lists. Python begins
            counting at 0.
        


        
colours = ("red", "blue", "green")

print(colours[0])   # red
print(colours[1])   # blue
print(colours[-1])  # green


    


    


        
 Why can’t we change a tuple?


        
days = ("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday")

# days[0] = "Sunday"   ❌ This creates an error


        

            This is useful when the data should stay safe, such as coordinates,
            RGB colours, dates, or settings that must not be edited by mistake.
        


        

             GPS coordinates
             RGB colours
             Dates
             Fixed results
        


    


    


        
 A tuple with one item


        

            For a one-item tuple, the comma is important. Without the comma,
            Python sees only a normal value inside parentheses.
        


        


            

                Not a tuple
                
fruit = ("mango")

                
This is a string.

            


            

                A real one-item tuple
                
fruit = ("mango",)

                
The comma makes it a tuple.

            


        


    


    


        
 Tuple packing and unpacking


        

            Python can place several values into a tuple automatically. This is
            called packing.
        


        
student = "Asha", 24, "Taiwan"

print(student)


        

            We can also unpack each tuple value into its own variable.
        


        
name, age, country = student

print(name)      # Asha
print(age)       # 24
print(country)   # Taiwan


    


    


        
 Try tuple unpacking


        

            This tuple stores a student's name, subject, and score. Click the
            button to unpack its values into three separate variables.
        


        

            student = ("Asha", "Python", 92)
        


        

        

            Click the button to see how tuple unpacking works.
        


    


    


        
 Small practice


        
Create a tuple for your favourite place using this format:


        
place = ("Kaohsiung", "Taiwan", 22.6273, 120.3014)

# Print the city name.
# Print the latitude.
# Try changing the country and observe the error.


    


    

        
        

            Coming next:
            

                We will use if, elif, and
                else to make Python choose between different actions.
            

        

    

    


        

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                If tuples cannot change, why not always use lists?
            

            

                A tuple protects data that should stay fixed, such as coordinates or dates, and tells other readers that it is not meant to change. Tuples are also slightly faster and can be used as dictionary keys.
            

        


        

            
                Is there any way to change a tuple?
            

            

                Not in place. You create a new tuple instead: colours = colours + ("yellow",). Or convert it to a list, change it, and convert it back with tuple().
            

        


        

            
                Do I always need brackets to make a tuple?
            

            

                No, the comma is what makes a tuple: point = 3, 4 is a tuple. Brackets make it easier to read, and you need them for an empty tuple: ().
            

        

        

            
                What happens if the number of variables does not match when unpacking?
            

            

                Python shows a ValueError, such as too many values to unpack. The number of variables on the left must match the number of items in the tuple.
            

        

        

            
                Can a tuple contain a list?
            

            

                Yes, but the list inside can still change: data = ([1, 2], 3) then data[0].append(5) works. The tuple only fixes which items it holds. For fully fixed data, put only fixed values inside.
            

        


    

    

        

        
    








    
19. Arrays: Working with Numerical Data


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Arrays are made for groups of numbers

            

                Arrays store many values in one variable. They are especially useful
                for temperatures, marks, sensor data, images, scientific data, and
                mathematical calculations.
            

        

    


    

        
 List versus array


        


            

                
Python list

                
values = [10, "hello", True]

                
A list can store different data types.

                
Useful for general programming.

            


            

                
Python array

                
from array import array

values = array("i", [10, 20, 30])

                
An array normally stores one type of value.

                
Useful when many values have the same type.

            


        

    


    

        
 Creating an array with Python


        

            Python has an array module. The type code
            "i" means integer values.
        


        
from array import array

marks = array("i", [78, 85, 92, 64])

print(marks)
print(marks[0])     # 78
print(marks[-1])    # 64


        

            
            

                Use array("f", [...]) when you need decimal values,
                such as temperature or height.
            

        

    


    

        
 Changing array values


        
from array import array

temperatures = array("f", [28.5, 29.0, 30.2])

temperatures[1] = 31.5
temperatures.append(29.8)

print(temperatures)


        

            

                .append(value)
                
Add one value at the end.

            


            

                .insert(index, value)
                
Add a value at a chosen position.

            


            

                .remove(value)
                
Remove a matching value.

            


            

                .pop()
                
Remove the final value.

            

        

    


    

        
 NumPy arrays for mathematics


        

            In science, engineering, data analysis, and machine learning, Python
            programmers usually use NumPy. NumPy arrays make
            calculations with many numbers fast and simple.
        


        
import numpy as np

numbers = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])

print(numbers + 10)
# [12 14 16 18]

print(numbers * 2)
# [ 4  8 12 16]


        

            
            

                To use NumPy for the first time, install it in your terminal:
                pip install numpy
            

        

    


    

        
 Two-dimensional arrays


        

            A two-dimensional array looks like a table: rows and columns.
            This is useful for marksheets, image pixels, and numerical grids.
        


        
import numpy as np

marks = np.array([
    [80, 75, 90],
    [65, 88, 72],
    [95, 91, 86]
])

print(marks[0, 1])  # 75
print(marks[2, 0])  # 95


        

            807590
            658872
            959186
        

    


    

        
 Useful NumPy calculations


        

            

                numbers.sum()
                Add all values
            


            

                numbers.mean()
                Find the average
            


            

                numbers.max()
                Find the largest value
            


            

                numbers.min()
                Find the smallest value
            

        


        
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([78, 85, 92, 64])

print(scores.sum())   # 319
print(scores.mean())  # 79.75
print(scores.max())   # 92
print(scores.min())   # 64

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Should I use the array module or NumPy?
            

            

                For calculations, use NumPy. The built-in array module only stores numbers compactly. It cannot do maths on all values at once like numbers * 2.
            

        


        

            
                What happens if I put a decimal into array("i", ...)?
            

            

                Python shows a TypeError, because "i" only allows whole numbers. Use "f" or "d" for decimal values.
            

        


        

            
                Why does a list times 2 repeat the list, but a NumPy array times 2 doubles each number?
            

            

                List operations work on the container: [1, 2] * 2 gives [1, 2, 1, 2]. NumPy does maths on every value: np.array([1, 2]) * 2 gives [2 4].
            

        

        

            
                I get ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'. What should I do?
            

            

                NumPy is not installed for the Python you are running. Run pip install numpy in the terminal, or %pip install numpy inside Jupyter, then run your code again.
            

        

        

            
                Why does a NumPy array print without commas?
            

            

                That is only how NumPy displays arrays; the values are all there. If you need a normal Python list, use numbers.tolist().
            

        


    

    

        

        
    








    
20. Dictionaries and Key–Value Data


    

        Stage II · Core Python
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Find information using a meaningful name

            

                A dictionary stores information as key–value pairs.
                Instead of remembering a position such as [0], we can
                use a meaningful key such as "name" or "age".
            

        

    


    


        
 What is a dictionary?


        

            Dictionaries use curly brackets { }. Each key is followed
            by a colon, then its value.
        


        
student = {
    "name": "Asha",
    "age": 24,
    "subject": "Python"
}

print(student)


        

            
            

                Think of a dictionary like a real dictionary: you look up a word
                (the key) to find its meaning (the value).
            

        


    


    


        
 Keys and values


        

            

                Key
                "name"
                "age"
                "subject"
            


            

                
                
                
            


            

                Value
                "Asha"
                24
                "Python"
            

        


    


    


        
 Accessing a value


        

            Write the dictionary name followed by the key inside square brackets.
        


        
student = {
    "name": "Asha",
    "age": 24,
    "subject": "Python"
}

print(student["name"])     # Asha
print(student["subject"])  # Python


        

            
            

                The key must be written exactly as it appears in the dictionary.
                "Name" and "name" are different keys.
            

        


    


    


        
 Common dictionary operations


        


            

                dictionary["key"]
                
Read a value

                
student["age"]

            


            

                dictionary["key"] = value
                
Add or change a value

                
student["city"] = "Kaohsiung"

            


            

                .get()
                
Safely read a value

                
student.get("email")

            


            

                .keys()
                
See all keys

                
student.keys()

            


            

                .values()
                
See all values

                
student.values()

            


            

                .pop()
                
Remove a key–value pair

                
student.pop("age")

            


        


    


    


        
 Adding and updating data


        
student = {
    "name": "Asha",
    "age": 24
}

student["city"] = "Kaohsiung"
student["age"] = 25

print(student)


        

            Dictionaries are mutable, so you can add, remove, and
            update their values after creating them.

21. Decision Making with if, elif, and else


    

        Stage III · Logic and Functions
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Programs become useful when they can make choices

            

                In human life, we make decisions in every moment. From deciding if we should get out of bed, to spending money on a 
                new gadget, to choosing a career path, we are constantly evaluating conditions and making choices.
                Most of time we think of decisions as a simple if this, then that statement. For example, if it is raining, then take an umbrella. 
                Likewise, Programming languages like Python allow us to make decisions in our code using if statements and make the problem easier to solve.
            

        

    


    


        
 We make decisions every day


        


            

                
                
If it is raining, take an umbrella.

            


            

                
                
If the battery is low, I will reduce scrolling social media or stop playing games until I reach home.

            


            

                
                
If I get a mark of 99 or above, then I will be proud of my achievement.

            


        


        

            Python follows the same pattern: it checks a condition, then selects
            the instruction that belongs to that condition.
        


    


    


        
 The if statement


        

            Use if when you want Python to do something only when a
            condition is True.
        


        
temperature = 32

if temperature > 30:
    print("It is a hot day.")


        

            Read this as:
            If the temperature is greater than 30, print “It is a hot day.”
        


        


    

    

        
How to write an if statement


        
if condition:
    action_to_do


        
    
            
  1. Write the word if.
    2. 
            
  2. Write a condition that becomes True or False.
    3. 
            
  3. Add a colon : at the end.
    4. 
            
  4. On the next line, indent the action using spaces.
    5. 
        


        
age = 20

if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote.")


        

            Read it as: if the condition age >= 18
            is true, then print the message.
        


        

            Parentheses are optional for one simple condition:
        


        
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")

if (age >= 18):
    print("Adult")


       
    



    




    
 How indentation works


    

        Indentation means adding spaces at the beginning of a line.
        In Python, indentation tells Python that the block is written 1 space after belongs to 
        if statement and should only run when the condition is True. 
        Once the indentation ends, Python knows that the block is finished and will continue with the next instruction.
    


    
age = 20

if age >= 18:
    print("You are an adult.")
    print("You can vote.")

print("This line runs for everyone.")


    

        

            The two lines with four spaces belong to the
            if block. They run only when age >= 18 is
            True.
        


        

            The final print() has no spaces before it, so it is
            outside the if block and always runs.
        

    


    
Correct indentation


    
temperature = 30

if temperature > 25:
    print("It is warm.")


    
Wrong indentation


    
temperature = 30

if temperature > 25:
print("It is warm.")  # ❌ IndentationError


    

        
        

            Use four spaces for one indentation level.
            Do not mix tabs and spaces, because Python may show an error.
        

    




    


        
 How Python follows an if statement


        

            
Start

            


            

                Is temperature > 30?
            


            

                

                    Yes · True
                    
                    
Print “Hot day”

                


                

                    No · False
                    
                    
Skip this instruction

                

            

        


    

    


    
 Checking more than one condition


    

        Sometimes Python must check two or more questions before deciding what to do.
        Use and, or, and not inside an
        if condition.
    


    


        

            
and — every condition must be true


            
if condition_a and condition_b:
    action


            

                Python runs the action only when both conditions
                are True.
            


            
age = 20
has_ticket = True

if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("You may enter the concert.")

        


        

            
or — at least one condition must be true


            
if condition_a or condition_b:
    action


            

                Python runs the action when one or both conditions
                are True.
            


            
is_weekend = False
is_holiday = True

if is_weekend or is_holiday:
    print("No classes today!")

        


    


    


        
Checking three or more conditions


        

            You can continue adding and or or:
        


        
if condition_a and condition_b and condition_c:
    action


        
age = 22
has_ticket = True
has_id = True

if age >= 18 and has_ticket and has_id:
    print("Everything is correct. You may enter.")


    


    


        
Using brackets to group conditions


        

            Parentheses ( ) are optional, but they make long
            conditions easier to read. They are especially useful when
            and and or are used together.
        


        
age = 16
has_parent_permission = True
has_ticket = True

if (age >= 18 or has_parent_permission) and has_ticket:
    print("You may enter.")


        

            Read this as: the person must have a ticket, and they must be either
            18 or older or have parent permission.
        


    


    

        
        

            Use and when all requirements are necessary.
            Use or when any one option is enough.
        

    




    


        
 Adding else: what happens otherwise?


        

            Use else when you want Python to do something when the
            if condition is False.
        


        
temperature = 22

if temperature > 30:
    print("It is a hot day.")
else:
    print("The weather is comfortable.")


        

            
            

                An else does not need a condition. It simply means:
                “if none of the previous conditions were true, do this.”
            

        


    


    


        
 What happens when you have more than two choices?


        

            If you have more choices then you can use elif means else if. Use it when your
            program has several possible paths.
        


        
mark = 72

if mark >= 90:
    print("Excellent!")
elif mark >= 70:
    print("Very good!")
elif mark >= 50:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Keep practising. You can improve!")


        

            
            

                Python checks conditions from top to bottom.
                

                    When it finds the first true condition, it runs that block and
                    skips all remaining elif and else blocks.
                    Then if first one is false it checks the next elif and so on until it finds a true condition or reaches the else block. 
                    It traverses the conditions in order and stops at the first one that is true.
                

            

        


    


    


        
 The basic structure


        
if condition_1:
    # runs when condition_1 is True

elif condition_2:
    # runs when condition_2 is True

else:
    # runs when all earlier conditions are False


        


            

                
                Use a colon after if, elif, and else.
            


            

                
                Indent the code inside each block with four spaces.
            


            

                
                You can write one if, many elifs, and one else.
            


        


    


    


        
 Try the Grade Decision Maker


        

            Enter a mark from 0 to 100. Watch how the same if–elif–else
            logic chooses a different message.
        


        

            

            
        


        

            Enter a mark to let Python make a decision.
        


        

            Python follows this logic
            if mark >= 90: ...
        


    


    


        
 Where are decisions used in real programs?


        

             Password checking
             Online shopping discounts
             Weather warnings
             Health-data alerts
             Games and AI decisions
             Data analysis rules
