            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                if, elif, and else are confusing. How do I remember the order?
            

            

                The order is always if then elifs then else. If there is no elif then it will be only if then else.  
            


        

        

            
                Can a statement start with elif?
            

            

                No it can't. If is the parent or root structure. Without if elif and else has no meaning. 
            

            
        

        

    




    

        

        
    








    
22. Nested Conditions and match–case


    

        Stage III · Logic and Functions
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Sometimes one decision is not enough

            

                Real-life decisions often happen in steps. If you take one decision then in that decision there might be 2-3 possibilities. 
                Suppose you want to order dinner. You want to choose between Indian cuision or maxican cuision. If you choose Indian what food
                 you want to order or if you choose Mexican what food you want to order from the menu as there are various options available to opt. 
                 Basically nested condition is condition inside condition or so on. 
            

        

    


    


        
 What is a nested condition?


        

            A nested condition is simply an if statement written
            inside another if statement.
        


        
mark = 85

if mark >= 50:
    print("You passed!")

    if mark >= 80:
        print("You also earned a distinction.")


        

            Read the logic like this:
            First check whether the student passed. Then check whether the mark is 80 or above.
        


    


    


        
 Follow the decision step by step


        


            
Student mark = 85

            

            

                Is mark >= 50?
            


            


                

                    Yes
                    

                    

                        Print “You passed!”
                    


                    

                    

                        Is mark >= 80?
                    


                    

                    

                        Print “Distinction!”
                    

                


                

                    No
                    

                    

                        Print “Keep practising.”
                    

                


            


        


    


    


        
 Indentation is extra important here


        

            Indentation tells Python which instructions belong inside each condition.
            Basically, body of each condition follow indentation. Parent If will start and then 1st indent for the body  
            then the 2nd if follows same indentation and then  body of 2nd if start with further a tab space or another indentation (more inside)
        


        


            

                 Correct

                
if age >= 18:
    if has_ticket:
        print("You may enter.")

            


            

                 Incorrect

                
if age >= 18:
if has_ticket:
    print("You may enter.")

            


        


    


    


        
 When should you use nested conditions?


        


            

                
                
Login systems

                
Check the username first, then check the password.

            


            

                
                
Exam results

                
Check pass or fail, then decide the grade.

            


            

                
                
Ticket systems

                
Check age first, then check whether a ticket exists.

            


        


    


    


        
 A cleaner choice: match–case


        

            Another type of decision making function is match–case. when one value needs to match one of many
            exact choices. It is especially useful for menu options, days, colours,
            commands, or simple categories.
        


        
day = "Saturday"

match day:
    case "Monday":
        print("Start of the week.")
    case "Saturday" | "Sunday":
        print("It is the weekend!")
    case _:
        print("It is a weekday.")


        

            
            

                case _ is the default case. It means “anything else”
                and works like else.
            

        


    


    

        

        
    








    
23. for Loops and Iteration


    

        Stage III · Logic and Functions
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Let Python repeat work for you

            

                Computers are there to reduce your labour. It takes care of boring repeatation part. Let say you are given a task to print 1 to 5.
                You will write print statement 5 times for 1 to 5. But what will happen you are assigned to print 1 to 1000.
                Then you may hesitate little bit to do so. To overcome the hesitations, programming language comes with a great solution. That is  loop.. We will tell computer to ireratate and print untill it reaches 1000.
                Programming sometimes makes us lazy but most of time reduce our work load.
            

        

    


    


        
 What is iteration?


        

            Iteration means visiting items/ performing task one by one. A
            loop takes one item, performs an action, then moves
            to the next item until no items remain.
        


        

            List: ["Put instant noodles on bowl", "Pour hot water", "Cover and keep it for 5 minutes"]
            
            First: Put instant noodles on bowl
            
            Then: Pour hot water
            
            Finally:Cover and keep it for 5 minutes
        


    


    


        
 How does a loop work?


        

            A loop starts with a value, checks a condition, runs some work, changes
            the value, and then checks the condition again.
        


        


            

        


        
Example


        
count = 1              # 1. Initialization

while count <= 5:       # 2. Condition
    print(count)        # 3. Loop body
    count = count + 1   # 4. Increment


    


    


        
 Two types of loops in Python


        
Python mainly has two types of loops:


        

            

                for
                
For loop

                

                    Use it when you want to repeat code for each item in a list,
                    range, string, or other collection.
                

            


            

                while
                
While loop

                

                    Use it when you want to repeat code while a condition remains
                    True.
                

            

        


        

            
            

                In this section, we will focus on the for loop.
            

        


    


    


        
 How Python writes a for loop


        
for variable_name in collection:
    action_to_repeat


        

            

                1. for
                
Start the loop.

            


            

                2. Variable name
                
Stores the current item name, for example i.

            


            

                3. in
                
a conjuction which  “take each item from this collection.”

            


            

                4. Collection
                
The list, range, or variable Python should go through.

            


            

                5. Colon :
                
Shows that the loop block is beginning.

            


            

                6. Indentation
                
After colon we add indentation for the body of the for loop

            

        


        
for drink in ["tea", "coffee", "juice"]:
    print(drink)


    


    


        
 What can we use after in?


        

            Most of time we can't type full list on collection, so we will learn How can we put the collections.
            It is a collection of values that Python can
            visit one by one.
        


        


            

                
1. A list written directly if it is small.


                
for vowel in ["a", "e", "i","o","u"]:
    print(vowel)


                
Python prints each vowel one by one.

            

            

                
2. predefine list 


                
marks=[78, 85, 92, 64]
for mark in marks:
    print(n)


                
Python takes each value from the variable marks.

                
 Don't confuse with the variable mark and marks. If you get confused then use little different varible naming like m and marks

            

            

                
3. Importing from .csv file or other file 


                
df=csv.load("Cell_count.csv")
N=df[:1]
for n in N:
    print(n)


                
Python takes each value csv file.

                
We will read how to load csv file later on this tutorial. 

            

            

                
4. A range of numbers


                
for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)


                
Python prints: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

                
Notice:It starts from 1 but goes till 5 if you use range. If you want to print till 6 then range should be (1,7)

            

            

                
5. A range of numbers with by default starting with zero.


                
for number in range(6):
    print(number)


                
Python prints: 0,1, 2, 3, 4, 5

            


        


    


    


        
 How does Python increment?


        

            In a for loop, Python automatically goes to the next item.
            You usually do not need to write count = count + 1.
        


        
for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)


        

            With range(), Python moves by 1 by default:
        


        
range(1, 6)

# 1, 2, 3, 4, 5


        

            
            

                The final number in range() is not included.
                Therefore, range(1, 6) stops at 5.
            

        


        

            You can also choose a different increment, called a step.
        


        
for number in range(0, 11, 2):
    print(number)

# 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10


        

            
            

                range(start, stop, step) means:
                start here, stop before this number, and move by this step.
            

        


    


    


        
 Let's feel proud of ownself.

        
Small task: Print the statement "I am proud of myself" 100 times and feel pround that you reached on the core of the topic.

        
stat = "I am proud of myself"

for i in range(1000):
    print(stat)


    


    


        
 Small practice

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why does range(1, 6) stop at 5 and not 6?
            

            

                The stop number in range() is never included. Think of it as "go up to, but not including, 6". A nice side effect: range(5) runs exactly 5 times (0, 1, 2, 3, 4).
            


        

        

            
                Is i a special word? Do I have to use it?
            

            

                No. i is just a short, popular variable name. You can use any valid name, such as number, city, or mark. A meaningful name makes the code easier to read.
            


        

        

            
                What happens to the loop variable after the loop finishes?
            

            

                It keeps the last value it received. After for n in range(1, 6): finishes, n is still 5.
            


        

        

            
                What if the list is empty?
            

            

                Then the loop body never runs. Python finds nothing to visit, skips the loop, and continues with the next line. No error.
            


        

        

            
                I wrote for i in 5: and got TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable. Why?
            

            

                A single number is not a collection, so Python cannot visit its items one by one. Use range(5) to make a sequence of numbers: for i in range(5):
            


        

        

            
                How does Python know which lines are inside the loop?
            

            

                By indentation. Every line indented under the for line repeats. The first line that goes back to the left edge runs only once, after the loop ends.
                
for i in range(3):
    print("Inside")   # runs 3 times
print("Outside")      # runs once

            


        

        

            
                Can I count backwards with range()?
            

            

                Yes. Use a negative step: range(10, 0, -1) gives 10, 9, 8, … 1. The start must be bigger than the stop, otherwise nothing is produced.
            


        

        

            
                Can I loop over a word or sentence?
            

            

                Yes. A string is a collection of characters, so for letter in "hello": visits h, e, l, l, o. Spaces count as characters too.
            


        

        

            
                Can I put a for loop inside another for loop?
            

            

                Yes. This is called a nested loop. The inner loop runs completely for every single step of the outer loop. It is useful for tables, grids, and patterns.
            


        

        

            
                When should I use for and when should I use while?
            

            

                Use for when you know what you are going through (a list, a string, or a fixed number of times). Use while when you repeat until a condition changes, for example "keep asking until the password is correct". We will learn while in the next lesson.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
24. While Loops and Repetition


    

        Stage III · Logic and Functions
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Repeat while something is true

            

                A while loop repeats code while a condition
                remains True. It is useful when you do not know exactly
                how many times a program should repeat.
            

        

    


    


        
 Basic while loop syntax


        
while condition:
    action_to_repeat


        

            Read it like this:
            While this condition is true, repeat the indented code.
        


        
count = 1

while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1


        

            
            

                Unlike a for loop, a while loop does
                not automatically increament. You must update the
                variable yourself.
            

        


    


    


        
 The three important parts


        


            

                1
                
Initialization

                
Give the variable a starting value before the loop.

                count = 1
            


            

                2
                
Condition

                
Python checks this before every repetition.

                count <= 5
            


            

                3
                
Update

                
Change the value so the loop can eventually stop.

                count = count + 1
            


        


    


    
    


        
 Useful examples


        


            

                
Countdown


                
number = 5

while number > 0:
    print(number)
    number = number - 1

print("Go!")

            


            

                
Keep asking until correct


                
password = ""

while password != "python123":
    password = input("Enter password: ")

print("Correct password!")

            


        


    


    


        
 Be careful: infinite loops


        

            An infinite loop happens when the condition never
            becomes False.
        


        


            

                
Wrong: value never changes


                
count = 1

while count <= 5:
    print(count)


                

                    count stays 1 forever, so the loop never stops.
                

            


            

                
Correct: value changes


                
count = 1

while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1


                

                    Eventually, count becomes 6 and the condition is false.
                

            


        


    


    


        
 for loop or while loop?


        


            

                
Use for

                
When you know the items or number of repetitions.


                
for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)

            


            

                
Use while

                
When repetition should continue until something changes.


                
while password != "python123":
    password = input("Password: ")

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                My program never stops. What happened, and how do I stop it?
            

            

                You made an infinite loop: the condition never became False. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop the program (in Jupyter, click the stop ■ button). Then check that the variable in the condition is updated inside the loop.
            


        

        

            
                Why do I have to write count = count + 1 myself?
            

            

                A while loop only checks a condition. It does not know which variable should change. A for loop moves to the next item automatically, but a while loop needs you to do it.
            


        

        

            
                Can a while loop run zero times?
            

            

                Yes. Python checks the condition first. If it is already False, for example count = 10 and while count <= 5:, the body never runs.
            


        

        

            
                Is count += 1 the same as count = count + 1?
            

            

                Yes. += is a shortcut. You can also use -=, *=, and /=.
            


        

        

            
                What is while True:? Isn't that an infinite loop?
            

            

                It is an infinite loop on purpose. It is used for menus and games that should keep running until the user chooses to exit. You stop it from inside with break, which we learn in the next lesson.
            


        

        

            
                Why does my password loop accept "Yes" but not "yes"?
            

            

                Python compares text exactly, including capital letters. Use .lower() to make the input lowercase first: answer = input("Type yes: ").lower()
            


        

        

            
                Can I write any for loop as a while loop?
            

            

                Yes, but it is usually longer. Use for when you know the items or the number of repetitions, and while when you repeat until something changes.
            


        

        

            
                Why did my loop print one number too many (or too few)?
            

            

                Check < versus <=. while count < 5 stops at 4, while while count <= 5 includes 5. Also check whether you update the variable before or after printing it.

                We will learn how to control loops using range,
                break, continue, and common loop patterns.
            

        

    


    

        

        
    







    
25. range(), break, continue, and Loop Patterns


    

        Stage III · Logic and Functions
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Control how your loops move

            

                We already learnt about the loops. Also we learnt about infinite loop in previous section. What will happen if the loop does come to an end? 
                What will happen once if the processes takes long time? To answer this question sometime our computer 
                crashes due to overload. So there should be some thing which can prevent from infinite loop. The answer is yes and they are called breaking of loop.
            

        

    


    


        
 Creating numbers with range()


        

            range() creates a sequence of numbers. It is commonly
            used with a for loop.
        


        
for number in range(5):
    print(number)

# 0, 1, 2, 3, 4


        


            

                range(stop)
                
Start at 0

                
The stop value is not included.

                
range(5)

                
0, 1, 2, 3, 4

            


            

                range(start, stop)
                
Choose the start

                
Python stops just before the final value.

                
range(1, 6)

                
1, 2, 3, 4, 5

            


            

                range(start, stop, step)
                
Choose the step

                
Move forward or backward by a chosen amount.

                
range(0, 11, 2)

                
0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10

            


        


        

            
            

                The default step is 1. For a countdown, use a
                negative step such as range(10, 0, -1).
            

        


        
for number in range(10, 0, -1):
    print(number)

print("Blast off!")


    


    


        
 Stop a loop early with break


        

            break immediately stops the current loop. Python does
            not continue with the remaining values.
        


        
for number in range(1, 11):
    if number == 6:
        break

    print(number)

# 1, 2, 3, 4, 5


        

            Think of break as:
            "Stop searching. We found what we need!"
        


        
names = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Mina", "Sara"]

for name in names:
    if name == "Mina":
        print("Mina found!")
        break


    


    


        
 Skip one turn with continue


        

            continue skips the remaining code in the current
            repetition and moves directly to the next repetition.
        


        
for number in range(1, 8):
    if number == 4:
        continue

    print(number)

# 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7


        

            Think of continue as:
            "Skip this one. Move to the next item."
        


        
for number in range(1, 11):
    if number % 2 == 0:
        continue

    print(number)

# Prints only odd numbers


    


    


        
 break versus continue


        


            

                
break

                
Stops the whole loop immediately.

                
if number == 5:
    break

    If your result is giving Nan value, you try to search if there is any Nan value present in the data or there is some other problem. For that case:
    
for number in Data:
    if number == Nan:
        break

            


            

                
continue

                
Skips only the current repetition.

                
if number == 5:
    continue

    If you don't care about Nan value of the data, You want to count the data which are not Nan, For that case:
    
count=1
    for number in Data:
        if number == Nan:
            continuek
        count=count+1 
        print(count)

            

            

        


    


    


        
 Useful loop patterns


        


            

                
Count up

                
for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)

            


            

                
Count down

                
for number in range(5, 0, -1):
    print(number)

            


            

                
Skip unwanted values

                
for number in range(1, 11):
    if number % 2 == 0:
        continue
    print(number)

            


            

                
Stop when found

                
for number in range(1, 11):
    if number == 7:
        break
    print(number)

            


        


    


    


        
 A useful search pattern: for ... else


        

            The else part runs only if the loop finishes normally
            without using break.
        


        
target = "Mina"
names = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Sara"]

for name in names:
    if name == target:
        print("Name found!")
        break
else:
    print("Name not found.")

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Does break stop the whole program?
            

            

                No. It stops only the loop it is inside. Python continues with the first line after that loop.
            


        

        

            
                In a loop inside another loop, which loop does break stop?
            

            

                Only the innermost loop that contains the break. The outer loop keeps running.
            


        

        

            
                Why does range(10, 0) print nothing?
            

            

                The default step is +1, so Python cannot count up from 10 to 0. Add a negative step: range(10, 0, -1).
            


        

        

            
                Can the step in range() be a decimal like 0.5?
            

            

                No. range() only works with whole numbers. For decimals, loop over whole numbers and divide, for example for i in range(5): print(i / 2). Later, NumPy's np.arange() also allows decimal steps.
            


        

        

            
                What does pass do? Is it the same as continue?
            

            

                No. pass does nothing. It is a placeholder for a block you will write later. continue jumps straight to the next repetition and skips the rest of the loop body.
            


        

        

            
                When does the else part of a loop run?
            

            

                Only when the loop finishes normally. If the loop ends because of break, the else part is skipped. That makes it useful for "searched everything, did not find it" messages.
            


        

        

            
                Why do I see range(0, 5) instead of numbers when I print a range?
            

            

                A range creates its numbers only when they are needed. To see them all at once, convert it to a list: print(list(range(5))) gives [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].
            


        

        

            
                Do break and continue work in while loops too?
            

            

                Yes, both work in for and while loops. In a while loop, be careful with continue: if it skips the line that updates your counter, the loop may never end.

 In this lesson

        
Functions are one big idea, so this lesson covers it in four parts:

Part 1 Functions and reusable code



    

        

            
        


        

            
Write once, use many times

            

                A function is a named block of code that performs
                one task. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, create a
                function once and call it whenever you need it.
            

        

    


    


        
 Why do we need functions?


        

            Imagine that you want to print a welcome message many times. Writing
            the same print() lines again and again makes code longer
            and harder to update.
        


        


            

                
Without a function


                
print("Welcome to Python!")
print("Have a good lesson.")

print("Welcome to Python!")
print("Have a good lesson.")

            


            

                
With a function


                
def welcome():
    print("Welcome to Python!")
    print("Have a good lesson.")

welcome()
welcome()

            


        


    


    


        
 Function syntax


        
def function_name():
    action_to_do

function_name()


        


            

                def
                
Tells Python that you are defining a function.

            


            

                function_name
                
Choose a meaningful name for the task.

            


            

                ()
                
Parentheses are part of function syntax.

            


            

                :
                
The colon begins the function block.

            


            

                indentation
                
Indented lines belong inside the function.

            


            

                function_name()
                
This calls and runs the function.

            


        


    


    


        
 Define first, then call


        

            Creating a function does not run it immediately. Python runs the code
            inside the function only when you call it.
        


        
def show_message():
    print("Python is fun!")

# The function is created,
# but nothing has printed yet.

show_message()

# Now Python prints:
# Python is fun!


        

            
            

                Think of a function as a recipe. Writing the recipe does not cook
                the food. Calling the function is like starting the recipe.
            

        


    


    


        
 Simple function examples


        


            

                
Print a line


                
def draw_line():
    print("-" * 30)

draw_line()
print("Python Lesson")
draw_line()

            


            

                
Show a menu


                
def show_menu():
    print("1. Start")
    print("2. Practice")
    print("3. Exit")

show_menu()

            


            

                
Say hello


                
def say_hello():
    print("Hello, learner!")

say_hello()
say_hello()

            


        


    


    


        
 Important rules


        
    
            
  • Use def to create a function.
    • 
            
  • Use a meaningful name, such as show_menu.
    • 
            
  • Always add parentheses () after the function name.
    • 
            
  • Always add a colon : after ().
    • 
            
  • Indent the code inside the function.
    • 
            
  • Call the function using its name and parentheses.
    • 
        


        

            
            

                show_menu means the function itself.
                show_menu() means “run the function.”
            

        


    


    


        
 Try the Function Builder


        

            Choose a function name and a message. The lab creates a simple Python
            function for you.

            Welcome to Python!
Welcome to Python!

    print("Welcome to Python!")

say_welcome()
say_welcome()

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                I wrote a function, but nothing happens when I run the file. Why?
            

            

                Defining a function only creates it. You must also call it, for example show_menu(), on its own line without indentation.
            


        

        

            
                Why do I get NameError: name 'greet' is not defined?
            

            

                Either the name is spelled differently (Python is case-sensitive), or you called the function before the line where it is defined. Put the def block above the call.
            


        

        

            
                What names can I give a function?
            

            

                The same rules as variables: letters, numbers, and underscores, not starting with a number, and no Python keywords. By convention, use lowercase words joined with underscores, such as show_report. A verb in the name helps explain what the function does.
            


        

        

            
                Can two functions have the same name?
            

            

                You can write it, but the second definition replaces the first one. Python keeps only the latest one, so give each function a unique name.
            


        

        

            
                Can a function call another function?
            

            

                Yes. This is very common. Small functions that each do one job can be combined inside a bigger function.
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between print() and my own functions?
            

            

                Nothing special. print() is a built-in function that Python already wrote for you. Your functions work the same way: you call them by name with parentheses.
            


        

        

            
                Why do I get IndentationError after def?
            

            

                A function body cannot be empty, and every line inside it must be indented. If you have nothing to write yet, put pass inside.
            


        

        

            
                When should I make a function?
            

            

                A good rule: if you copy and paste the same lines a second time, put them in a function. Functions also help when a long program becomes hard to read. Give each clear task its own name.
            


        


    


    
Part 2 Parameters, arguments, *args, and **kwargs



    

        

            
        


        

            
Give information to a function

            

                Functions become more useful when they can work with different
                values. Parameters receive information, while
                arguments are the real values we send to a function.
            

        

    


    


        
 Parameter versus argument


        


            

                
Parameter

                

                    A parameter is a temporary variable written inside the function
                    definition.
                


                
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")


                
name is a parameter.

            


            

                
Argument

                

                    An argument is the real value sent when calling the function.
                


                
greet("Asha")


                
"Asha" is an argument.

            


        


        

            
            

                Python puts the argument "Asha" into the parameter
                name, then runs the function.
            

        


    


    


        
 One parameter


        
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Asha")
greet("Ravi")
greet("Mina")


        

            The same function runs three times, but each call uses a different
            argument.
        


    


    


        
 More than one parameter


        

            Separate parameters and arguments with commas. The values are matched
            in the same order.
        


        
def introduce(name, city):
    print(f"{name} lives in {city}.")

introduce("Asha", "Kaohsiung")
introduce("Ravi", "Taipei")


        

            
            

                Order matters. introduce("Kaohsiung", "Asha") gives
                the wrong meaning because Python matches values by position.
            

        


    


    


        
 Default parameters


        

            A default parameter already has a value. You can use it or replace it
            when calling the function.
        


        
def greet(name, message="Hello"):
    print(f"{message}, {name}!")

greet("Asha")
greet("Ravi", "Welcome")


        

            Hello, Asha!
            Welcome, Ravi!
        


    


    


        
 Extra positional arguments: *args


        

            Use *args when you do not know how many positional
            arguments will be sent. Python collects them into a tuple.
        


        
def show_numbers(*numbers):
    for number in numbers:
        print(number)

show_numbers(10, 20, 30)
show_numbers(5, 8, 12, 19)


        

            
            

                The name args is a common convention. The star
                * is the important part.
            

        


    


    


        
 Extra named arguments: **kwargs


        

            Use **kwargs when you want to send an unknown number of
            named values. Python collects them into a dictionary.
        


        
def show_profile(**info):
    for key, value in info.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value}")

show_profile(
    name="Asha",
    city="Kaohsiung",
    subject="Python"
)


        

            
            

                The name kwargs is also a convention. The two stars
                ** tell Python to collect named arguments.
            

        


    


    


        
 Parameter order


        
When one function uses different parameter types, use this order:


        
def example(required, default_value="Hello", *args, **kwargs):
    pass


        

            1. Required parameters
            2. Default parameters
            3. *args
            4. **kwargs
        


    


    


        
 Try the Function Call Builder


        

            Enter two arguments and see how Python sends them into a function.
        


        


            

            

        


        

        

            Python output
            Asha lives in Kaohsiung.
        


        

            Python code
            
def introduce(name, city):
    print(f"{name} lives in {city}.")

introduce("Asha", "Kaohsiung")

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Parameter or argument? I keep mixing them up.
            

            

                The parameter is the name in the def line (the empty box). The argument is the real value you put in the box when you call the function.
            


        

        

            
                What does TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument mean?
            

            

                The function expects more values than you sent. Count the parameters in the def line and send the same number of arguments, or give the extra parameter a default value.
            


        

        

            
                Do I have to use the names args and kwargs?
            

            

                No. Only the * and ** matter. *numbers and **info work the same way. args and kwargs are just names that many programmers use.
            


        

        

            
                What type is args inside the function? And kwargs?
            

            

                *args becomes a tuple, for example (10, 20, 30). **kwargs becomes a dictionary, for example {"name": "Asha"}. You can loop over both.
            


        

        

            
                Can a parameter have the same name as a variable outside the function?
            

            

                Yes. The parameter is a separate, temporary variable that exists only inside the function. Changing it does not change the outside variable. We look at this more in the next lesson on scope.
            


        

        

            
                Why should I not use a list as a default value, like def add(item, items=[])?
            

            

                The default list is created only once and is shared between calls, so items from earlier calls remain. Use items=None, then inside the function write if items is None: items = [].
            


        

        

            
                When should I use keyword arguments like city="Taipei"?
            

            

                When a function has many parameters, or when the meaning of a value is not obvious. rectangle(width=5, height=3) is easier to read than rectangle(5, 3), and the order no longer matters.
            


        

        

            
                print() accepts any number of values. Does it use *args?
            

            

                Yes, it works the same way. That is why print("a", "b", "c") works. Its sep and end options are keyword arguments with default values.
            


        


    


    
Part 3 Return values and variable scope



    

        

            
        


        

            
Functions can send a result back

            

                A function does not only print messages. It can calculate, create,
                or find something, then send that result back using
                return.
            

        

    


    


        
 print() versus return


        


            

                
print()

                
Shows a value on the screen.


                
def show_sum(a, b):
    print(a + b)

show_sum(3, 4)


                
Output: 7

            


            

                
return

                
Sends a value back so we can store or use it later.


                
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

 Return value syntax


        
def function_name(parameters):
    result = something
    return result


        


            

                1. Call the function

                2. Function calculates
                3 + 4

def calculate_area(length, width):

    return area

room_area = calculate_area(8, 5)

 A function stops at return


        

            When Python reaches return, the function ends immediately.
            Code written after it does not run.
        


        
def check_number(number):
    if number < 0:
        return "Negative"

    return "Zero or positive"

print(check_number(-5))


    


    


        
 What if there is no return?


        

            Every Python function returns something. If you do not write
            return, Python automatically returns None.
        


        
def say_hello():
    print("Hello!")

result = say_hello()

print(result)
# None


        

            
            

                Use print() when you only want to show information.
                Use return when you need the result later.
            

        


    


    


        
 What is variable scope?


        

            Scope means where a variable can be used in a program.
            A variable created inside a function is usually a
            local variable.
        


        


            

                
Local variable

                
Created inside a function. It exists only inside that function.


                
def show_score():
    score = 95
    print(score)

show_score()

# print(score) ❌ Error

            


            

                
Global variable

                
Created outside a function. It can be read inside a function.


                
course = "Python"

def show_course():
    print(course)

show_course()

            


        


    


    


        
 A safer way to work with values


        

            Avoid changing global variables inside functions when possible.
            Instead, send values in through parameters and send results back with
            return.
        


        


            

                
Less clear: changing a global value


                
score = 0

def add_points():
    global score
    score = score + 10

            


            

                
Better: return a new value


                
def add_points(score):

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Should my function use print() or return?
            

            

                Use return when the result will be used again: stored, compared, or used in another calculation. Use print() only when you just want to show something. Most useful functions return a value and leave printing to the code that calls them.
            


        

        

            
                Can a function return more than one value?
            

            

                Yes. return a, b sends back a tuple, and you can unpack it: low, high = min_max(numbers).
            


        

        

            
                Why does my variable show None?
            

            

                The function you stored did not return anything, or it used print() instead of return. A function without return always gives back None.
            


        

        

            
                Can I write more than one return in a function?
            

            

                Yes, for example one inside each if branch. Only the first return that Python reaches runs, and the function stops there.
            


        

        

            
                Why does my code after return never run?
            

            

                return ends the function immediately. Move the lines you need above the return statement.
            


        

        

            
                What does the global keyword do, and should I use it?
            

            

                global name lets a function change a variable outside it. It works, but it makes programs harder to follow, because any function could change the value. Prefer parameters and return.
            


        

        

            
                Why can a function read a global variable but not change it?
            

            

                As soon as you assign x = ... inside a function, Python treats x as a new local variable. Reading is allowed, but assigning creates a local copy unless you declare global x.
            


        

        

            
                Can I return a list or a dictionary?
            

            

                Yes. A function can return any Python value: numbers, strings, lists, dictionaries, even other functions.
            


        


    


    
Part 4 Lambda, map(), filter(), and useful built-ins



    

        

            
        


        

            
Small tools for working with data

            

                Python has many built-in tools for common tasks. In this lesson,
                you will learn short lambda functions,
                map(), filter(), and useful built-ins
                such as sum(), max(), and
                sorted().
            

        

    


    


        
 What is a lambda function?


        

            A lambda function is a short, unnamed function. It is
            useful for one small expression.
        


        
lambda parameters: expression


        


            

                
Normal function


                
def square(number):
    return number * number

            


            

                
Lambda function


                
square = lambda number: number * number

            


        


        
square = lambda number: number * number

print(square(5))
# 25


        

            
            

                Use a normal def function for long or complicated
                work. Use lambda for one short expression.
            

        


    


    


        
 Change every item with map()


        

            map() applies a function to every item in a collection.
        


        
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]

squares = list(map(lambda number: number * number, numbers))

print(squares)
# [1, 4, 9, 16]


        

            Read it like this:
            Apply number * number to every item in
            numbers.
        


        
words = ["python", "code", "fun"]

upper_words = list(map(lambda word: word.upper(), words))

print(upper_words)
# ['PYTHON', 'CODE', 'FUN']


    


    


        
 Keep selected items with filter()


        

            filter() keeps only the items for which a condition is
            True.
        


        
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

even_numbers = list(
    filter(lambda number: number % 2 == 0, numbers)
)

print(even_numbers)
# [2, 4, 6]


        

            Read it like this:
            Keep a number only when number % 2 == 0 is true.
        


        
marks = [45, 72, 38, 90, 65]

passed_marks = list(
    filter(lambda mark: mark >= 50, marks)
)

print(passed_marks)
# [72, 90, 65]


    


    


        
 Using filter() and map() together


        

            First filter the values you need. Then use map() to
            change those values.
        


        
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

even_numbers = filter(
    lambda number: number % 2 == 0,
    numbers
)

doubled_evens = list(
    map(lambda number: number * 2, even_numbers)
)

print(doubled_evens)
# [4, 8, 12]


    


    


        
 Useful built-in functions

Find the smallest value.

Find the largest value.

            


            

                sorted(values)
                
Create a sorted version.

            


            

                abs(number)
                
Find distance from zero.

            


            

                round(number, 2)
                
Round to two decimal places.

            


            

                enumerate(values)
                
Get item positions and values.

print(len(numbers))      # 4
print(sum(numbers))      # 65
print(min(numbers))      # 5
print(max(numbers))      # 30

 Number items with enumerate()

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why does print(map(...)) show <map object at 0x...>?
            

            

                map() and filter() do not calculate everything immediately. They produce values one by one when needed. Wrap them in list() to see all the results.
            


        

        

            
                Why is my map result empty the second time I use it?
            

            

                A map or filter object can be used only once. After you loop over it (or turn it into a list), it is empty. Save the result with result = list(map(...)) and reuse result.
            


        

        

            
                Can a lambda have several lines or use if?
            

            

                A lambda can contain only one expression. You can use a one-line condition such as lambda n: "Even" if n % 2 == 0 else "Odd". Anything longer should be a normal def function.
            


        

        

            
                Is lambda faster than def?
            

            

                No, it is just shorter. Both create a function. Choose whichever is easier to read.
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between sorted(numbers) and numbers.sort()?
            

            

                sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. .sort() changes the original list and returns None, so x = numbers.sort() gives None.
            


        

        

            
                Should I use map()/filter() or a list comprehension?
            

            

                Both work. Many Python programmers find list comprehensions such as [n * 2 for n in numbers if n > 0] easier to read. map() is handy when you already have a function, for example map(int, texts).
            


        

        

            
                Why does sum(["1", "2"]) give an error?
            

            

                sum() only adds numbers. Convert the text first: sum(map(int, ["1", "2"])) gives 3.
            


        

        

            
                Why does round(2.5) give 2 and not 3?
            

            

                Python rounds exact halves to the nearest even number ("banker's rounding"), so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4. This reduces bias when you round many numbers.

27. Mini Project: A Menu-Driven Python Program


    

        Stage III · Logic and Functions
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Make your program wait for a choice

            

                A menu-driven program shows choices to the user, accepts their
                input, and performs the matching action. It combines
                while loops, if statements,
                functions, input, and output.
            

        

    


    

        
 The project idea


        

            We will create a small Student Score Helper. The user
            can choose to calculate a total, find an average, check whether a
            student passed, or exit the program.
        


        

            Program menu
            
1. Calculate total marks
2. Calculate average marks
3. Check pass or fail
4. Exit

        

    


    

        
 How does a menu program work?


        

            

                1
                Show the menu
                
Display all available choices.

            


            

                2
                Ask for input
                
Let the user select an option.

            


            

                3
                Check the choice
                
Use if, elif, and else.

            


            

                4
                Repeat or exit
                
Keep showing the menu until the user chooses exit.

            

        

    


    

        
 Basic menu structure


        
while True:
    print("\n--- Student Score Helper ---")
    print("1. Calculate total marks")
    print("2. Calculate average marks")
    print("3. Check pass or fail")
    print("4. Exit")

    choice = input("Choose an option (1-4): ")

    if choice == "1":
        print("You selected total marks.")

    elif choice == "2":
        print("You selected average marks.")

    elif choice == "3":
        print("You selected pass or fail.")

    elif choice == "4":
        print("Goodbye!")
        break

    else:
        print("Invalid choice. Please try again.")


        

            
            

                while True: keeps the menu running. The
                break statement stops the loop when the user chooses
                option 4.
            

        

    


    

        
 Make the program cleaner with functions


        

            Instead of writing everything inside one large loop, create a function
            for each task. This makes your code easier to read and reuse.
        


        
def calculate_total():
    mark1 = float(input("Enter first mark: "))
    mark2 = float(input("Enter second mark: "))
    total = mark1 + mark2
    print(f"Total marks: {total}")


def check_result():
    mark = float(input("Enter the mark: "))

    if mark >= 50:
        print("Result: Pass")
    else:
        print("Result: Fail")

    


    

        
 Complete mini project


        
def calculate_total():
    mark1 = float(input("Enter first mark: "))
    mark2 = float(input("Enter second mark: "))

    total = mark1 + mark2
    print(f"Total marks: {total}")


def calculate_average():
    mark1 = float(input("Enter first mark: "))
    mark2 = float(input("Enter second mark: "))

    average = (mark1 + mark2) / 2
    print(f"Average marks: {average}")


def check_result():
    mark = float(input("Enter the mark: "))

    if mark >= 50:
        print("Result: Pass")
    else:
        print("Result: Fail")


while True:
    print("\n--- Student Score Helper ---")
    print("1. Calculate total marks")
    print("2. Calculate average marks")
    print("3. Check pass or fail")
    print("4. Exit")

    choice = input("Choose an option (1-4): ")

    if choice == "1":
        calculate_total()

    elif choice == "2":
        calculate_average()

    elif choice == "3":
        check_result()

    elif choice == "4":
        print("Thank you for using the program!")
        break

    else:
        print("Invalid choice. Please enter 1, 2, 3, or 4.")

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why compare choice == "1" and not choice == 1?
            

            

                input() always returns text. The text "1" is not equal to the number 1, so compare with a string, or convert first with int(choice).
            


        

        

            
                My program crashes when the user types a letter instead of a mark. How do I stop that?
            

            

                float("abc") raises ValueError. Use try/except to catch it and ask again (see practice question 14). Error handling gets its own lesson later.
            


        

        

            
                Is while True bad practice?
            

            

                No. It is the normal pattern for menus, as long as there is a clear break (an exit option). Without a break, the program would never end.
            


        

        

            
                How do I clear the screen between menus?
            

            

                Use import os, then os.system("cls") on Windows or os.system("clear") on macOS/Linux. It is optional. Printing an empty line with print() is often enough.
            


        

        

            
                How do I keep data, like marks or tasks, after the program closes?
            

            

                Variables are lost when the program ends. Save the data to a file (text, CSV, or JSON) and load it again when the program starts. File handling comes in a later lesson.
            


        

        

            
                Should I use if/elif or match–case for menus?
            

            

                Both work. match–case (Python 3.10+) can look cleaner when you compare one value against many exact choices. if/elif works on every Python version and handles ranges like mark >= 50.
            


        

        

            
                What does if __name__ == "__main__": mean?
            

            

                It runs main() only when you run this file directly. If another file imports your functions, the menu will not start automatically. You will use this more when we learn modules.
            


        

        

            
                Why does the menu sometimes show \n in my code?
            

            

                \n means "new line". print("\n--- Menu ---") prints an empty line before the title, which separates each menu from the previous one.

 What is a Python library?


        

            A library is a collection of ready-made functions that someone
            else has already written and tested. Instead of writing everything from scratch,
            we load the library and use its functions directly.
        

        

            Built-in functions like print() and len() are always
            available. Functions for specialised work, such as statistics, plotting, numerical
            calculation and machine learning, live inside separate libraries.
        


        

            

                
                    

                        Library
                        Used for
                        Example function
                    

                
                
                    

                        math
                        Basic mathematics (comes with Python)
                        math.sqrt(16) → 4.0
                    

                    

                        statistics
                        Mean, median, standard deviation (comes with Python)
                        statistics.mean([2, 4, 6]) → 4
                    

                    

                        numpy
                        Fast numerical work with arrays
                        numpy.array([1, 2, 3])
                    

                    

                        pandas
                        Reading and analysing tables of data
                        pandas.read_csv("data.csv")
                    

                    

                        matplotlib
                        Drawing graphs and plots
                        matplotlib.pyplot.plot(x, y)
                    

                    

                        sklearn
                        Machine learning
                        sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression()
                    

                
            

        


        
 How to use a function from a library


        

            Using a library takes two steps:
        

        
    
            
  1. Import the library at the top of your code with import.
    2. 
            
  2. Call its function using the pattern library.function().
    3. 
        


        
import math

print(math.sqrt(25))     # square root
print(math.pi)           # value of pi
print(math.floor(7.8))   # round down


        
Output:

        
5.0
3.141592653589793
7


        

            The dot (.) means "look inside". math.sqrt reads as
            "the sqrt function inside the math library".
        


        

            
            

                math and statistics come with Python. Libraries like
                numpy, pandas and matplotlib must be
                installed first with pip install, as shown in Section 3. If you
                import a library that is not installed, Python shows
                ModuleNotFoundError.
            

        


        
 Giving a library a short name (alias)


        

            Some library names are long to type again and again. We can give a library a
            short nickname, called an alias, using as:
        


        
import numpy as np

marks = np.array([60, 75, 90])
print(np.mean(marks))


        
Output:

        
75.0


        

            Here numpy is the real library name and np is the
            alias. After this line, we write np.mean() instead of
            numpy.mean(). Both mean the same function.
        


        
The Python community uses these standard aliases. Use them so others can read your code easily:


        
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


        
 Importing only one function


        

            If you need just one or two functions, use from ... import ....
            Then you can call the function directly, without the library name in front:
        


        
from math import sqrt, pi

print(sqrt(49))   # no "math." needed
print(pi)


        
Output:

        
7.0
3.141592653589793


        

            
            

                Avoid from math import *. It loads every name from the library
                and can silently replace your own variables with the same name.
            

        

    

    

        
 What is NumPy?


        

            NumPy stands for Numerical Python. It is the most widely used
            Python library for working with numbers. It gives us fast tools for
            mathematics, statistics and handling large amounts of numerical data.
        

        

            Many other libraries are built on top of NumPy, including
            pandas, matplotlib, scipy and
            scikit-learn. Learning NumPy first makes all of them easier to
            understand.
        


        
What can NumPy do?

        
    
            
  • Maths on many values at once: add, multiply or take the square root of a whole set of numbers in one line.
    • 
            
  • Statistics: mean, median, standard deviation, minimum and maximum.
    • 
            
  • Create number sequences: ranges, evenly spaced values, and arrays of zeros or ones.
    • 
            
  • Tables and matrices: work with data in rows and columns, and do matrix calculations.
    • 
            
  • Random numbers: generate random values for simulations and testing.
    • 
        


        
Installing and importing NumPy

        
Install it once from the terminal:

        
pip install numpy

        
Then import it at the top of your code:

        
import numpy as np

print(np.sqrt(81))        # 9.0
print(np.pi)              # 3.141592653589793
print(np.round(2.678, 1)) # 2.7


        

            
            

                We normally import NumPy as np. This is the standard
                short name used in Python science and data projects.
            

        


        
What is a NumPy array?

        

            The main object in NumPy is the array (its full name is
            ndarray, meaning "n-dimensional array"). An array looks like a Python
            list, but every item has the same data type and the items are stored together in
            memory. This lets NumPy do a calculation on all the items at once, which is much
            faster than looping through a list one item at a time.
        


        
import numpy as np

temperatures = np.array([25.4, 26.1, 27.8, 28.2])

print(temperatures)          # [25.4 26.1 27.8 28.2]
print(np.mean(temperatures)) # 26.875

    


    

        
 List versus NumPy array


        


            

                Python list
                
marks = [60, 70, 80]

print(marks * 2)
# [60, 70, 80, 60, 70, 80]

                

                    Multiplying a list repeats the items. It does not multiply
                    every number.
                

            


            

                NumPy array
                
marks = np.array([60, 70, 80])

print(marks * 2)
# [120 140 160]

                

                    NumPy performs the calculation on every value automatically.
                

            


        

    


    

        
 Array calculations happen element by element


        

            One operation can work on an entire array. This is called
            vectorized computation.
        


        
marks = np.array([60, 70, 80])

print(marks + 5)   # [65 75 85]
print(marks - 10)  # [50 60 70]
print(marks * 2)   # [120 140 160]
print(marks / 2)   # [30. 35. 40.]


        

            
array + number
Add to every item

            
array - number
Subtract from every item

            
array * number
Multiply every item

            
array / number
Divide every item

        

    


    

        
 Useful ways to create arrays


        


            

                np.array()
                
Create from values

                
numbers = np.array([2, 4, 6])

            


            

                np.arange()
                
Create a sequence

                
numbers = np.arange(1, 6)
# [1 2 3 4 5]

            


            

                np.linspace()
                
Create evenly spaced values

                
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 5)
# [0.  2.5 5.  7.5 10.]

            


            

                np.zeros()
                
Create zeros

                
data = np.zeros(5)
# [0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]

            


        

    


    

        
 One-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays


        

            An array can be one row of data, or a grid containing rows and columns.
        


        


            

                
1D array: one line of values

                
wind_speed = np.array([3.2, 4.1, 5.6])

print(wind_speed.shape)
# (3,)

            


            

                
2D array: rows and columns

                
grid = np.array([
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6]
])

print(grid.shape)
# (2, 3)

            


        


        

            (2, 3) means:
            2 rows
            
            3 columns
        

    


    

        
 Fast calculations with built-in functions


        
sea_level = np.array([1.2, 1.6, 1.4, 1.9, 1.5])

print(np.mean(sea_level))  # Average
print(np.max(sea_level))   # Largest value
print(np.min(sea_level))   # Smallest value
print(np.sum(sea_level))   # Total value
print(np.std(sea_level))   # Standard deviation


        

            
np.mean()
Average

            
np.max()
Maximum

            
np.min()
Minimum

            
np.sum()
Total

            
np.std()
Spread of values

        

    


    

        
 Select values using a condition


        

            NumPy can quickly find values that match a condition. This is very
            useful when working with measurements, temperatures, rainfall, or data grids.
        


        
temperature = np.array([21, 26, 31, 18, 29])

hot_days = temperature[temperature > 25]

print(hot_days)
# [26 31 29]


        

            
            

                For NumPy arrays, use & for “and” and
                | for “or”. Put each condition inside brackets.
            

        


        
temperature = np.array([21, 26, 31, 18, 29])

comfortable = temperature[
    (temperature >= 20) & (temperature <= 28)
]

print(comfortable)
# [21 26]

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                I get ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'. What should I do?
            

            

                NumPy is not part of plain Python, so install it once: run pip install numpy in the terminal (or %pip install numpy in a Jupyter cell). Anaconda already includes it.
            


        

        

            
                Why does NumPy print [1 2 3] without commas?
            

            

                That is just how NumPy displays arrays, so you can tell them apart from lists. The data is the same. Use array.tolist() if you need a normal list.
            


        

        

            
                Can a NumPy array hold numbers and text together?
            

            

                An array holds one data type. If you mix them, NumPy converts everything to text, and maths no longer works. For mixed tables, use Pandas (coming soon).
            


        

        

            
                Why does arr[(arr > 5) and (arr < 10)] give an error?
            

            

                and and or work on single True/False values, not on whole arrays. Use & and |, and put each condition in brackets: arr[(arr > 5) & (arr < 10)].
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between np.arange() and np.linspace()?
            

            

                arange(start, stop, step) uses a step size and stops before stop, like range(). linspace(start, stop, count) asks how many values you want and includes stop.
            


        

        

            
                What do axis=0 and axis=1 mean?
            

            

                In a 2D array, axis=0 works down the rows, giving one result per column. axis=1 works across the columns, giving one result per row.
            


        

        

            
                If I change a slice of an array, why does the original array change too?
            

            

                NumPy slices are views of the same data, not copies (to save memory). Use part = arr[0:3].copy() when you want an independent copy.
            


        

        

            
                Why is NumPy faster than a Python loop?
            

            

                The loop over the numbers happens inside NumPy's compiled C code, and the numbers are stored close together in memory. Python does not have to handle each number one by one.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
29. Pandas Series and DataFrames


    

        Stage IV · Scientific Python and Data
        Planned
    


    

        

            
        


        

            
Turn messy data into an organized table

            

                Pandas is a Python library for working with
                tabular data: CSV files, Excel sheets, measurements, survey data,
                student records, weather observations, and research datasets.
            

        

    


    

        
 Install and import Pandas


        
Install Pandas once in your terminal or command prompt:


        
pip install pandas


        
Then import it in your Python file:


        
import pandas as pd


        

            
            

                We use pd as the short name for Pandas, just as we
                use np for NumPy.
            

        

    


    

        
 What is a Series?


        

            A Series is one labelled column of data. It is similar
            to a NumPy array, but each value can have a meaningful label called an
            index.
        


        
import pandas as pd

temperature = pd.Series(
    [28.5, 29.1, 30.2],
    index=["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
)

print(temperature)


        

            Output
            
Mon    28.5
Tue    29.1
Wed    30.2
dtype: float64

        


        

            

                
                    
IndexValue

                
                
                    
Mon28.5

                    
Tue29.1

                    
Wed30.2

                
            

        

    


    

        
 What is a DataFrame?


        

            A DataFrame is a complete table with rows and columns.
            Think of it like an Excel sheet inside Python.
        


        
import pandas as pd

students = {
    "Name": ["Asha", "Ravi", "Mina"],
    "Age": [21, 22, 20],
    "Score": [88, 76, 92]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(students)

print(df)


        

            

                
                    

                        Index
                        Name
                        Age
                        Score
                    

                
                
                    
0Asha2188

                    
1Ravi2276

                    
2Mina2092

                
            

        

    


    

        
 Important DataFrame words


        

            

                
                
Row

                
One complete record, such as information about one student.

            


            

                
                
Column

                
One type of information, such as Name, Age, or Score.

            


            

                
                
Index

                
The row label or position, usually starting from zero.

            


            

                
                
Dataset

                
The full collection of related rows and columns.

            

        

    


    

        
 Read a CSV file


        

            CSV means Comma-Separated Values. It is one of the
            most common formats for datasets.
        


        
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("weather_data.csv")

print(df.head())


        

            

                pd.read_csv()
                
Reads the CSV file into a DataFrame.

            


            

                df.head()
                
Shows the first five rows.

            

        

    


    

        
 Select rows and columns


        


            

                
Select one column

                
print(df["Score"])

                
Returns the complete Score column as a Series.

            


            

                
Select more than one column

                
print(df[["Name", "Score"]])

                
Use double square brackets for multiple columns.

            


            

                
Select a row with iloc

                
print(df.iloc[0])

                
Selects the first row by its numeric position.

            


            

                
Filter using a condition

                
high_scores = df[df["Score"] >= 80]

print(high_scores)

                
Keeps only rows where the score is 80 or higher.

            


        

    


    

        
 Inspect your data quickly


        
print(df.head())        # First 5 rows
print(df.tail())        # Last 5 rows
print(df.shape)         # Rows and columns
print(df.columns)       # Column names
print(df.info())        # Data types and missing values
print(df.describe())    # Statistics for numerical columns


        

            
            

                Always inspect your dataset before analysis. Check its column
                names, data types, missing values, and units first.

 Why Pandas is useful


        
    
            
  • It reads CSV and Excel-style data easily.

  • It keeps rows and columns organised with meaningful names.

  • It helps you filter, sort, clean, group, and summarise data.
