            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why start with a question instead of just exploring the data?
            

            

                Exploring is useful, but without a question it is easy to make dozens of plots and find "patterns" by chance. A question keeps the analysis focused and tells you when you are finished.
            


        

        

            
                Mean or median: which one should I report?
            

            

                The mean is sensitive to extreme values, and the median is not. If the data is skewed or has outliers (rainfall, income, river flow), the median often describes the "typical" value better. Reporting both is fine.
            


        

        

            
                Should I remove outliers?
            

            

                Only if you have a reason: a sensor error, a typing mistake, or a physically impossible value. Real extreme events (a typhoon, a heat wave) are often the most interesting data. Document every removal.
            


        

        

            
                Why does df.info() show my numbers as object?
            

            

                At least one value in the column is not a number, for example "NA", "-", or "12,5" with a comma. Use pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") and then look at the rows that became NaN.
            


        

        

            
                Does a strong correlation mean one variable causes the other?
            

            

                No. Two variables can move together because of a third factor (for example, season), or by coincidence. Causation needs experimental design or strong physical reasoning.
            


        

        

            
                How do I make my analysis reproducible?
            

            

                Keep raw data unchanged, do every step in code (not by hand in Excel), fix random seeds, record package versions, and save outputs with clear names.
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between std() in Pandas and NumPy?
            

            

                Pandas uses the sample standard deviation by default (ddof=1). NumPy uses the population version (ddof=0). With small datasets the numbers differ slightly. Say which one you used.
            


        

        

            
                How much data do I need?
            

            

                It depends on how variable the data is and how small an effect you want to detect. More data gives more reliable results. For formal studies, a power analysis estimates the required sample size.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    


    






    
35. Regression Plots


    

        Stage V · Python for Researchers
        Planned
    


    

        

        

            
Can one variable help explain another?

            

                Regression helps us describe the relationship between variables.
                For example, do study hours relate to exam score? Does salinity
                change with depth? Does temperature increase over time?
            

        

    


    

        
 The linear regression idea


        

            y = mx + b
            y = predicted value
            m = slope
            x = input variable
            b = intercept
        


        

            The regression line is the straight line that best represents the
            overall pattern in a scatter plot.
        

    


    

        
 What is regression?


        

            Regression means finding the line (or curve) that best follows your data,
            so you can describe how y changes when x changes.
            Six students give us six dots. Regression replaces the six dots with one rule:
        


        

            score = 7.97 × hours + 35.6
        


        

            
        


        

             real measurement
             regression line
             residual = real − predicted
        


        

            
            

                How does Python choose "the best" line? It tries to make the red
                gaps as small as possible. Each gap is squared (so negatives do not cancel
                positives) and added up. The line with the smallest total is the winner. This is
                called the least squares method.
            

        

    


    

        
 Why do we need regression?


        

            

                
                
To measure "how much"

                

                    "Score goes up with study time" is vague. The slope says it exactly:
                    each extra hour adds about 8 points.
                    In research: "SST rose by 0.02 °C per year".
                

            


            

                
                
To predict

                

                    Put a new x into the equation: 7 hours gives
                    7.97 × 7 + 35.6 ≈ 91 points.
                    In research: estimate a value where you have no measurement.
                

            


            

                
                
To summarise many points

                

                    Ten thousand data points become two numbers (slope and intercept)
                    that you can report in one sentence of a paper.
                

            


            

                
                
To compare

                

                    Is warming faster at station A or B? Compare their slopes. Is a new
                    sensor consistent with the old one? Regress one on the other.
                

            

        


        

            But a line can be drawn through any cloud of dots, even random ones.
            So we also need a number that says how well the line fits.
            That number is R².
        

    


    

        
 What is R²?


        

            R² (read "R squared", also called the coefficient of determination)
            answers one question:
        


        

            What fraction of the ups and downs in y can the line explain?
        


        

            The exam scores are different from each other: some are 45, some are 85. R² compares
            two pictures of that difference:
        


        

            

            
        


        

            

                Total variation
                

                1121.5
            

            

                Left over
                

                9.5
            

        


        

            
R² = 1 − SSresSStot

            
= 1 − 9.51121.5

            
= 0.99

        


        

            
            In words: 99% of the differences between the students' scores are explained by
            their study hours. Only 1% is left for everything else (sleep, luck, the exam questions…).
        


        

            
            

                For a straight line with one x, R² is simply the correlation coefficient r
                squared. That is why the code below uses result.rvalue ** 2.
                Because it is squared, R² tells you how well the line fits, not
                which direction it goes. Look at the slope for the direction.
            

        

    


    

        
 How to read an R² value


        

            

                
                R² ≈ 0
                
The line explains almost nothing. Knowing x does not help you guess y.

            


            

                
                R² ≈ 0.5
                
A clear trend, but with a lot of spread. Other factors matter too.

            


            

                
                R² ≈ 0.95
                
The dots sit close to the line. x explains most of the change in y.

            

        


        

            0 · no fit
            1 · perfect fit
        


        

            
            

                There is no universal "good" R². A calibration of a lab instrument
                is usually expected to be very close to 1. Field and environmental data are noisy, so a
                lower R² can still describe a real and useful relationship. Compare with
                published studies in your own field.
            

        

    


    

        
 Four R² traps to avoid


        

            

                1
                

                    
High R² does not mean x causes y

                    
Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. The cause is the heat, not the ice cream.

                

            

            

                2
                

                    
Always look at the plot, not only the number

                    

                        Curved data, one extreme outlier, or two separate groups can all give the
                        same R². A famous example is Anscombe's quartet: four very different
                        datasets with almost identical R².
                    

                

            

            

                3
                

                    
A low R² is not automatically useless

                    

                        A slope can be real even when the spread is large. Check the p-value of the
                        slope and how many data points you have.
                    

                

            

            

                4
                

                    
Do not predict far outside your data

                    

                        The line was fitted for 1 to 6 hours. At 20 hours it predicts 195 points, which
                        is impossible. A regression only describes the range you measured.
                    

                

            

        

    


    

        
 Try it in Python


        

            
                
                1. Fit the line and make a predictionSlope, intercept, and the score for 7 hours
                
            
            

                
 fit_line.py

                
from scipy.stats import linregress

hours = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
scores = [45, 51, 58, 68, 74, 85]

result = linregress(hours, scores)

print(f"Slope:     {result.slope:.2f} points per hour")
print(f"Intercept: {result.intercept:.2f}")

new_hours = 7
predicted = result.slope * new_hours + result.intercept
print(f"Predicted score for {new_hours} hours: {predicted:.1f}")

                

                    Output
                    
Slope:     7.97 points per hour
Intercept: 35.60
Predicted score for 7 hours: 91.4

                

            

        


        

            
                
                2. Calculate R² by hand, step by stepTotal variation, left-over variation, then R²
                
            
            

                
 r_squared.py

                
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import linregress

hours = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
scores = np.array([45, 51, 58, 68, 74, 85])

result = linregress(hours, scores)
predicted = result.slope * hours + result.intercept

# Step 1: total variation = squared gaps to the mean
ss_tot = np.sum((scores - scores.mean()) ** 2)

# Step 2: left-over variation = squared gaps to the line (residuals)
residuals = scores - predicted
ss_res = np.sum(residuals ** 2)

# Step 3: the fraction that the line explains
r_squared = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

print(f"SS_tot (total):      {ss_tot:8.2f}")
print(f"SS_res (left over):  {ss_res:8.2f}")
print(f"R² by hand:    {r_squared:.4f}")
print(f"R² from SciPy: {result.rvalue ** 2:.4f}")

                

                    Output
                    
SS_tot (total):       1121.50
SS_res (left over):      9.49
R² by hand:    0.9915
R² from SciPy: 0.9915

                

                
    
                    
  • Both ways give the same answer. In practice you just use result.rvalue ** 2.
    • 
                    
  • Writing it out once helps you remember what the number really means.
    • 
                

            

        


        

            
                
                3. Show the equation and R² on the plotThe style you see in papers and reports
                
            
            

                
 plot_with_r2.py

                
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import linregress

hours = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
scores = np.array([45, 51, 58, 68, 74, 85])

result = linregress(hours, scores)
line = result.slope * hours + result.intercept

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(hours, scores, color="steelblue", s=60, label="Measured")
ax.plot(hours, line, color="teal", label="Regression line")

label = (
    f"y = {result.slope:.2f}x + {result.intercept:.2f}\n"
    f"R² = {result.rvalue ** 2:.3f}"
)
ax.text(0.05, 0.95, label, transform=ax.transAxes,
        va="top", fontsize=11,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="lightgray"))

ax.set_xlabel("Study hours")
ax.set_ylabel("Exam score")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()

                
    
                    
  • transform=ax.transAxes places the text by position in the box (0 to 1), so it stays in the top-left corner whatever the data range.
    • 
                

            

        

    


    

        
 Regression plot with Seaborn


        
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "hours": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
    "score": [45, 51, 58, 68, 74, 85]
})

sns.regplot(
    data=df,
    x="hours",
    y="score",
    color="teal"
)

plt.title("Study Hours and Exam Score")
plt.show()

    


    

        
 How to read a regression plot


        

            
Positive slope
As x increases, y usually increases.

            
Negative slope
As x increases, y usually decreases.

            
Flat slope
There may be little linear relationship.

            
Scatter
More spread means the prediction is less certain.

        

    


    

        
 R²: how much variation is explained?


        
from scipy.stats import linregress

result = linregress(df["hours"], df["score"])

print(result.slope)
print(result.intercept)
print(result.rvalue ** 2)  # R²


        

            
            

                A strong relationship does not automatically prove causation.
                Always consider other variables, measurement quality, and your
                scientific context.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                What is the shaded area around the Seaborn regression line?
            

            

                It is a 95% confidence interval for the line: the range where the true average line probably lies. It is wider where you have fewer points. Turn it off with ci=None.
            


        

        

            
                What is a "good" R² value?
            

            

                It depends on the field. Controlled lab experiments often reach 0.9 or higher, while field and social data with many influences may be meaningful at 0.3. R² tells you how much variation the line explains, not whether the model is correct.
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between correlation (r) and R²?
            

            

                r runs from −1 to 1 and shows direction and strength. For a simple straight-line fit, R² is just r², which loses the sign and shows the fraction of variation explained.
            


        

        

            
                Does the order of x and y matter?
            

            

                Yes. Regression predicts y from x, and swapping them gives a different line. Put the variable you control or think of as the cause on x, and the response on y. The correlation r stays the same.
            


        

        

            
                linregress returns NaN. Why?
            

            

                Your data probably contains missing values. Remove them first, for example with df = df.dropna(subset=["hours", "score"]).
            


        

        

            
                When should I not use a straight-line regression?
            

            

                When the scatter plot is clearly curved, when the residuals show a pattern, or when the data are counts or yes/no values. Then try a polynomial, a log transform, or another model.
            


        

        

            
                Is regplot enough for a scientific paper?
            

            

                It is great for a quick look. For a paper, also report the slope with its uncertainty, R², the number of points, and the test you used, usually from linregress or statsmodels.
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between regplot and lmplot?
            

            

                regplot draws one regression on one axes. lmplot makes a whole figure and can split the data by groups using hue, col, or row.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
36. Choosing the Right Plot: Line, Bar, Scatter, and Histogram


    

        Stage V · Python for Researchers
        Planned
    


    

        

        

            
One dataset can tell different stories

            

                The best plot is the one that makes your result easiest to
                understand. A line plot, bar chart, scatter plot, and histogram
                answer different types of questions. Choose a plot based on your
                question, not because it looks fancy.
            

        

    


    

        
 Four basic plot types


        

            

                
                
Line plot

                
Best for changes over ordered time or distance.

                plt.plot(time, temperature)
            


            

                
                
Bar chart

                
Best for comparing separate categories or groups.

                plt.bar(city, rainfall)
            


            

                
                
Scatter plot

                
Best for checking a relationship between two numerical variables.

                plt.scatter(depth, salinity)
            


            

                
                
Histogram

                
Best for checking how values are distributed.

                plt.hist(scores, bins=10)
            

        

    


    

        
 Four basic plotting commands


        
# Line plot
plt.plot(days, temperature)

# Bar chart
plt.bar(cities, rainfall)

# Scatter plot
plt.scatter(depth, salinity)

# Histogram
plt.hist(exam_scores, bins=10)

 3D bar chart

                        ax.bar3d()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
Bars standing on a floor. The floor has two categories (city and month), and the bar height is the value (rainfall).

                        
 Use it for A value for every combination of two categories, when you want an eye-catching overview, for example in a talk.

                        
 Watch out Front bars hide back bars, and perspective makes heights hard to compare. Put the smallest row in front and try different view_init() angles. In a paper, a heatmap of the same table is usually easier to read.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 bar3d_chart.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May"]
cities = ["Tainan", "Hualien", "Taipei"]    # smallest values in front

# rows = cities, columns = months (example rainfall in mm)
rainfall = np.array([
    [19, 25, 41, 85, 180],
    [68, 101, 87, 81, 213],
    [83, 170, 180, 177, 251],
])

# One (x, y) position on the floor for every bar
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(len(months)), np.arange(len(cities)))
x = x.ravel()
y = y.ravel()
heights = rainfall.ravel()

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")    # turn on 3D

colors = plt.cm.viridis(heights / heights.max())    # taller bar = brighter colour
ax.bar3d(x, y, np.zeros_like(heights),     # where each bar starts
         dx=0.6, dy=0.6, dz=heights,       # bar width, depth, height
         color=colors, shade=True)

ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(months)) + 0.3, months)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(cities)) + 0.3, cities)
ax.set_zlabel("Rainfall (mm)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_title("Monthly Rainfall by City")
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-55)       # camera angle: height, rotation
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)    # shrink a little so labels fit

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • projection="3d" turns a normal axes into a 3D axes.
    • 
                            
  • bar3d(x, y, z, dx, dy, dz): where each bar starts (x, y, z) and its width, depth, and height.
    • 
                            
  • np.meshgrid() + ravel() make one floor position for every cell of the table.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    2
                    

                        
 Error bars and box plot

                        ax.errorbar() · ax.boxplot()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
Both show the spread of each group, not only the average. An error bar shows mean ± a range. A box plot shows the median, the middle 50%, and outliers of all values.

                        
 Use it for Comparing groups in an experiment: control vs treatment, station A vs B, before vs after.

                        
 Watch out An error bar can mean SD, standard error, or a 95% confidence interval, and they differ a lot. Always write which one in the caption. With fewer than about 10 values per group, show the points themselves.

                    
                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 errorbar_boxplot.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)    # fixed seed: same "random" data every run

groups = ["Control", "Low dose", "High dose"]
data = [
    rng.normal(50, 5, 30),    # 30 plants per group
    rng.normal(56, 8, 30),
    rng.normal(63, 6, 30),
]

means = [d.mean() for d in data]
stds = [d.std(ddof=1) for d in data]    # sample standard deviation

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)

# (a) Error bars: one dot for the mean, a whisker for the spread
ax1.errorbar(groups, means, yerr=stds,
             fmt="o", markersize=8, capsize=6, color="steelblue")
ax1.set_title("(a) Error bars: mean ± 1 SD")
ax1.set_ylabel("Plant height (cm)")

# (b) Box plot: median, quartiles, and outliers of all 30 values
ax2.boxplot(data)
ax2.set_xticks([1, 2, 3], groups)
ax2.set_title("(b) Box plot: median and quartiles")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • yerr=stds sets the length of each whisker. capsize draws the small caps.
    • 
                            
  • fmt="o" draws dots only, with no line joining the groups.
    • 
                            
  • boxplot(data) takes a list of arrays, one per group, and calculates everything itself.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    3
                    

                        
 Pie chart

                        ax.pie()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
A circle cut into slices. Each slice is a share of one whole, and all slices add up to 100%.

                        
 Use it for Two to five parts of one total, such as land use, energy mix, or survey answers.

                        
 Watch out People compare angles badly, so with many or similar slices use a sorted bar chart instead. Never use a 3D pie: the front slices look bigger than they are.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 pie_chart.py

                        
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sources = ["Gas", "Coal", "Renewables", "Nuclear"]
share = [42, 39, 13, 6]    # percent (example values)
colors = ["#3776ab", "#5d6b7a", "#21845b", "#d9822b"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))

ax.pie(share,
       labels=sources,
       colors=colors,
       autopct="%1.0f%%",          # write the percentage on each slice
       startangle=90,              # first slice starts at 12 o'clock
       counterclock=False,         # go clockwise, like a clock
       wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white", "linewidth": 2},
       textprops={"fontsize": 11})

ax.set_title("Electricity Sources (example)")
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • autopct="%1.0f%%" writes each percentage on its slice (%% prints a % sign).
    • 
                            
  • startangle=90 and counterclock=False start at 12 o'clock and go clockwise, as people read a clock.
    • 
                            
  • wedgeprops adds white edges, so neighbouring slices are easy to separate.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    4
                    

                        
 Contour plot

                        ax.contour() · ax.contourf()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
A surface seen from above. Each line joins points with the same value, like height lines on a hiking map or isobars on a weather map.

                        
 Use it for Smooth 2D fields: topography, pressure, temperature, concentration.

                        
 Watch out Lines close together mean the value changes fast (a steep slope). Too many levels make the plot busy; too few hide detail. Try 8 to 15.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 contour_plot.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# A grid of x, y points
x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 200)
y = np.linspace(-3, 3, 200)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

# A "landscape" with two hills
Z = 3 * np.exp(-(X**2 + Y**2)) + 2 * np.exp(-((X - 1.5)**2 + (Y + 1.2)**2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

filled = ax.contourf(X, Y, Z, levels=15, cmap="viridis")         # coloured bands
lines = ax.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=8, colors="white", linewidths=0.8)  # lines
ax.clabel(lines, fontsize=8, fmt="%.1f")                            # numbers on lines

fig.colorbar(filled, ax=ax, label="Height (km)")
ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
ax.set_title("Contour Plot of Two Hills")
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • np.meshgrid(x, y) turns two 1D axes into 2D grids X and Y. Z must have the same shape.
    • 
                            
  • contourf fills the bands with colour. contour draws only the lines. Using both is common.
    • 
                            
  • clabel() writes the value on each line.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    5
                    

                        
 Surface plot (surf)

                        ax.plot_surface()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
The same X, Y, Z data as the contour plot, shown as a 3D landscape. MATLAB users know it as surf.

                        
 Use it for Showing the overall shape of a 2D function or field, especially in teaching and presentations.

                        
 Watch out Hills can hide valleys behind them, and exact values are hard to read. In a paper, show a contour plot next to it, or instead of it.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 surface_plot.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 80)
y = np.linspace(-3, 3, 80)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 3 * np.exp(-(X**2 + Y**2)) + 2 * np.exp(-((X - 1.5)**2 + (Y + 1.2)**2))

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

surface = ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z, cmap="viridis",
                          edgecolor="none", antialiased=True)

fig.colorbar(surface, ax=ax, shrink=0.6, pad=0.1, label="Height (km)")
ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
ax.set_zlabel("Height (km)")
ax.set_title("Surface Plot of the Same Two Hills")
ax.view_init(elev=30, azim=-125)      # rotate so both hills are visible
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)    # shrink a little so labels fit

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • cmap="viridis" colours the surface by height, so it can share a colorbar.
    • 
                            
  • view_init(elev, azim) sets the camera: elevation (up/down) and azimuth (rotation).
    • 
                            
  • In a normal Python window (not a notebook image) you can drag the plot with the mouse to rotate it.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    6
                    

                        
 imshow

                        ax.imshow()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
Shows a 2D array as a picture: every number becomes one coloured pixel.

                        
 Use it for Regular grids (model output, satellite data), matrices, and photos.

                        
 Watch out By default row 0 is drawn at the top, so maps appear upside-down. Use origin="lower". Without extent, the axes show index numbers instead of real coordinates. For uneven grids, use pcolormesh().

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 imshow_grid.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# A 2D grid of sea-surface temperature (example values)
lon = np.linspace(118, 124, 60)
lat = np.linspace(20, 27, 70)
LON, LAT = np.meshgrid(lon, lat)
sst = 29 - 0.8 * (LAT - 20) + 0.6 * np.sin(LON * 1.5)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))

image = ax.imshow(sst,
                  cmap="coolwarm",
                  origin="lower",                 # row 0 at the bottom (south)
                  extent=[118, 124, 20, 27],      # real axis values: x0, x1, y0, y1
                  aspect="auto")

fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="SST (°C)")
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")
ax.set_title("imshow: a grid shown as an image")
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • origin="lower" puts the first row at the bottom, so south is at the bottom.
    • 
                            
  • extent=[x0, x1, y0, y1] labels the axes with longitude and latitude.
    • 
                            
  • aspect="auto" lets the pixels stretch to fill the axes.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    7
                    

                        
 Bubble chart

                        ax.scatter(s=…, c=…)
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
A scatter plot where the size of each dot shows a third variable, and the colour can show a fourth.

                        
 Use it for Points that each have several properties: earthquakes (location, magnitude, depth), cities (position, population).

                        
 Watch out s sets the area, not the radius. Big bubbles cover small ones, so use alpha and an edge colour. Always add a size legend, otherwise nobody knows what a big bubble means.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 bubble_chart.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 40

lon = rng.uniform(120.0, 122.5, n)
lat = rng.uniform(21.8, 25.3, n)
magnitude = rng.uniform(3.0, 6.5, n)
depth = rng.uniform(5, 80, n)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))

bubbles = ax.scatter(lon, lat,
                     s=magnitude**3 * 2,     # bubble AREA grows with magnitude
                     c=depth,                # colour shows depth
                     cmap="plasma_r",
                     alpha=0.7, edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.5)

fig.colorbar(bubbles, ax=ax, label="Depth (km)")

# Legend that explains the bubble sizes
handles, labels = bubbles.legend_elements(
    prop="sizes", num=4, func=lambda s: np.cbrt(s / 2), fmt="M {x:.1f}")
ax.legend(handles, labels, title="Magnitude", loc="upper left",
          labelspacing=1.4, borderpad=1)

ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")
ax.set_title("Earthquakes (example data)")
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • s= sets the bubble size and c= the colour value. cmap picks the colours.
    • 
                            
  • legend_elements(prop="sizes") builds the size legend. func converts sizes back to magnitudes.
    • 
                            
  • The colorbar explains the colours, and the legend explains the sizes. Both are needed.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    8
                    

                        
 Heatmap

                        sns.heatmap()
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
A table where each cell is coloured by its value, with named rows and columns.

                        
 Use it for Month × station tables, correlation matrices, any table you want to scan for patterns.

                        
 Watch out Write numbers in the cells (annot=True) only when there are few cells. For correlations use a diverging colormap with vmin=-1, vmax=1, so 0 is the neutral colour.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 heatmap_table.py

                        
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
          "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
stations = ["Taipei", "Taichung", "Tainan", "Hualien"]

# Example monthly mean temperature: yearly average + a seasonal wave
yearly = np.array([23.5, 23.8, 25.1, 23.7])
season = 6 * np.sin((np.arange(12) - 3) * np.pi / 6)
table = pd.DataFrame((yearly[:, None] + season).round(1),
                     index=stations, columns=months)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.5))

sns.heatmap(table,
            annot=True, fmt=".1f",        # write the number in every cell
            cmap="YlOrRd",
            linewidths=0.5, linecolor="white",
            cbar_kws={"label": "Temperature (°C)"},
            ax=ax)

ax.set_title("Monthly Mean Temperature (example)")
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • Give sns.heatmap() a pandas DataFrame: its index and columns become the axis labels.
    • 
                            
  • annot=True, fmt=".1f" writes each value with one decimal.
    • 
                            
  • cbar_kws={"label": ...} adds a label with units to the colorbar.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


        

            
 Four ways to show a 2D grid of values

            

                

                    
                        
PlotBest forMain strength

                    
                    
                        
imshowRegular grids, imagesFast and simple, one pixel per value

                        
sns.heatmapTables with named rows and columnsLabels and numbers in the cells

                        
contourfSmooth fieldsShows lines of equal value

                        
plot_surfaceShowing the 3D shapeIntuitive, but hides parts

 Quick plot decision guide


        

            

                
                    

                        Your question
                        Data type
                        Recommended plot
                    

                
                
                    
How does a value change over time?Time + numberLine plot

                    
Which group is larger?Category + numberBar chart

                    
Are two variables related?Number + numberScatter / regression plot

                    
How are values distributed?One numerical variableHistogram / box plot

                    
Where is data located?Latitude + longitudeMap / spatial plot

                    
How does a field vary over space?X + Y + valueHeatmap / contour plot

                
            

        

    


    

        
 Ask these questions before plotting


        
    
            
  1. What is my main research question?

  3. Am I showing a trend, comparison, relationship, or distribution?
    4. 
            
  4. Will the reader understand the axes and units immediately?
    5. 
            
  5. Would a simpler 2D plot communicate the idea better than a 3D plot?
    6.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                What is the difference between a bar chart and a histogram?
            

            

                A bar chart compares separate categories (cities, groups), so the bars have gaps. A histogram groups one numerical variable into ranges (bins), so the bars touch and show the distribution.
            


        

        

            
                Should the y-axis of a bar chart always start at 0?
            

            

                Yes. Bar length represents the value, so a cut axis exaggerates differences. Line plots may start elsewhere when you are showing changes.
            


        

        

            
                Should I join scatter points with lines?
            

            

                Only if the points have a natural order, like time or distance. For independent measurements (different students, different stations), lines would suggest a connection that does not exist.
            


        

        

            
                How many bins should my histogram have?
            

            

                There is no single answer. Start with bins="auto", then try a few values. Too few bins hide the shape, and too many make it look noisy.
            


        

        

            
                When is a box plot better than a histogram?
            

            

                When you compare the spread of several groups side by side. A box plot shows the median, quartiles, and outliers compactly, while a histogram shows the full shape of one distribution.
            


        

        

            
                Why are my bar labels overlapping?
            

            

                Use plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right"), switch to horizontal bars with plt.barh, or make the figure wider.
            


        

        

            
                Why does my line plot zigzag strangely?
            

            

                The x values are probably not sorted, so the line jumps back and forth. Sort the data by x (for example df.sort_values("date")) before plotting.
            


        

        

            
                Are pie charts a good choice?
            

            

                Rarely in research. People compare lengths more accurately than angles, so a bar chart usually communicates the same information more clearly.
            


        

        

            
                Can one figure answer two questions at once?
            

            

                Usually it is clearer to make one figure per message. If two views belong together, put them in separate panels (subplots) labelled (a) and (b) instead of mixing them in one plot.
            


        

        

            
                When should I show all data points instead of averages?
            

            

                Whenever you have few points (fewer than about 20 per group). Bar charts of means hide how much the data varies. Strip or swarm plots show every observation.
            


        

        

            
                How many colours should a plot have?
            

            

                As few as possible. Use colour to separate a few groups or to highlight the important element. More than 6–7 distinct colours become hard to tell apart.
            


        

        

            
                Is a violin plot better than a box plot?
            

            

                A violin plot also shows the shape, such as two peaks, which a box plot hides. It needs enough data to estimate the shape reliably, and some readers find it harder to read.
            


        

        

            
                How do I choose between a heatmap and a contour plot?
            

            

                A heatmap shows exact values in each cell and suits blocky grids or tables. A contour plot shows smooth fields with lines of equal value and suits continuous quantities like temperature or pressure.
            


        

        

            
                Where can I find examples of good plots?
            

            

                The Matplotlib and Seaborn galleries show code for every plot type. "From Data to Viz" (data-to-viz.com) is a decision tree that helps you choose a plot. Figures in leading journals in your field are good models too.
            


        

        

            
                My plot looks correct, but people misunderstand it. Why?
            

            

                Ask someone to describe what they see before you explain it. Common causes: missing units, unclear title, too many elements, or a colour scale with no legend. Simplify until the main message is obvious.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
37. 3D Data Analysis and Visualization


    

        Stage V · Python for Researchers
        Planned
    


    

        

        

            
When two axes are not enough

            

                Three-dimensional plots can show three variables together, such
                as longitude, latitude, and sea-surface temperature—or x, y, and
                height across a surface.
            

        

    



    

        
 Five common 3D plots


        

            Click a plot type to open it. Each card shows a real picture made by the code
            in its Show code box. Click the picture to see it full size.
        


        

            
            
            
            
            
        


            

                

                    1
                    

                        
 3D scatter

                        ax.scatter(x, y, z)
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
Separate points in space. Each point has an x, y, and z position, and colour can show a fourth value.

                        
 Use it for Measurements at different positions: water samples, sensors, particles, stars.

                        
 Watch out It is hard to judge how deep a point is, and points hide each other. Colour by a value, use a few clear ticks, and try several angles.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 scatter_3d.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 150

# Example water samples: position, depth, and temperature
lon = rng.uniform(120, 122, n)
lat = rng.uniform(21, 23, n)
depth = rng.uniform(0, 500, n)
temperature = 28 - 0.035 * depth + rng.normal(0, 0.8, n)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

points = ax.scatter(lon, lat, -depth,           # minus: deeper = lower
                    c=temperature, cmap="coolwarm", s=25)

fig.colorbar(points, ax=ax, shrink=0.6, pad=0.12, label="Temperature (°C)")

ax.set_xticks([120, 121, 122])    # a few clear ticks are easier to read
ax.set_yticks([21, 22, 23])
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")
ax.set_zlabel("Depth (m)", labelpad=8)
ax.zaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda value, pos: f"{abs(value):.0f}")   # show 500, not -500
ax.set_title("3D Scatter: Water Samples")
ax.view_init(elev=20, azim=-60)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • projection="3d" creates 3D axes. scatter then takes three 1D arrays.
    • 
                            
  • -depth puts deeper samples lower. The formatter shows the numbers as positive depths.
    • 
                            
  • shrink and pad keep the colorbar small and away from the axis labels.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    2
                    

                        
 3D line

                        ax.plot(x, y, z)
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
A path through space, drawn in order. The same plot() you know, with a third array.

                        
 Use it for Trajectories: profiling floats, drones, particles, a balloon rising and drifting.

                        
 Watch out From a 3D view it is hard to tell where the path is horizontally. Draw its shadow on the floor and mark the start and end.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 line_3d.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# A float that dives to 500 m and comes back up 4 times while drifting
t = np.linspace(0, 4, 400)                      # number of dive cycles
lon = 121 + 0.3 * t + 0.05 * np.sin(3 * t)
lat = 22 + 0.2 * t
depth = 500 * (1 - np.cos(2 * np.pi * t)) / 2   # 0 -> 500 -> 0 m

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

ax.plot(lon, lat, -depth, color="tab:blue", linewidth=2, label="Float path")

# "Shadow" of the path on the floor helps the eye read the position
floor = -600
ax.plot(lon, lat, np.full_like(lon, floor), color="gray",
        linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, label="Track seen from above")

ax.scatter(lon[0], lat[0], 0, color="green", s=60, label="Start")
ax.scatter(lon[-1], lat[-1], 0, color="red", s=60, label="End")

ax.set_zlim(floor, 0)
ax.set_xticks([121.0, 121.5, 122.0])
ax.set_yticks([22.0, 22.4, 22.8])
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")
ax.set_zlabel("Depth (m)", labelpad=8)
ax.zaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda value, pos: f"{abs(value):.0f}")
ax.set_title("3D Line: Path of a Profiling Float")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.view_init(elev=20, azim=-50)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.8)

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • ax.plot(lon, lat, -depth) joins the points in the order of the arrays.
    • 
                            
  • np.full_like(lon, floor) makes the same path at a constant depth: the shadow.
    • 
                            
  • set_zlim(floor, 0) makes sure the shadow is inside the box.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    3
                    

                        
 Surface plot

                        ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z)
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
A continuous field Z over an x–y grid, drawn as a coloured landscape. Here a contour map of the same data is projected on the floor.

                        
 Use it for Topography and bathymetry, model output on a grid, mathematical functions.

                        
 Watch out X, Y, and Z must be 2D grids of the same shape (np.meshgrid). Hills hide valleys: the contour floor shows the hidden parts.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 surface_3d.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# A grid of x, y points (km)
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 120)
y = np.linspace(-5, 5, 120)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

# Sea floor with an underwater mountain (seamount), in km
Z = -4 + 3 * np.exp(-(X**2 + Y**2) / 3) + 0.2 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

surface = ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z, cmap="viridis",
                          edgecolor="none", alpha=0.95)

# The same field as a contour map on the floor of the box
ax.contourf(X, Y, Z, zdir="z", offset=-6, levels=15, cmap="viridis")

ax.set_zlim(-6, 0)
fig.colorbar(surface, ax=ax, shrink=0.6, pad=0.1, label="Height (km)")
ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
ax.set_zlabel("Height (km)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_title("Surface + Contour Floor: a Seamount")
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-60)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • np.meshgrid(x, y) builds the 2D grids. Z is calculated on the whole grid at once.
    • 
                            
  • contourf(..., zdir="z", offset=-6) draws the contour map flat at height −6.
    • 
                            
  • set_zlim(-6, 0) must include the offset, otherwise the floor map is outside the box.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    4
                    

                        
 Wireframe

                        ax.plot_wireframe(X, Y, Z)
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
The same kind of surface drawn as a net of lines. You can see through it.

                        
 Use it for Seeing the shape and what is behind it, or a quick, fast first look at a surface.

                        
 Watch out There is no colour, so there are no values to read. Too many lines become a grey blur: use rstride and cstride.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 wireframe_3d.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-6, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(-6, 6, 80)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

# Ripples spreading out from a stone dropped in water
R = np.sqrt(X**2 + Y**2)
Z = np.cos(2 * R) * np.exp(-R / 3)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

ax.plot_wireframe(X, Y, Z,
                  rstride=3, cstride=3,      # draw every 3rd row and column
                  color="steelblue", linewidth=0.7)

ax.set_xlabel("x (m)")
ax.set_ylabel("y (m)")
ax.set_zlabel("Height (m)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_title("Wireframe: Water Ripples")
ax.view_init(elev=30, azim=-60)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • Same X, Y, Z grids as plot_surface.
    • 
                            
  • rstride=3, cstride=3 draws every 3rd row and column line.
    • 
                            
  • Swap plot_wireframe for plot_surface and the code still works.
    • 
                        

                    

                

            


            

                

                    5
                    

                        
 3D bar chart

                        ax.bar(…, zs=…, zdir="y")
                    

                


                

                    
                    

                        
Normal bar charts placed one behind the other, one row per group.

                        
 Use it for A value for each category and group: months × years, sites × seasons.

                        
 Watch out Front rows hide back rows, and heights are hard to compare across rows. For a paper, grouped 2D bars or a heatmap are usually clearer.

                    

                


                

                    
                        
                        Show the code for this plotComplete and ready to run: it makes exactly the picture above
                        
                    
                    

                        
 bars_3d.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = np.arange(1, 13)
years = [2023, 2024, 2025]
colors = ["#3776ab", "#21845b", "#d9822b"]

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
season = 120 + 110 * np.sin((months - 3) * np.pi / 6)    # wet summer

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")

# One row of bars per year, placed one behind the other
for i, (year, color) in enumerate(zip(years, colors)):
    rain = np.clip(season + rng.normal(0, 25, 12), 0, None)    # rain cannot be negative
    ax.bar(months, rain, zs=i, zdir="y",       # zs: which row; zdir: rows go along y
           color=color, alpha=0.85, edgecolor="white")

ax.set_yticks(range(len(years)), years)
ax.set_xticks(months, ["J", "F", "M", "A", "M", "J",
                       "J", "A", "S", "O", "N", "D"])
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_zlabel("Rainfall (mm)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_title("3D Bars: Monthly Rainfall in Three Years")
ax.view_init(elev=22, azim=-62)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • zs=i tells Matplotlib which row the bars go in.
    • 
                            
  • zdir="y" places the rows along the y-axis.
    • 
                            
  • np.clip(..., 0, None) keeps rainfall from becoming negative after adding random noise.
    • 
                        

                    

                

                

                    
                        
                        Grid version: square 3D bars with ax.bar3d()City × month, the version shown in Lesson 36
                        
                    
                    

                        
 bar3d_grid.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May"]
cities = ["Tainan", "Hualien", "Taipei"]    # smallest values in front

# rows = cities, columns = months (example rainfall in mm)
rainfall = np.array([
    [19, 25, 41, 85, 180],
    [68, 101, 87, 81, 213],
    [83, 170, 180, 177, 251],
])

# One (x, y) position on the floor for every bar
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(len(months)), np.arange(len(cities)))
x = x.ravel()
y = y.ravel()
heights = rainfall.ravel()

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")    # turn on 3D

colors = plt.cm.viridis(heights / heights.max())    # taller bar = brighter colour
ax.bar3d(x, y, np.zeros_like(heights),     # where each bar starts
         dx=0.6, dy=0.6, dz=heights,       # bar width, depth, height
         color=colors, shade=True)

ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(months)) + 0.3, months)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(cities)) + 0.3, cities)
ax.set_zlabel("Rainfall (mm)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_title("Monthly Rainfall by City")
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-55)       # camera angle: height, rotation
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)    # shrink a little so labels fit

plt.show()

                    

                

            


    


    

        
 Essential points for 3D plots


        

            3D plots fail in the same few ways again and again. These ten points fix most of them.
        


        


            

                1
                

                    
Turn on 3D for every 3D axes

                    
Write projection="3d" when you create the axes. You can mix 2D and 3D axes in one figure.

                

                    
                        
                        Mix a 3D and a 2D plot in one figureprojection is set per axes
                        
                    
                    

                        
 mix.py

                        
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4.5))

ax1 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1, projection="3d")    # left: 3D
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2)                     # right: normal 2D

plt.show()

                    

                

                

            


            

                2
                

                    
Know which shape your data must have

                    
Points and lines take simple lists. Surfaces need grids. This is the most common 3D error: "Argument Z must be 2-dimensional".

                    

                        

                            
Plotx, y, z must beExample shape

                            
                                
scatter, plot1D arrays of the same length(150,)

                                
plot_surface, plot_wireframe, contourf2D grids of the same shape(100, 100)

                            
                        

                    

                

                    
                        
                        Make grids from a formula or from a tablenp.meshgrid and DataFrame.pivot
                        
                    
                    

                        
 grid.py

                        
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# From formulas: make the grid first, then calculate Z on it
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
y = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)
print(X.shape, Y.shape, Z.shape)    # (100, 100) three times

# From a table with x, y, and value columns
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [0, 1, 0, 1],
                   "y": [0, 0, 1, 1],
                   "value": [5, 6, 7, 9]})
grid = df.pivot(index="y", columns="x", values="value")
X, Y = np.meshgrid(grid.columns, grid.index)
Z = grid.values

                    

                

                

            


            

                3
                

                    
Choose the camera angle on purpose

                    
The default angle is rarely the best one. The same data can look completely different:

                    
                    

                        elev = how high the camera is (0 = side view, 90 = straight down)
                        azim = how far the camera walks around the plot, in degrees
                    

                

                    
                        
                        Code for the three viewsview_init(elev, azim)
                        
                    
                    

                        
 three_views.py

                        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 80)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, x)
Z = -4 + 3 * np.exp(-(X**2 + Y**2) / 3) + 0.2 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)

views = [(30, -60, "Default-like view"),
         (75, -90, "From above"),
         (0, -90, "From the side")]

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 4.5))

for i, (elev, azim, name) in enumerate(views, start=1):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, i, projection="3d")
    ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z, cmap="viridis", edgecolor="none")
    ax.view_init(elev=elev, azim=azim)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nelev={elev}, azim={azim}")
    ax.set_xticks([])    # hide numbers: only the angle matters here
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_zticks([])

plt.show()

                    

                

                

            


            

                4
                

                    
Label all three axes, with units, and keep them visible

                    
The z label is often cut off, and tick numbers often overlap. Add labelpad, use fewer ticks, and shrink the box slightly.

                

                    
                        
                        Readable labels and tickslabelpad, set_xticks, set_box_aspect
                        
                    
                    

                        
 labels.py

                        
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")
ax.set_zlabel("Depth (m)", labelpad=8)    # push the label away from the numbers

ax.set_xticks([120, 121, 122])            # fewer ticks = no overlapping numbers
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.85)        # shrink the box so labels are not cut off

                    

                

                

            


            

                5
                

                    
Make depth go down

                    
Axes grow upward, but depth grows downward. Without a fix, the deep ocean appears at the top.

                

                    
                        
                        Two ways to show depth correctlynegative values or invert_zaxis()
                        
                    
                    

                        
 depth.py

                        
# Option 1: plot negative depth, but show positive numbers
ax.plot(lon, lat, -depth)
ax.zaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda value, pos: f"{abs(value):.0f}")

# Option 2: plot depth as it is and flip the axis
ax.plot(lon, lat, depth)
ax.invert_zaxis()

                    

                

                

            


            

                6
                

                    
Check the proportions

                    
Matplotlib draws the box as a cube, even if your area is 100 km wide and 1 km deep. That stretches the height a lot. Set real proportions, or say clearly how much you stretched it.

                

                    
                        
                        Set the box proportionsset_box_aspect((x, y, z))
                        
                    
                    

                        
 aspect.py

                        
# Default: the box is a cube, whatever the units are
ax.set_box_aspect((1, 1, 1))

# Wide and flat box, e.g. 10 km x 10 km area but only 4 km deep
ax.set_box_aspect((10, 10, 4))

# Say it in the caption if you stretch the height on purpose:
# "Vertical exaggeration x 50"

                    

                

                

            


            

                7
                

                    
Help the eye read depth

                    
A 3D picture is still flat on the screen. Colour by value (with a colorbar), draw shadows or contours on the floor, mark start and end points, and use transparency (alpha) to see what is behind.

                

            


            

                8
                

                    
Remember what 3D hides

                    
Parts of the data are always behind other parts. Matplotlib also draws each object as one flat layer, so two crossing surfaces can appear in the wrong order. For complex 3D scenes, use Plotly or PyVista.

                

            


            

                9
                

                    
Rotate while exploring, choose views when publishing

                    
In a normal Python window you can drag the plot with the mouse. A printed page cannot rotate, so save a few good angles, or add a 2D version.

                

                    
                        
                        Save several angles, and rotate in Jupyterview_init in a loop, %matplotlib widget
                        
                    
                    

                        
 save.py

                        
# Save the same 3D figure from several angles for a paper
for azim in [-60, 0, 60, 120]:
    ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=azim)
    fig.savefig(f"surface_azim{azim}.png", dpi=300)

# In Jupyter, make plots rotatable (after: pip install ipympl)
# %matplotlib widget

                    

                

                

            


            

                10
                

                    
Keep it fast

                    
A 1000 × 1000 surface has a million cells and can freeze your computer. Draw fewer points: the picture usually looks the same.

                

                    
                        
                        Reduce the data before plottingslicing, rcount/ccount, random sample
                        
                    
                    

                        
 fast.py

                        
# Draw every 4th grid point: 16 times fewer polygons
ax.plot_surface(X[::4, ::4], Y[::4, ::4], Z[::4, ::4], cmap="viridis")

# Or let Matplotlib reduce it: at most 50 x 50 patches
ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z, rcount=50, ccount=50, cmap="viridis")

# Large scatter: plot a random sample of 5000 points
idx = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(x), size=5000, replace=False)
ax.scatter(x[idx], y[idx], z[idx], s=2)

                    

                

                

            


        

    


    

        
 3D or 2D?


        

            

                
Use 3D when…

                
    
                    
  • the shape is the message (a seamount, a valley, a trajectory)
    • 
                    
  • you are exploring data and can rotate it
    • 
                    
  • you present on a screen, or the reader can open an interactive figure
    • 
                

            

            

                
Prefer 2D when…

                
    
                    
  • readers must read exact values
    • 
                    
  • the figure is printed in a paper
    • 
                    
  • a contour map, heatmap, or map with colour shows the same thing
    • 
                

            

        


        

            
            

                Many good papers show both: a 3D view to give the reader the shape, and a 2D map
                next to it for the exact values.
