            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                I get ValueError: Unknown projection '3d'. Why?
            

            

                In very old Matplotlib versions you had to import the 3D toolkit first: from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D. Updating Matplotlib with pip install -U matplotlib also fixes it.
            


        

        

            
                Why does plot_surface say "Argument Z must be 2-dimensional"?
            

            

                Surfaces need grids, not simple lists. Build X, Y with np.meshgrid, then calculate Z from them so all three have the same 2D shape.
            


        

        

            
                How do I rotate a 3D plot with the mouse?
            

            

                In a normal Python window you can drag the plot. In Jupyter, run %matplotlib widget (after pip install ipympl), or use Plotly, which is always interactive.
            


        

        

            
                Is a 3D plot better than a 2D contour map?
            

            

                Usually not for reading exact values. In print, 3D perspective distorts sizes and hides parts of the data. Contour maps and heatmaps are often clearer. Use 3D when the shape itself is the message.
            


        

        

            
                My surface looks blocky. How do I make it smoother?
            

            

                Use more grid points in np.linspace (for example 100 instead of 20). For measured data, you may need to interpolate onto a finer grid first.
            


        

        

            
                Why is depth shown upside down?
            

            

                Depth increases downward, but axes increase upward. Plot negative depth (-depth) or call ax.invert_zaxis().
            


        

        

            
                What does cmap mean?
            

            

                It is the colour map: how numbers become colours. viridis and cividis are readable and colour-blind friendly. Avoid jet and rainbow maps, because they create false boundaries.
            


        

        

            
                My 3D plot is very slow. What can I do?
            

            

                Reduce the number of points: use every 2nd or 4th grid point (X[::4, ::4]), or plot a sample of a large scatter dataset.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
38. More about Plot Components


    

        Stage V · Python for Researchers
        Planned
    


    

        

        

            
Small details make a plot easy to read

            

                A plot is built from parts: markers, lines, axes, a legend, text, colours, and often a
                colorbar. Each part has settings. Knowing them turns a default plot into a clear figure
                that you can put in a report or a paper.
            

        

    


    

        
 The parts of a plot


        
Every red label below is explained in one of the tabs further down. Click the picture to see it full size.


                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Code for this pictureThe red labels are only for teaching
                            
                        
                        

                            
 plot_anatomy.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = np.arange(0, 25, 2)
measured = 24 + 4 * np.sin((hours - 9) * np.pi / 12)
model = 24 + 3.5 * np.sin((hours - 8) * np.pi / 12)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.5), layout="constrained")

ax.plot(hours, model, "--", color="gray", label="Model")
points = ax.scatter(hours, measured, c=measured, cmap="coolwarm",
                    s=70, edgecolor="black", zorder=3, label="Measured")
cbar = fig.colorbar(points, ax=ax, label="Temperature (°C)")

ax.set_title("Air Temperature on 19 Oct 2026")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")
ax.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 25, 4))
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.annotate("Daily maximum", xy=(14, measured[7]), xytext=(17, 27.3),
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->"})

# ---- red labels that name each part (only for this teaching picture) ----
def callout(text, xy, xytext, coords="data"):
    ax.annotate(text, xy=xy, xycoords=coords, xytext=xytext, textcoords=coords,
                color="#c0392b", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold",
                bbox={"boxstyle": "round", "fc": "#fff3f1", "ec": "#c0392b"},
                arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "-|>", "color": "#c0392b"})

callout("Title", (0.64, 1.03), (0.80, 0.93), "axes fraction")
callout("Legend", (0.19, 0.93), (0.30, 0.82), "axes fraction")
callout("Marker", (hours[2], measured[2]), (5.5, 21.2))
callout("Line style", (6.4, 22.5), (1.0, 24.4))
callout("Text / annotation", (19, 27.2), (16.8, 25.9))
callout("Tick + tick label", (0.5, 0.0), (0.42, 0.12), "axes fraction")
callout("Axis label", (0.5, -0.1), (0.66, 0.08), "axes fraction")
callout("Grid", (21, 21.6), (19.3, 21.0))
ax.annotate("Colorbar", xy=(0, 0.15), xycoords=cbar.ax,    # point at the colorbar itself
            xytext=(0.98, -0.16), textcoords="axes fraction",
            color="#c0392b", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold",
            bbox={"boxstyle": "round", "fc": "#fff3f1", "ec": "#c0392b"},
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "-|>", "color": "#c0392b"})

plt.show()

                        

                    

    


    

        
 Customise each part


        

            Click a tab to open it. Each tab shows real pictures with the code that made them.
            The cheat sheet at the end of each tab lists the settings at a glance.
        


        

            
            
            
            
            
            
            
        


            

                

                    1
                    

                        
 Colorbar

                    

                

                
The colorbar translates colours back into numbers. This tab covers its colours, size, range, distance, position, and pointed ends.


                

                    
0 What is a colorbar?

                    

                        When colour stands for a number (height, temperature, depth), the reader
                        needs a key to turn the colour back into its number. That key is the colorbar.
                        It works like a legend, but for a continuous range of values. You create it with
                        fig.colorbar(mappable), where the mappable is what
                        imshow, contourf, pcolormesh, plot_surface,
                        or scatter(c=...) returned.
                    

                    

                        

                        
    
                            
  1. Colormap (cmap): the list of colours, from low to high. Here "viridis".
    2. 
                            
  2. Top value (vmax): the brightest colour means 30 °C or more.
    3. 
                            
  3. Bottom value (vmin): the darkest colour means 15 °C or less.
    4. 
                            
  4. Label with units: without it, readers cannot know what 25 means.
    5. 
                            
  5. Pointed ends (extend): some values are beyond the range and were painted with the end colour.
    6. 
                        

                    


                    

                        
                        

                            How to read it: pick a colour in the plot, find the same colour on the
                            bar, and read the number next to it. In the picture at the top of this lesson, the
                            darkest red marker matches the top of the colorbar, so it is about 28 °C.
                        

                    

                


                

                    
1 Colormap names cmap="viridis"

                    
The colormap is chosen by its name. Pick the family that matches your data:

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Sequential for values that only go one way (height, rainfall, concentration).
    • 
                        
  • Diverging for values above and below a meaningful centre (anomalies, differences, correlations).
    • 
                        
  • Cyclic when the end wraps round to the start: wind direction (0° = 360°), time of day, phase.
    • 
                        
  • Qualitative maps are for separate groups: use a legend, not a colorbar.
    • 
                        
  • Avoid jet and rainbow maps: their bright bands create edges that are not in the data, and many colour-blind readers cannot read them.
    • 
                        
  • Add _r to any name to reverse it: "Blues_r", "RdBu_r".
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Code that draws these stripsimshow of a 0 → 1 gradient
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colormap_names.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

groups = {
    "Sequential: low → high": ["viridis", "plasma", "cividis", "Blues", "YlOrRd"],
    "Diverging: below ↔ above a centre": ["RdBu_r", "coolwarm", "BrBG"],
    "Cyclic: angles, wind direction, time of day": ["twilight"],
    "Qualitative: separate groups (use a legend)": ["tab10"],
    "Avoid: rainbow": ["jet"],
}

gradient = np.linspace(0, 1, 256).reshape(1, -1)    # one row: 0 ... 1
rows = sum(len(names) + 1 for names in groups.values())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, 1, figsize=(8, rows * 0.42))
row = 0
for title, names in groups.items():
    axes[row].set_axis_off()
    axes[row].text(0, 0.2, title, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold",
                   transform=axes[row].transAxes)
    row += 1
    for name in names:
        axes[row].imshow(gradient, aspect="auto", cmap=name)
        axes[row].set_axis_off()
        axes[row].text(-0.01, 0.5, f'"{name}"', ha="right", va="center",
                       family="monospace", transform=axes[row].transAxes)
        row += 1

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.18, right=0.98, hspace=0.45)
plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Reverse a colormap and list all names_r and matplotlib.colormaps
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colormap_tips.py

                            
ax.imshow(data, cmap="Blues")      # light = low, dark = high
ax.imshow(data, cmap="Blues_r")    # _r reverses it: dark = low, light = high

# See every colormap name that Matplotlib knows
import matplotlib
print(sorted(matplotlib.colormaps))

                        

                    

                


                

                    
2 Size: length and thickness shrink · aspect

                    

                        shrink sets the length as a fraction of the plot height (1 = full height).
                        aspect sets the thickness: the bar is aspect times longer than
                        it is wide, so a bigger number gives a thinner bar (default 20).
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_size.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(0, 4, 60)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 20 + 8 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)    # values from about 12 to 28

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6), layout="constrained")

im0 = axes[0].imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
fig.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0])                   # default size
axes[0].set_title("default")

im1 = axes[1].imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
fig.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.6)       # 60% of the plot height
axes[1].set_title("shrink=0.6  (shorter)")

im2 = axes[2].imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
fig.colorbar(im2, ax=axes[2], aspect=40)        # length = 40 x width
axes[2].set_title("aspect=40  (thinner)")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Range: which values get which colour vmin · vmax · ticks · norm

                    

                        By default the colours stretch from the smallest to the largest value. Set
                        vmin and vmax to choose the range yourself, especially when several
                        plots must be compared. ticks= chooses which numbers appear on the bar.
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • (a) Automatic: fine for one plot on its own.
    • 
                        
  • (b) vmin=15, vmax=25: values outside this range get the end colours.
    • 
                        
  • (c) plt.get_cmap("viridis", 6): 6 clear steps are easier to read than a smooth gradient.
    • 
                        
  • (d) norm=LogNorm(vmin=1, vmax=1000): for skewed data like rainfall, where most values are small.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_range.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm

x = np.linspace(0, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(0, 4, 60)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 20 + 8 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)    # values from about 12 to 28

rain = 10 ** (3 * np.exp(-((X - 3)**2 + (Y - 2)**2)))    # 1 to 1000 mm: very skewed

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.4), layout="constrained")

im = axes[0].imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("(a) automatic: min to max")

im = axes[1].imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower", vmin=15, vmax=25)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], ticks=[15, 17.5, 20, 22.5, 25])
axes[1].set_title("(b) vmin=15, vmax=25, own ticks")

steps = plt.get_cmap("viridis", 6)              # only 6 colours
im = axes[2].imshow(Z, cmap=steps, origin="lower", vmin=12, vmax=28)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("(c) 6 discrete steps")

im = axes[3].imshow(rain, cmap="Blues", origin="lower", norm=LogNorm(vmin=1, vmax=1000))
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[3], label="Rain (mm)")
axes[3].set_title("(d) log scale: LogNorm")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
4 Distance from the plot pad

                    

                        pad is the gap between the plot and the colorbar, as a fraction of the plot size.
                        The default is 0.05 for a bar on the right. Increase it when the colorbar touches
                        tick labels; decrease it to save space.
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_pad.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(0, 4, 60)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 20 + 8 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)    # values from about 12 to 28

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))

for ax, pad in zip(axes, [0.0, 0.05, 0.2]):
    image = ax.imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, pad=pad)        # gap between plot and colorbar
    ax.set_title(f"pad={pad}" + ("  (default)" if pad == 0.05 else ""))

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
5 Position location="right" | "left" | "top" | "bottom"

                    

                        location puts the colorbar on any side and turns it horizontal for top and bottom.
                        Use the bottom for wide maps, and the right for tall plots.
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_location.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(0, 4, 60)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 20 + 8 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)    # values from about 12 to 28

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.8), layout="constrained")

for ax, place in zip(axes, ["right", "left", "top", "bottom"]):
    image = ax.imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, location=place, label="Value")
    ax.set_xlabel(f'location="{place}"', family="monospace", fontsize=11)

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        Two more positions are very common in research figures: one shared colorbar for
                        several panels (pass a list of axes to ax=), and a small colorbar inside the
                        plot (draw it in an inset_axes and pass it as cax=).
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_shared_inset.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(0, 4, 60)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 20 + 8 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)    # values from about 12 to 28

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4), layout="constrained")

# (a) + (b): one shared colorbar under both panels (same vmin and vmax!)
for ax, data, title in zip(axes[:2], [Z, Z + 3], ["(a) January", "(b) July"]):
    image = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis", origin="lower", vmin=12, vmax=31)
    ax.set_title(title)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes[:2], location="bottom", shrink=0.6, label="SST (°C)")

# (c): a small colorbar INSIDE the plot, in the lower-left corner
image = axes[2].imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
cax = axes[2].inset_axes([0.06, 0.86, 0.45, 0.06])   # x, y, width, height (0-1)
fig.colorbar(image, cax=cax, orientation="horizontal")
cax.tick_params(labelsize=8, colors="white")
axes[2].set_title("(c) small colorbar inside the plot")

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • A shared colorbar is only correct when all panels use the same vmin and vmax.
    • 
                            
  • inset_axes([x, y, width, height]) uses fractions of the plot: [0.06, 0.86, 0.45, 0.06] is top-left.
    • 
                            
  • cax= means "draw the colorbar in exactly this axes". It replaces ax=.
    • 
                        

                        

                    

                


                

                    
6 Arrows at the ends extend="neither" | "min" | "max" | "both"

                    

                        When your data go beyond vmin or vmax, those values are painted with the
                        end colour. A pointed end tells the reader that some values are further out
                        than the numbers on the bar.
                    

                    
                    

                        

                            
SettingArrowUse when

                            
                                
"neither"none (default)all data are inside vmin–vmax

                                
"min"bottom (or left)some values are below vmin

                                
"max"top (or right)some values are above vmax

                                
"both"both endsvalues on both sides are cut off

                            
                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_extend.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 6, 80)
y = np.linspace(0, 4, 60)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = 20 + 8 * np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)    # values from about 12 to 28

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.4), layout="constrained")

for ax, ext in zip(axes, ["neither", "min", "max", "both"]):
    # Data go from 12 to 28, but the colour range is only 15 to 25
    image = ax.imshow(Z, cmap="viridis", origin="lower", vmin=15, vmax=25)
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, extend=ext)
    ax.set_title(f'extend="{ext}"', family="monospace")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Give out-of-range values their own colourset_over and set_under
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_over_under.py

                            
cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
cmap.set_over("red")      # colour for values ABOVE vmax
cmap.set_under("white")   # colour for values BELOW vmin

image = ax.imshow(data, cmap=cmap, vmin=15, vmax=25)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, extend="both")

                        

                    

                


                

                    
7 Label and numbers set_label · tick_params

                    
Always give the colorbar a label with units, and make its numbers as large as the other tick labels.

                    

                        
                            
                            Label, tick size, tick positions, and number formatcbar.set_label, cbar.ax.tick_params
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_text.py

                            
cbar = fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax)

cbar.set_label("Sea-surface temperature (°C)", fontsize=12, labelpad=10)
cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=10)               # size of the numbers
cbar.set_ticks([15, 20, 25, 30])                # which numbers to show
cbar.ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.0f} °C") # 15 -> "15 °C" (vertical bar)

                        

                    

                


                

                    
8 Three colorbar rules, shown in one figure

                    
                    
    
                        
  1. Same range when you compare panels. (a) and (b) both use vmin=15, vmax=30 and share one colorbar. With separate automatic ranges, January and July could look equally warm, even though July is 5 °C warmer.
    2. 
                        
  2. Centre a diverging colormap on zero. In (c), vmin=-limit, vmax=limit makes white mean "no difference". Blue is cooler than average, red is warmer.
    3. 
                        
  3. Always label it with units. A colorbar without a label is a decoration, not information.
    4. 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Code for the three panelsShared colorbar for (a) and (b), diverging colorbar for (c)
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_rules.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(118, 124, 60)
y = np.linspace(20, 27, 70)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

january = 24 - 0.9 * (Y - 20) + 0.5 * np.sin(X * 1.5)
july = january + 5
anomaly = july - july.mean()        # difference from the average

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))

# (a) and (b): SAME vmin and vmax, so one colour = one temperature
for ax, data, title in zip(axes[:2], [january, july], ["(a) January", "(b) July"]):
    image = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis", origin="lower",
                      extent=[118, 124, 20, 27], vmin=15, vmax=30)
    ax.set_title(title)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes[:2], label="SST (°C)", shrink=0.9)

# (c): values above AND below zero -> diverging colormap centred on 0
limit = np.abs(anomaly).max()
image_c = axes[2].imshow(anomaly, cmap="RdBu_r", origin="lower",
                         extent=[118, 124, 20, 27], vmin=-limit, vmax=limit)
axes[2].set_title("(c) Anomaly")
fig.colorbar(image_c, ax=axes[2], label="Difference (°C)", extend="both")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
 Cheat sheet

                    

                        

                            
Write thisWhat it does

                            
                            
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax)Add a colorbar for image next to ax

                            
cmap="viridis"Colormap name (inside imshow, contourf, scatter…)

                            
vmin=15, vmax=25Colour range (inside imshow, contourf, scatter…)

                            
shrink=0.7Length: 70% of the plot

                            
aspect=30Thickness: bigger = thinner

                            
pad=0.1Gap between plot and bar

                            
location="bottom"Side: right, left, top, bottom

                            
orientation="horizontal"Horizontal bar (when using cax=)

                            
extend="both"Pointed ends for out-of-range values

                            
ticks=[15, 20, 25]Numbers shown on the bar

                            
label="SST (°C)"Label with units

                            
ax=[ax1, ax2]One colorbar shared by several panels

                            
cax=small_axesDraw the bar inside a given axes

                            
                        

                    

                


            


            

                

                    2
                    

                        
 Markers and lines

                    

                

                
Markers show the measured points and lines show how they connect. Their shape, size, colour, and style tell the reader what kind of data they see.


                

                    
1 Marker shapes marker="o"

                    
A marker shows each measured point. Choose the shape with one character:

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Use different shapes as well as different colours for different groups, so the plot still works in black and white.
    • 
                        
  • "+", "x", and "|" are lines only: they have no fill colour.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 marker_shapes.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

markers = ["o", "s", "^", "v", "D", "p", "h", "*", "+", "x", ".", "|"]
names = ["circle", "square", "triangle up", "triangle down", "diamond", "pentagon",
         "hexagon", "star", "plus", "x", "point", "vertical line"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.4))

for i, (marker, name) in enumerate(zip(markers, names)):
    col, row = i % 6, i // 6
    ax.plot(col, -row, marker=marker, markersize=18,
            color="#3776ab", markeredgecolor="#112d3a")
    ax.text(col, -row - 0.32, f'"{marker}"\n{name}', ha="center", va="top",
            family="monospace", fontsize=9)

ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 5.6)
ax.set_ylim(-1.9, 0.5)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
2 Marker size, fill, and edge markersize · markerfacecolor · markeredgecolor

                    
Every marker has a size, an inside (face) colour, and an edge colour:

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Hollow markers (markerfacecolor="white" or "none") let overlapping points stay visible.
    • 
                        
  • markevery=4 keeps a long line readable: it draws a marker on every 4th point only.
    • 
                        
  • Short names also work: ms = markersize, mfc = face colour, mec = edge colour, mew = edge width.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 marker_options.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.arange(0, 10.5, 0.5)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5), layout="constrained")

ax.plot(x, np.full_like(x, 5), marker="o", markersize=4)
ax.plot(x, np.full_like(x, 4), marker="o", markersize=10)
ax.plot(x, np.full_like(x, 3), marker="o", markersize=10,
        markerfacecolor="white", markeredgewidth=2)
ax.plot(x, np.full_like(x, 2), marker="s", markersize=9,
        markerfacecolor="gold", markeredgecolor="black")
ax.plot(x, np.full_like(x, 1), marker="D", markersize=8, markevery=4)
ax.plot(x, np.full_like(x, 0), marker="o", markersize=10, linestyle="none")

labels = ["markersize=4", "markersize=10", 'markerfacecolor="white"  (hollow)',
          'face "gold", edge "black"', "markevery=4  (every 4th point)",
          'linestyle="none"  (markers only)']
for y, text in zip([5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0], labels):
    ax.text(10.8, y, text, va="center", family="monospace", fontsize=10)

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 18)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 5.7)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Line styles and the format string linestyle · linewidth · "o--"

                    

                        plot() accepts a short format string that combines a marker and a line
                        style: "o-" is circles joined by a solid line, "s--" is squares with a dashed line.
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Use solid lines for measurements and dashed lines for models or predictions. Readers expect this.
    • 
                        
  • linewidth (or lw): 1.5–2 for the main line, 1 for background lines.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 line_styles.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 11)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.2), layout="constrained")

ax.plot(x, x * 0 + 5, "-", linewidth=2)          # solid
ax.plot(x, x * 0 + 4, "--", linewidth=2)         # dashed
ax.plot(x, x * 0 + 3, ":", linewidth=2)          # dotted
ax.plot(x, x * 0 + 2, "-.", linewidth=2)         # dash-dot
ax.plot(x, x * 0 + 1, "o-", linewidth=1)         # circles joined by a line
ax.plot(x, x * 0 + 0, "s--", linewidth=3)        # squares + thick dashed line

labels = ['"-"  solid', '"--"  dashed', '":"  dotted', '"-."  dash-dot',
          '"o-"  marker + line', '"s--", linewidth=3']
for y, text in zip([5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0], labels):
    ax.text(10.6, y, text, va="center", family="monospace", fontsize=11)

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 16)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 5.7)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
4 plot() vs scatter(): two kinds of size markersize vs s

                    

                        This confuses almost everyone once. In plot(), markersize is the
                        diameter. In scatter(), s is the area.
                        So s=100 looks about the same as markersize=10.
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Same size in plot() and scatter()markersize = diameter, s = area
                            
                        
                        

                            
 marker_sizes.py

                            
# plot(): markersize is the DIAMETER in points
ax.plot(x, y, "o", markersize=10)

# scatter(): s is the AREA in points²
ax.scatter(x, y, s=100)            # about the same size as markersize=10

# scatter can give every point its own size and colour
ax.scatter(x, y, s=sizes, c=values, cmap="viridis",
           marker="^", edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.5)

                        

                    

                


                

                    
 Cheat sheet

                    

                        

                            
Write thisWhat it does

                            
                            
marker="o"Marker shape

                            
markersize=8  (ms)Diameter in plot()

                            
s=64Area in scatter()

                            
markerfacecolor="white"  (mfc)Inside colour: white or "none" for hollow

                            
markeredgecolor="black"  (mec)Edge colour

                            
markeredgewidth=1.5  (mew)Edge thickness

                            
markevery=5Marker on every 5th point

                            
linestyle="--"  (ls)"-", "--", ":", "-.", or "none"

                            
linewidth=2  (lw)Line thickness

                            
"o--"Format string: marker + line style

                            
                        

                    

                


            


            

                

                    3
                    

                        
 Legend

                    

                

                
The legend names each line or group. A good legend is close to the data and never covers it.


                

                    
1 Make a legend label="..." + ax.legend()

                    

                        Give every line a label= when you draw it, then call ax.legend() once.
                        Lines without a label (or with a label that starts with _) are left out.
                    

                


                

                    
2 Position loc · bbox_to_anchor · ncol

                    

                        loc chooses the corner: "best", "upper right",
                        "upper left", "lower left", "lower right", "center",
                        and more. To put the legend outside the plot, combine loc with
                        bbox_to_anchor: loc says which corner of the legend is pinned, and
                        bbox_to_anchor says where to pin it (in plot fractions).
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • (a) loc="best" finds the emptiest corner. Good for quick work.
    • 
                        
  • (b) loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1): the legend's upper-left corner is pinned just right of the plot.
    • 
                        
  • (c) loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.12), ncol=3: centred below, in 3 columns.
    • 
                        
  • Use layout="constrained" (or bbox_inches="tight" when saving) so an outside legend is not cut off.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_positions.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.2), layout="constrained")

for ax in axes:
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="Station A")
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x) * 0.7 + 0.3, label="Station B")
    ax.plot(x, np.cos(x) * 0.5, label="Station C")

axes[0].legend(loc="best")
axes[0].set_title('(a) loc="best": inside, least overlap')

axes[1].legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1))
axes[1].set_title("(b) outside, to the right")

axes[2].legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.12), ncol=3)
axes[2].set_title("(c) below the plot, ncol=3")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Style title · frameon · fontsize · markerscale

                    
A legend can have a title, no frame, its own font size, and bigger symbols than the plot.

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_style.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2), layout="constrained")

# (a) A styled legend
axes[0].plot(x, np.sin(x), label="Measured")
axes[0].plot(x, np.sin(x - 0.3), "--", label="Model run 1")
axes[0].plot(x, np.sin(x + 0.3), ":", label="_nolegend_")     # hidden from legend
axes[0].legend(title="Data source", frameon=False, fontsize=11,
               loc="lower left", title_fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_title("(a) title, no frame, one line hidden")

# (b) Tiny scatter points: make their legend symbols bigger
for name, shift in [("Site 1", 0), ("Site 2", 2)]:
    axes[1].scatter(rng.normal(shift, 1, 300), rng.normal(0, 1, 300),
                    s=4, alpha=0.5, label=name)
axes[1].legend(markerscale=4, loc="upper left")
axes[1].set_title("(b) markerscale=4 for small points")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
4 Show and hide the legend legend() · remove() · set_visible()

                    

                        A legend appears only when you call ax.legend(). You can remove it completely,
                        hide it and show it again, or leave out just one line:
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_show_hide.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4), layout="constrained")

for ax in axes:
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="Station A")
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x + 1), label="Station B")
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x + 2), label="Station C")

# (a) SHOW: call legend()
axes[0].legend(loc="lower left")
axes[0].set_title("(a) shown: ax.legend()")

# (b) HIDE: make the legend, then remove it
axes[1].legend(loc="lower left")
axes[1].get_legend().remove()
axes[1].set_title("(b) hidden: ax.get_legend().remove()")

# (c) HIDE ONE ENTRY: give that line a label starting with "_"
axes[2].lines[1].set_label("_hidden")
axes[2].legend(loc="lower left")
axes[2].set_title('(c) one entry hidden: label="_hidden"')

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            All the ways to show or hide a legendremove(), set_visible(), _nolegend_, legend=False
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_hide_ways.py

                            
ax.plot(x, y1, label="Station A")     # only lines WITH a label appear

# 1. Show the legend
ax.legend()

# 2. Hide it again (it is removed from the plot)
ax.get_legend().remove()

# 3. Hide it but keep it, so you can show it later
legend = ax.legend()
legend.set_visible(False)     # disappear
legend.set_visible(True)      # appear again

# 4. Leave one line out of the legend
ax.plot(x, y2, label="_nolegend_")    # any label that starts with _

# 5. pandas and seaborn draw a legend automatically: switch it off
df.plot(x="day", y=["temp", "rain"], legend=False)
sns.lineplot(data=df, x="day", y="temp", hue="station", legend=False)

                        

                    

                    

                        Interactive version: in a normal Python window, clicking a name in the legend can
                        hide or show its line, and a key can make the whole legend disappear and come back. This is
                        very handy when many lines overlap.
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Click a legend entry to hide its line, press T to hide the legendpick_event and key_press_event
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_interactive.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

lines = []
for name, shift in zip(["A", "B", "C"], [0, 1, 2]):
    line, = ax.plot(x, np.sin(x + shift), label=f"Station {name}")
    lines.append(line)

legend = ax.legend(loc="upper right", title="Click a name")

# Link every legend symbol and name to its line in the plot
link = {}
for symbol, text, line in zip(legend.get_lines(), legend.get_texts(), lines):
    symbol.set_picker(5)      # clickable (5 points tolerance)
    text.set_picker(True)
    link[symbol] = line
    link[text] = line


def on_click_legend(event):
    """Clicking a legend entry hides or shows its line."""
    line = link[event.artist]
    line.set_visible(not line.get_visible())
    for item, target in link.items():           # fade the hidden entry
        if target is line:
            item.set_alpha(1.0 if line.get_visible() else 0.25)
    fig.canvas.draw_idle()


def on_key(event):
    """Pressing T makes the whole legend disappear or appear."""
    if event.key == "t":
        legend.set_visible(not legend.get_visible())
        fig.canvas.draw_idle()


fig.canvas.mpl_connect("pick_event", on_click_legend)
fig.canvas.mpl_connect("key_press_event", on_key)
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • set_picker(5) makes the legend symbol clickable. Matplotlib then sends a pick_event.
    • 
                            
  • link remembers which plot line belongs to each legend entry.
    • 
                            
  • set_visible(not ...) switches between shown and hidden. The faded entry shows which lines are off.
    • 
                            
  • It needs an interactive window: run it as a .py file, or use %matplotlib widget in Jupyter. A saved PNG cannot be clicked.
    • 
                        

                        

                    

                    
    
                        
  • remove() deletes the legend. Call ax.legend() again to bring it back.
    • 
                        
  • set_visible(False) keeps the legend object, so set_visible(True) shows exactly the same legend again.
    • 
                    

                


                

                    
5 One legend for two axes or for the whole figure

                    

                        With twinx(), each y-axis has its own legend. Collect the lines and build one legend.
                        For several panels with the same lines, use one fig.legend() instead of repeating it.
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Combine the legends of two y-axesline1 + line2
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_twin_axes.py

                            
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()
line1 = ax1.plot(months, temp, color="tab:red", label="Temperature")
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
line2 = ax2.plot(months, rain, color="tab:blue", label="Rainfall")

# Each axes has its own legend. Combine them into ONE legend:
lines = line1 + line2
ax1.legend(lines, [line.get_label() for line in lines], loc="upper left")

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            One legend for the whole figurefig.legend(loc="outside right upper")
                            
                        
                        

                            
 legend_figure.py

                            
# One legend for the whole figure, outside on the right
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, layout="constrained")
axes[0].plot(x, y1, label="Model")
axes[1].plot(x, y2, label="Model")
fig.legend(*axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="outside right upper")

Write thisWhat it does

loc="upper left"Which corner
