                    4
                    

                        
 Axes and ticks

                    

                

                
The axes give every point its meaning: labels, units, range, ticks, and scale.


                

                    
1 From default to clean axes

                    

                        The default axes have no labels, no units, and empty space at the ends. Ten seconds of
                        work makes a big difference:
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • set_xlabel / set_ylabel: always with units in brackets.
    • 
                        
  • set_xlim / set_ylim: choose the visible range.
    • 
                        
  • set_xticks(range(0, 25, 3)): a tick every 3 hours. minorticks_on() adds small ticks.
    • 
                        
  • grid(alpha=0.3): a light grid helps reading values without shouting.
    • 
                        
  • spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False): removes the frame lines you do not need.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axes_clean_up.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = np.arange(0, 24.5, 0.5)
temp = 24 + 4 * np.sin((hours - 9) * np.pi / 12)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2), layout="constrained")

# (a) Default: no labels, no units, automatic everything
ax1.plot(hours, temp)
ax1.set_title("(a) Default")

# (b) Cleaned-up axes
ax2.plot(hours, temp)
ax2.set_title("(b) Cleaned up")
ax2.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")
ax2.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax2.set_xlim(0, 24)                       # no empty space at the ends
ax2.set_ylim(18, 30)
ax2.set_xticks(range(0, 25, 3))           # a tick every 3 hours
ax2.minorticks_on()                       # small ticks in between
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)                       # light grid
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)    # remove the box top and right
ax2.tick_params(labelsize=10)

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
2 Scale, direction, and a second y-axis set_yscale · invert_yaxis · twinx

                    
Four axis tricks you will use again and again:

                    
                    
    
                        
  • (a) → (b) Log scale turns fast growth into a straight line and shows the small values too.
    • 
                        
  • (c) Inverted axis for depth or pressure, which grow downward.
    • 
                        
  • (d) Second y-axis for two quantities with different units. Colour each label like its data, so readers know which axis belongs to which.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axes_scales.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7.5), layout="constrained")

# (a) and (b): the same fast-growing numbers on a linear and a log axis
hours = np.arange(0, 11)
bacteria = 100 * 2 ** hours
for ax, scale in zip(axes[0], ["linear", "log"]):
    ax.plot(hours, bacteria, "o-")
    ax.set_yscale(scale)
    ax.set_title(f'({"a" if scale == "linear" else "b"}) set_yscale("{scale}")')
    ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Number of bacteria")

# (c) Depth goes down: invert the y-axis
depth = np.array([0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400])
temp = np.array([28, 27.8, 26, 22, 17, 12, 8])
axes[1, 0].plot(temp, depth, "o-")
axes[1, 0].invert_yaxis()
axes[1, 0].set_title("(c) invert_yaxis() for depth")
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Depth (m)")

# (d) Two different units: a second y-axis
months = np.arange(1, 13)
temp_m = 24 + 5 * np.sin((months - 4) * np.pi / 6)
rain_m = 120 + 100 * np.sin((months - 3) * np.pi / 6)
ax_left = axes[1, 1]
ax_left.plot(months, temp_m, color="tab:red", marker="o")
ax_left.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)", color="tab:red")
ax_right = ax_left.twinx()                 # shares x, new y on the right
ax_right.bar(months, rain_m, color="tab:blue", alpha=0.3)
ax_right.set_ylabel("Rainfall (mm)", color="tab:blue")
ax_left.set_title("(d) twinx(): two y-axes")
ax_left.set_xlabel("Month")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Dates and percentages on the axes mdates · PercentFormatter

                    

                        Tick labels can be formatted: month names instead of crowded dates, or 75%
                        instead of 0.75.
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axes_dates_percent.py

                            
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter

dates = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", "2026-12-31", freq="D")
temp = 24 + 5 * np.sin((dates.dayofyear - 110) * 2 * np.pi / 365)
humidity = 0.75 + 0.1 * np.sin(dates.dayofyear * 2 * np.pi / 365)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4), layout="constrained")

ax1.plot(dates, temp)
ax1.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(interval=2))    # every 2 months
ax1.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b"))       # Jan, Mar, ...
ax1.set_title("(a) Dates: one label every 2 months")
ax1.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")

ax2.plot(dates, humidity)
ax2.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1, decimals=0))   # 0.75 -> 75%
ax2.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b"))
ax2.set_title("(b) Percent labels on the y-axis")
ax2.set_ylabel("Relative humidity")

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • MonthLocator(interval=2) decides where ticks go. DateFormatter("%b") decides how they look.
    • 
                            
  • Other formats: "%Y-%m-%d" → 2026-10-20, "%d %b" → 20 Oct, "%H:%M" → 14:30.
    • 
                        

                        

                    

                


                

                    
4 Turn the axis off, or only parts of it axis("off") · set_xticks([]) · spines

                    

                        Images, maps, diagrams, and empty panels often look better without axes. You can switch
                        off everything at once, or only the parts you do not need:
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • (b) ax.axis("off"): frame, ticks, numbers, and labels all disappear. The title stays.
    • 
                        
  • (c) set_xticks([]) and set_yticks([]): no numbers, but a frame. Common for photos and microscope images.
    • 
                        
  • (d) Hide frame lines with spines and a whole axis with yaxis.set_visible(False).
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axis_off.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.4), layout="constrained")
for ax in axes:
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x))

axes[0].set_title("(a) normal")

axes[1].axis("off")                    # frame, ticks, numbers: all off
axes[1].set_title('(b) ax.axis("off")')

axes[2].set_xticks([])                 # no ticks or numbers ...
axes[2].set_yticks([])                 # ... but the frame stays
axes[2].set_title("(c) set_xticks([]), set_yticks([])")

axes[3].spines[["left", "top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
axes[3].yaxis.set_visible(False)       # hide the whole y-axis
axes[3].set_title("(d) only the x-axis left")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            More ways to hide parts of the axestick marks only, numbers only, frame only, empty panels
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axis_off_more.py

                            
ax.axis("off")                      # everything off
ax.axis("on")                       # and back on

ax.set_xticks([])                   # no x ticks and numbers (frame stays)
ax.tick_params(labelbottom=False)   # keep the tick marks, hide only the numbers
ax.tick_params(bottom=False)        # keep the numbers, hide only the tick marks
ax.xaxis.set_visible(False)         # the whole x-axis off
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False) # one frame line off
ax.set_frame_on(False)              # the whole frame off, ticks stay

# A 2 x 3 figure with only 5 plots: switch off the empty panel
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3)
axes[1, 2].axis("off")

                        

                    

                


                

                    
5 Axis labels and tick numbers: size, distance, and colour fontsize · labelpad · tick_params

                    

                        The label ("Time (hour)") and the tick numbers (0, 5, 10 …) are
                        set separately. The label is changed in set_xlabel(); the numbers and tick marks
                        in tick_params().
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • fontsize=14 in set_xlabel: size of the label. labelpad=10: gap between label and numbers.
    • 
                        
  • tick_params(labelsize=12): size of the numbers. length and width: size of the tick marks.
    • 
                        
  • direction="in" points ticks into the plot, as many journals prefer.
    • 
                        
  • tick_params(axis="y", colors="tab:red") colours the y numbers and ticks. Use only labelcolor= to colour just the numbers.
    • 
                        
  • For papers: labels about 10–12 pt and numbers 8–10 pt at the final printed size.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axis_label_sizes.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = np.arange(0, 24.5, 0.5)
temp = 24 + 4 * np.sin((hours - 9) * np.pi / 12)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4), layout="constrained")

# (a) Default sizes
ax1.plot(hours, temp, color="tab:red")
ax1.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")
ax1.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax1.set_title("(a) default")

# (b) Bigger labels, bigger numbers, longer ticks, a little more space
ax2.plot(hours, temp, color="tab:red")
ax2.set_xlabel("Time (hour)", fontsize=14, labelpad=10)     # labelpad: gap to the numbers
ax2.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="tab:red")
ax2.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=12,     # size of the numbers
                length=7, width=1.5,           # tick mark length and thickness
                direction="in")                # ticks point into the plot
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", colors="tab:red")    # y ticks and numbers in red
ax2.set_title("(b) fontsize=14, labelpad=10, labelsize=12", fontsize=13)

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            More label optionsword sizes, rotation, label on top, minor ticks
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axis_label_options.py

                            
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)", fontsize=14)           # size in points
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)", fontsize="large")      # or: small, medium, large, x-large
ax.set_ylabel("Depth (m)", labelpad=12)             # distance from the numbers
ax.set_ylabel("Depth (m)", rotation=0, ha="right")  # horizontal y label
ax.xaxis.set_label_position("top")                  # x label above the plot
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=12, rotation=45) # number size and angle
ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=3)             # the small ticks

                        

                    

                


                

                    
6 Tilt the tick labels by 45° labelrotation=45 · ha="right"

                    

                        Long names or dates on the x-axis run into each other. Tilting them by 45° fixes this.
                        But a plain rotation turns each label around its centre, so the labels
                        look shifted to the left of their bars. Add ha="right" and
                        rotation_mode="anchor" so the end of each label sits exactly
                        under its tick.
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • (b) tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45): quick, fine for short labels.
    • 
                        
  • (c) plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor"): the clean version for long labels.
    • 
                        
  • ha = horizontal alignment: which end of the text is fixed to the tick.
    • 
                        
  • Use 90° for very many labels, and fig.autofmt_xdate() for dates.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 tick_rotation.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

stations = ["Taipei Main", "Taichung Airport", "Tainan Harbour",
            "Kaohsiung Port", "Hualien Coast", "Taitung Mountain"]
rain = [210, 160, 120, 140, 230, 190]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.8), layout="constrained", sharey=True)
for ax in axes:
    ax.bar(stations, rain, color="#3776ab")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Rainfall (mm)")

# (a) No rotation: long names run into each other
axes[0].set_title("(a) no rotation: labels overlap")

# (b) Rotated 45°, but each label turns around its CENTRE
axes[1].tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45)
axes[1].set_title("(b) labelrotation=45: looks shifted")

# (c) Rotated 45°, and the END of each label sits under its bar
plt.setp(axes[2].get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")
axes[2].set_title('(c) 45°, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor"')

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            All the ways to rotate tick labelstick_params, setp, set_xticks, autofmt_xdate, barh
                            
                        
                        

                            
 tick_rotation_ways.py

                            
# 1. Any axis, any angle
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelrotation=90)

# 2. Best look at 45°: the END of each label sits under its tick
plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")

# 3. When you set the ticks yourself, rotate in the same line
ax.set_xticks(range(len(names)), names, rotation=45, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")

# 4. Dates: Matplotlib tilts and aligns them for you
fig.autofmt_xdate()                 # 30° by default
fig.autofmt_xdate(rotation=45)      # or choose the angle

# 5. Very long names: horizontal bars need no tilting at all
ax.barh(names, values)

                        

                    

                


                

                    
7 More axis settings

                    

                        
                            
                            Equal aspect, rotated ticks, own tick labels, shared axesset_aspect, tick_params, sharex
                            
                        
                        

                            
 axes_more.py

                            
ax.set_aspect("equal")                  # 1 unit in x = 1 unit in y (maps, circles)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)   # rotate crowded tick labels
ax.set_xticks([0, 6, 12, 18, 24], ["0h", "6h", "12h", "18h", "24h"])  # own labels
ax.set_xlim(right=24)                   # change only one end

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)   # panels share one x-axis

                        

                    

                


                

                    
 Cheat sheet

                    

                        

                            
Write thisWhat it does

                            
                            
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")Axis label with units

                            
ax.set_xlim(0, 24)Visible range

                            
ax.set_xticks([0, 6, 12])Tick positions (and optional labels)

                            
ax.minorticks_on()Small ticks between the big ones

                            
ax.tick_params(labelsize=10, rotation=45)Tick label size and angle

                            
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)Light grid

                            
ax.set_yscale("log")Logarithmic axis

                            
ax.invert_yaxis()Values grow downward (depth)

                            
ax2 = ax.twinx()Second y-axis on the right

                            
ax.set_aspect("equal")Same scale on x and y

                            
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)Remove frame lines

                            
ax.axis("off")Switch the whole axis off

                            
ax.set_xticks([])No x ticks and numbers

                            
ax.set_xlabel("...", fontsize=14, labelpad=10)Label size and its distance

                            
ax.tick_params(labelsize=12, length=6, direction="in")Number size, tick length, tick direction

                            
plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")Tilt x labels 45°, ends under the ticks

                            
                        

                    

                


            


            

                

                    5
                    

                        
 Text and annotations

                    

                

                
Titles, labels, notes, arrows, and math text: how to put words exactly where the reader needs them.


                

                    
1 Titles, labels, notes, and arrows set_title · text · annotate

                    

                        Text turns a plot into a message. Use it to name things, point at the important part,
                        and give context.
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • annotate(text, xy=point, xytext=place): an arrow from the text to a data point.
    • 
                        
  • ax.text(x, y, text) uses data coordinates. Add transform=ax.transAxes to use plot fractions (0–1), so the text stays in the corner even when the data change.
    • 
                        
  • bbox={...} puts a box behind the text.
    • 
                        
  • Math text goes between dollar signs: r"$T_{max}$", r"$\Delta T$", r"m$^2$". The r before the string keeps the backslashes.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 text_annotate.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = np.arange(0, 24.5, 0.5)
temp = 24 + 4 * np.sin((hours - 9) * np.pi / 12)
peak = np.argmax(temp)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(hours, temp, color="tab:red")

ax.set_title("Air Temperature", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Temperature, $T$ (°C)")             # math text between $ $

# 1. Arrow pointing at one point
ax.annotate(f"Maximum: {temp[peak]:.1f} °C",
            xy=(hours[peak], temp[peak]),            # point the arrow at this
            xytext=(hours[peak] + 3, temp[peak] - 1.5),    # put the text here
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": "black"})

# 2. A reference line with its own label
ax.axhline(25, color="gray", linestyle="--")
ax.text(0.3, 25.15, "Comfort limit 25 °C", color="gray")

# 3. A text box in the corner, placed by axes fraction (0-1)
ax.text(0.02, 0.95, "Station: Tainan\nData: hourly", va="top",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10,
        bbox={"boxstyle": "round", "facecolor": "white", "edgecolor": "lightgray"})

# 4. Math and Greek letters
ax.text(15, 21, r"$\Delta T = T_{max} - T_{min} = 8$ °C", fontsize=12)

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
2 Put a picture inside the plot inset_axes · OffsetImage · AnnotationBbox

                    

                        Besides text, you can place pictures in a plot: a photo of the site or instrument,
                        an icon that marks an event, or a logo. Read the picture with plt.imread(),
                        then choose one of two ways to place it:
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • 1. Picture in a corner: ax.inset_axes([x, y, width, height]) makes a small axes inside the plot (fractions 0–1). Show the picture there with imshow and hide its ticks with axis("off").
    • 
                        
  • 2. Icon at a data point: wrap the picture in OffsetImage(picture, zoom=0.3), then AnnotationBbox places it at xybox with an arrow to xy, just like annotate does for text.
    • 
                        
  • zoom sets the icon size. A PNG with a transparent background looks best for icons.
    • 
                        
  • Try it yourself with the two example pictures: station.png and sun.png. Save them next to your script.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 image_inside_plot.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.offsetbox import OffsetImage, AnnotationBbox

hours = np.arange(0, 24.5, 0.5)
temp = 24 + 4 * np.sin((hours - 9) * np.pi / 12)

# Read your pictures: any .png or .jpg file next to your script
station_photo = plt.imread("station.png")
sun_icon = plt.imread("sun.png")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(hours, temp, color="tab:red", linewidth=2)
ax.set_title("Air Temperature at Tainan Station")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)")
ax.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylim(19.5, 29)

# 1. A picture in a corner: a small axes INSIDE the plot
corner = ax.inset_axes([0.02, 0.52, 0.25, 0.45])    # x, y, width, height (0-1 of the plot)
corner.imshow(station_photo)
corner.axis("off")                                  # no ticks around the picture
corner.set_title("The station", fontsize=9)

# 2. An icon at a data point, with an arrow pointing to it
peak = np.argmax(temp)
icon = OffsetImage(sun_icon, zoom=0.3)              # zoom: size of the icon
sun_box = AnnotationBbox(icon,
                         xy=(hours[peak], temp[peak]),     # the data point
                         xybox=(20.5, 28.0),               # where the icon sits
                         frameon=False,
                         arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->"})
ax.add_artist(sun_box)
ax.text(20.5, 26.9, "hottest hour", ha="center", fontsize=10)

plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • plt.imread("station.png") reads the picture as an array of pixel colours.
    • 
                            
  • The inset is a normal axes: you can give it a title, a frame, or even a small plot of its own.
    • 
                            
  • ax.add_artist(sun_box) adds the icon to the plot. Without it, nothing appears.
    • 
                        

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            More ways: map under the data, logo on the figure, transparencyimshow(extent=...), fig.figimage, alpha
                            
                        
                        

                            
 image_more_ways.py

                            
picture = plt.imread("map.png")        # .png or .jpg

# 3. A picture stretched over a DATA area, e.g. a map under your points
ax.imshow(picture, extent=[118, 124, 20, 27], zorder=0)   # x0, x1, y0, y1
ax.plot(lon, lat, "ro", zorder=1)                         # data drawn on top
ax.set_aspect("auto")                                     # let the axes keep their shape

# 4. A logo on the whole FIGURE, in pixels from the bottom-left corner
fig.figimage(logo, xo=10, yo=10, alpha=0.6, zorder=10)

# 5. A half-transparent picture, so the data behind it stay visible
corner = ax.inset_axes([0.7, 0.6, 0.28, 0.38])
corner.imshow(picture, alpha=0.7)
corner.axis("off")

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Panel labels, figure title, and units with superscripts suptitle · transAxes

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Journals ask for panel labels (a), (b), (c). Put them just above the top-left corner: ax.text(0, 1.03, "(a)", transform=ax.transAxes).
    • 
                        
  • fig.suptitle() is one title above all panels. ax.set_title() is per panel.
    • 
                        
  • Units with powers: "W m$^{-2}$" → W m⁻², "km$^2$" → km².
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 text_panels.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 11})    # base size for ALL text in the figure

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6), layout="constrained")

for ax, letter, func in zip(axes, "abc", [np.sin, np.cos, np.tanh]):
    ax.plot(x, func(x - 5))
    ax.text(0.0, 1.03, f"({letter})", transform=ax.transAxes,   # just above the top-left corner
            fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", va="bottom")
    ax.set_xlabel("x (m)")

axes[0].set_ylabel(r"Heat flux (W m$^{-2}$)")     # superscript: m⁻²
fig.suptitle("Panel labels (a), (b), (c) and one title for the whole figure",
             fontsize=13)

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
4 Mathematical text r"$...$"

                    

                        Matplotlib understands maths written like LaTeX. Put it between dollar signs
                        inside a raw string r"...", in any title, label, legend, or text.
                        You do not need to install LaTeX.
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • ^ raises and _ lowers. Use braces for more than one character: $x^{10}$, $T_{max}$.
    • 
                        
  • Greek letters: a backslash and the name, \alpha, \Delta (capital first letter = capital Greek).
    • 
                        
  • Only the part between $ $ is maths: r"m$^2$" keeps the m upright and raises the 2.
    • 
                        
  • Use \mathrm{...} for units and words inside maths, so they are not italic.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Code that draws this tableIt prints the code and the result side by side
                            
                        
                        

                            
 math_text_table.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

examples = [
    ("Superscript", r"m$^2$, s$^{-1}$, $x^{10}$"),
    ("Subscript", r"$T_{max}$, CO$_2$, $x_i$"),
    ("Greek letters", r"$\alpha, \beta, \lambda, \mu, \sigma, \Delta, \Omega$"),
    ("Fraction", r"$\frac{dT}{dt}$, $\frac{1}{2}$"),
    ("Square root", r"$\sqrt{x}$, $\sqrt[3]{8}$"),
    ("Symbols", r"$\pm$, $\times$, $\approx$, $\leq$, $\infty$, $^\circ$C"),
    ("Sum, integral", r"$\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$, $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$"),
    ("Accents", r"$\bar{x}$, $\hat{y}$, $\vec{v}$, $\dot{x}$"),
    ("Upright units", r"$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $T_{\mathrm{surface}}$"),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 7.5))
ax.axis("off")

ax.text(0.0, 1.06, "What", fontsize=11, color="gray")
ax.text(0.14, 1.06, "What you type", fontsize=11, color="gray")
ax.text(0.66, 1.06, "What you see", fontsize=11, color="gray")

for i, (name, text) in enumerate(examples):
    y = 0.97 - i / len(examples)
    ax.text(0.0, y, name, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", va="center")
    ax.text(0.14, y, text.replace("$", r"\$"),         # show the code itself
            family="monospace", fontsize=10, va="center", color="#126b78")
    ax.text(0.66, y, text, fontsize=16, va="center")   # Matplotlib draws the maths

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    
The same maths in a real plot: title, axis labels, legend, and a formula on the plot.

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 math_text_plot.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.linspace(0, 5, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8), layout="constrained")

for tau in [0.5, 1, 2]:
    ax.plot(t, np.exp(-t / tau), label=rf"$\tau = {tau}$ s")     # rf: maths + a variable

ax.set_title(r"Exponential decay: $C(t) = C_0\,e^{-t/\tau}$", fontsize=14)
ax.set_xlabel(r"Time, $t$ (s)", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel(r"$C \,/\, C_0$", fontsize=12)
ax.text(2.4, 0.55, r"$\frac{dC}{dt} = -\frac{C}{\tau}$", fontsize=20, color="#126b78")
ax.legend(fontsize=12)

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Raw strings, variables in maths, maths font, full LaTeXr"...", rf"...", mathtext.fontset
                            
                        
                        

                            
 math_text_tips.py

                            
# 1. Maths goes between $ ... $, inside a raw string r"..."
ax.set_xlabel(r"Wavelength $\lambda$ (nm)")

# 2. Why r? Without it, Python reads \t as a TAB:
#    "$\tau$" breaks, r"$\tau$" works.

# 3. Maths + a Python variable: rf"..." and DOUBLE braces for LaTeX braces
tau = 2
ax.set_title(rf"$\tau = {tau}$ s,   $x^{{2}}$")   # {tau} = variable, {{2}} = LaTeX

# 4. Make maths use the same font as the normal text
plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "dejavusans"    # or "stix" for a journal look

# 5. Full LaTeX for everything (only if LaTeX is installed on your computer)
# plt.rcParams["text.usetex"] = True

                        

                    

                


                

                    
5 Colour of titles, labels, ticks, and text color · tick_params(colors=)

                    

                        Every piece of text takes color=. Colouring an axis label and its numbers like
                        its data line tells the reader immediately which axis belongs to which line.
                    

                    
                    
    
                        
  • set_title(..., color="navy"), set_xlabel(..., color="dimgray"): colour of titles and labels.
    • 
                        
  • tick_params(colors=...) colours tick marks and numbers. labelcolor= colours the numbers only.
    • 
                        
  • spines["left"].set_color(...) colours the axis line.
    • 
                        
  • bbox={"facecolor": ...} puts coloured text on a coloured box. Make sure the contrast is high enough to read.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 text_colours.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = np.arange(0, 24.5, 0.5)
temp = 24 + 4 * np.sin((hours - 9) * np.pi / 12)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(hours, temp, color="tab:red", linewidth=2)

ax.set_title("Air Temperature", color="navy", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (hour)", color="dimgray", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel(r"Temperature $T$ (°C)", color="tab:red", fontsize=12)    # maths in colour too

ax.tick_params(axis="y", colors="tab:red")        # y tick marks AND numbers
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelcolor="dimgray")    # only the x numbers
ax.spines["left"].set_color("tab:red")            # the y-axis line
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

ax.text(1, 27, "Hot afternoon", color="white", fontsize=11,
        bbox={"facecolor": "tab:red", "edgecolor": "none", "boxstyle": "round"})
ax.annotate("coldest", xy=(3, 20), xytext=(6, 20.6), color="tab:blue",
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": "tab:blue"})

plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Dark background for slides, and one text colour for everythingplt.style.context("dark_background"), rcParams
                            
                        
                        

                            
 text_colours_style.py

                            
# Dark slides: one line changes every colour
with plt.style.context("dark_background"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(hours, temp, color="gold")
    ax.set_title("Air Temperature")
    plt.show()

# One text colour for the whole figure
plt.rcParams.update({"text.color": "navy", "axes.labelcolor": "navy",
                     "xtick.color": "navy", "ytick.color": "navy"})

                        

                    

                


                

                    
6 Font sizes everywhere at once rcParams

                    

                        Changing fontsize= in every command is slow and easy to forget. Set the sizes once
                        at the top of your script with plt.rcParams.
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Set all font sizes in one placeplt.rcParams.update
                            
                        
                        

                            
 font_sizes.py

                            
# One place for all font sizes (put it at the top of your script)
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 11,          # default for everything
    "axes.titlesize": 13,     # ax.set_title
    "axes.labelsize": 12,     # ax.set_xlabel / set_ylabel
    "xtick.labelsize": 10,
    "ytick.labelsize": 10,
    "legend.fontsize": 10,
})

# Or change one piece of text only
ax.set_title("Air Temperature", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="navy")

                        

                    

                


                

                    
 Cheat sheet

                    

                        

                            
Write thisWhat it does

                            
                            
ax.set_title("...")Title of one panel

                            
fig.suptitle("...")Title of the whole figure

                            
ax.text(x, y, "...")Text at a data position

                            
transform=ax.transAxesPosition in plot fractions 0–1

                            
ax.annotate("...", xy=..., xytext=..., arrowprops={...})Text with an arrow

                            
ax.axhline(25) / ax.axvline(12)Horizontal / vertical reference line

                            
plt.imread("photo.png")Read a picture file

                            
ax.inset_axes([x, y, w, h]).imshow(photo)Picture in a corner of the plot

                            
AnnotationBbox(OffsetImage(icon), xy, xybox)Icon at a data point, with an arrow

                            
fontsize=12, fontweight="bold"Size and weight of one text

                            
ha="center", va="top"Alignment: horizontal / vertical

                            
r"$T_{max}$"Math text: subscript

                            
r"m$^{-2}$"Math text: superscript

                            
r"$\alpha$, $\Delta T$"Greek letters

                            
r"$\frac{dT}{dt}$"Fraction

                            
rf"$\tau = {tau}$"Maths with a Python variable

                            
color="navy"Colour of any title, label, or text

                            
ax.tick_params(colors="tab:red")Colour of tick marks and numbers

                            
                        

                    

                


            


            

                

                    6
                    

                        
 Plot colours

                    

                

                
How to write colours, which colours everyone can see, and how to use colour to guide the eye.


                

                    
1 Ways to write a colour color="..."

                    
Every plotting command accepts color=, written in any of these ways:

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Names like "tomato", "navy", "darkgreen": easy to read in code.
    • 
                        
  • Hex codes like "#3776ab": exact colours, for example from your institute's style.
    • 
                        
  • Grey levels as a string from "0" (black) to "1" (white).
    • 
                        
  • "C0" … "C9": the default colours, in the order Matplotlib uses them.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colour_formats.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

colors = ["tomato", "#3776ab", (0.2, 0.6, 0.3), "0.6", "C4", "tab:orange"]
labels = ['"tomato"\nname', '"#3776ab"\nhex code', "(0.2, 0.6, 0.3)\nRGB 0-1",
          '"0.6"\ngrey level', '"C4"\ncycle no. 4', '"tab:orange"\nTableau']

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.8), layout="constrained")
ax.bar(range(len(colors)), [5, 6, 4, 3, 5, 6], color=colors, edgecolor="black")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(colors)), labels, family="monospace", fontsize=10)
ax.set_title("Six ways to write a colour")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
2 Colour-blind safe palettes

                    

                        About 1 in 12 men has some colour-vision deficiency. Red and green are the usual problem.
                        The Okabe-Ito palette was designed to stay distinguishable for them:
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colour_palettes.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

palettes = {
    "Matplotlib default (C0-C9)": [f"C{i}" for i in range(10)],
    "Okabe-Ito (colour-blind safe)": ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
                                      "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000"],
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 2.8), layout="constrained")
for ax, (name, colors) in zip(axes, palettes.items()):
    for i, color in enumerate(colors):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i, 0), 0.95, 1, color=color))
        ax.text(i + 0.47, -0.15, color, ha="center", va="top",
                family="monospace", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 1)
    ax.set_title(name, loc="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
    ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Use a palette automatically, and fix one colour per groupaxes.prop_cycle and a colour dictionary
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colour_cycle.py

                            
# Use your own colours for every new line, automatically
from cycler import cycler

okabe_ito = ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7"]
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = cycler(color=okabe_ito)

# Colour by group from a dictionary: same group = same colour in every figure
group_colors = {"Control": "0.5", "Low dose": "#56B4E9", "High dose": "#D55E00"}
for name, values in groups.items():
    ax.plot(values, color=group_colors[name], label=name)

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Grey for context, colour for the message

                    

                        The strongest colour trick is to use less colour. Draw everything in grey and only
                        the important line in a strong colour. The reader's eye goes straight to it.
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colour_highlight.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
years = np.arange(2000, 2026)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5), layout="constrained")

# Context: all stations in light grey
for _ in range(15):
    ax.plot(years, 24 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.02, 0.15, len(years))),
            color="lightgray", linewidth=1)

# The story: one station in a strong colour, drawn on top
tainan = 24 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.06, 0.12, len(years)))
ax.plot(years, tainan, color="#d62728", linewidth=2.5)
ax.text(years[-1] + 0.3, tainan[-1], "Tainan", color="#d62728",
        fontweight="bold", va="center")

ax.set_title("Grey for context, one colour for the message")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean temperature (°C)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
4 Colour rules

                    
    
                        
  • Use as few colours as possible. More than 6–7 become hard to tell apart.
    • 
                        
  • Keep the same colour for the same thing in every figure of a paper or thesis.
    • 
                        
  • Do not rely on colour alone: add different markers or line styles too.
    • 
                        
  • Check your figure in greyscale: if two lines look identical, change one.
    • 
                        
  • Name lines directly at their ends (as above) instead of a legend when there are only a few.
    • 
                    

                


                

                    
 Cheat sheet

                    

                        

                            
Write thisWhat it does

                            
                            
color="tomato"Named colour

                            
color="#3776ab"Hex colour

                            
color=(0.2, 0.6, 0.3)RGB from 0 to 1

                            
color="0.6"Grey level (0 black … 1 white)

                            
color="C0"Default colour number 0

                            
edgecolor="black"Outline colour of bars, markers, patches

                            
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"]Your own default colour order

                            
                        

                    

                


            


            

                

                    7
                    

                        
 Opacity (alpha)

                    

                

                
Transparency lets overlapping data show through, and makes uncertainty bands possible.


                

                    
1 Transparency shows where data overlap alpha

                    

                        alpha goes from 1 (solid) to 0 (invisible). With thousands of
                        points, solid markers merge into one blob. Transparent markers show where the data are
                        dense: overlapping points add up to a darker colour.
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 alpha_scatter.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
x = rng.normal(0, 1, 5000)
y = x + rng.normal(0, 0.6, 5000)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4), layout="constrained",
                         sharex=True, sharey=True)

for ax, alpha in zip(axes, [1.0, 0.3, 0.05]):
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=8, alpha=alpha, color="tab:blue")
    ax.set_title(f"alpha={alpha}")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
2 Bands and overlapping shapes fill_between · hist

                    

                        A transparent band shows an uncertainty range without hiding the line or the grid.
                        Two transparent histograms can be compared in the same place.
                    

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            Show the code for this pictureComplete and ready to run
                            
                        
                        

                            
 alpha_band_hist.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
days = np.arange(60)
mean = 25 + 3 * np.sin(days / 9)
spread = 0.8 + 0.6 * np.abs(np.sin(days / 15))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.2), layout="constrained")

# (a) A transparent band shows the uncertainty around a line
ax1.fill_between(days, mean - spread, mean + spread,
                 color="tab:blue", alpha=0.25, label="± 1 SD")
ax1.plot(days, mean, color="tab:blue", label="Mean")
ax1.legend()
ax1.set_title("(a) fill_between(..., alpha=0.25)")
ax1.set_xlabel("Day")
ax1.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")

# (b) Two histograms on top of each other: both stay visible
ax2.hist(rng.normal(70, 8, 500), bins=25, alpha=0.5, label="Class A")
ax2.hist(rng.normal(78, 8, 500), bins=25, alpha=0.5, label="Class B")
ax2.legend()
ax2.set_title("(b) overlapping histograms, alpha=0.5")
ax2.set_xlabel("Score")

plt.show()

                        

                    

                


                

                    
3 Transparent backgrounds and RGBA colours transparent=True

                    

                        
                            
                            Save with no background, and colours with their own alphasavefig(transparent=True), (r, g, b, a)
                            
                        
                        

                            
 transparency_tips.py

                            
# Transparent background: the figure blends into slides of any colour
fig.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300, transparent=True)

# Colour with its own transparency: (red, green, blue, alpha)
ax.plot(x, y, color=(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5))

# Transparent face, solid edge: overlapping points stay outlined
ax.scatter(x, y, s=60, facecolor=(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.2), edgecolor="navy")

                        

                    

                    
    
                        
  • For a band, alpha=0.2–0.3. For overlapping histograms, 0.5. For dense scatter, 0.05–0.3.
    • 
                        
  • Transparent colours can look different on paper. Check a printed copy before submitting.
    • 
                    

                


                

                    
 Cheat sheet

                    

                        

                            
Write thisWhat it does

                            
                            
alpha=0.3Transparency of one plot element

                            
ax.fill_between(x, low, high, alpha=0.25)Transparent band

                            
color=(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5)Colour with its own alpha (RGBA)

                            
facecolor=(…, 0.2), edgecolor="navy"Transparent inside, solid outline

                            
fig.savefig("f.png", transparent=True)No background behind the figure

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Why does plt.colorbar() say "No mappable was found"?
            

            

                You called it after a plot that has no colour values, such as plt.plot. Save what imshow, contourf, or scatter(c=...) returns, and pass it: fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax).
            


        

        

            
                My colorbar is taller than my plot. How do I match them?
            

            

                Use shrink= (for example 0.8), or create the figure with layout="constrained", which sizes colorbars to fit the plot.
            


        

        

            
                Should I use plt.xlabel or ax.set_xlabel?
            

            

                Both work. plt. changes the current plot, ax. changes a specific one. With subplots, always use ax. so you know exactly which panel you change.
            


        

        

            
                Why is my legend empty or missing lines?
            

            

                Only lines with a label= appear. Also call ax.legend() after drawing all lines.
            


        

        

            
                How do I make all my figures look the same?
            

            

                Put your settings (font sizes, colours, line widths) in plt.rcParams at the top of every script, or save them in a style file and load it with plt.style.use("my_style.mplstyle").
            


        

        

            
                My saved figure cuts off the labels or the legend. Why?
            

            

                Save with fig.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight"), or create the figure with layout="constrained".
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
39. Making Animations with Matplotlib


    

        Stage V · Python for Researchers
        Planned
    


    

        

        

            
Show how data changes, not only the final result

            

                An animation is useful when time matters: a moving weather field,
                ocean current, changing temperature map, simulation result, or
                model training process.
            

        

    


    

        
 Animation has three important parts


        

            
1Figure
Create the axes and first plot.

            
2Update function
Change the plot for each frame.

            
3Frames
Tell Python how many time steps to show.

        

    


    

        
 A basic line animation


        
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot(x, np.sin(x))

ax.set_ylim(-1.2, 1.2)

def update(frame):
    y = np.sin(x + frame / 10)
    line.set_ydata(y)
    return line,

animation = FuncAnimation(
    fig,
    update,
    frames=100,
    interval=50
)

plt.show()

    


    

        
 Save an animation


        
# GIF file
animation.save("wave.gif", writer="pillow", fps=20)

# MP4 file
animation.save("wave.mp4", writer="ffmpeg", fps=20)


        

            
            

                Saving MP4 files usually requires FFmpeg. GIF files often work
                with Pillow, but they can become large for many frames.
            

        

    


    

        
 Animation Preview


        

            

            
        


        

            
        

    


    


        
            
            Open 20 thinking practice questions
        

        


            
1
Animate a sine wave that moves to the right.


            
2
Make the animation run faster by changing one setting.


            
3
Save the animation as a GIF.


            
4
Show the frame number as the title of each frame.


            
5
Animate a point moving around a circle.


            
6
Animate a line that grows one data point at a time.


            
7
Animate a bar chart where bar heights change.


            
8
Animate a 2D temperature map that changes over time.


            
9
Show the date of each map frame in the title.


            
10
Make the animation play only once instead of looping.


            
11
Display an animation inside a Jupyter notebook.


            
12
Save an MP4 video at 300 dpi quality.


            
13
Animate a scatter plot of moving particles.


            
14
Keep a fixed colour scale across all frames of a map.


            
15
Animate a trail: show the last 10 positions of a moving point.


            
16
Animate two lines at the same time.


            
17
Make a simple animation by saving one PNG per frame.

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                My animation shows only the first frame. Why?
            

            

                Keep a reference to the animation: write anim = FuncAnimation(...), not just FuncAnimation(...). Otherwise Python deletes it immediately. In Jupyter, show it with HTML(anim.to_jshtml()).
            


        

        

            
                Saving as MP4 says FFmpeg is not available. What do I do?
            

            

                FFmpeg is a separate program. Install it (for example conda install ffmpeg, or download it and add it to PATH), or save a GIF with writer="pillow" instead.
            


        

        

            
                What is the difference between interval and fps?
            

            

                interval (milliseconds) controls playback speed on screen. fps (frames per second) sets the speed of the saved file. 50 ms ≈ 20 fps.
            


        

        

            
                Why is there a comma in line, = ax.plot(...)?
            

            

                ax.plot returns a list of lines. The comma unpacks the first (and only) line, so you can update it later with line.set_ydata().
            


        

        

            
                Why should I update the data instead of redrawing the whole plot?
            

            

                Changing existing objects (set_data, set_ydata) is much faster than clearing and plotting again for every frame, especially for long animations.
            


        

        

            
                My GIF file is huge. How can I make it smaller?
            

            

                Use fewer frames, a lower dpi, a smaller figure size, or save as MP4, which compresses video much better than GIF.
            


        

        

            
                Can I put an animation in a paper?
            

            

                Printed papers need static figures, so show 3–4 key frames side by side. Many journals accept the animation as a supplementary video file.
            


        

        

            
                What does blit=True do?
            

            

                It redraws only the parts that changed, which makes animations smoother. Your update function must then return the changed objects. If titles or labels do not update, turn blit off.
            


        


    


    

        

        
    







    
40. Making Publication-Quality Graphs


    

        Stage V · Python for Researchers
        Planned
    


    

        

        

            
A good figure should explain itself

            
 
                A publication-quality graph is clear, honest, readable, and
                consistent. A reader should understand the main message without
                searching through your code or guessing the units. This won't gaurentee the publish of your 
                paper. But it will make your paper a good standard.  
            

        

    

    

        
 It looked fine on screen…


        

            Many students and early-career researchers struggle to make clear, good-quality figures.
            A plot looks perfect in the Python window, but once it is placed in the manuscript, it
            suddenly looks poor: the lines are blurry, the text is far too small (or too large),
            and the image is wider than the text column.
        


        

            The usual quick fix is to drag the picture smaller or larger in Word, or to set its width
            and height in LaTeX. But resizing a finished image cannot add detail. It only stretches or
            squeezes the pixels that are already there, so the figure becomes distorted and pixelated.
        


        

            
            
        


        

            
            Same data, same plot. The right-hand figure was saved at screen resolution in a large window,
            then stretched to fit the page. Click either picture to compare them at full size.
        


        
    

    

         Rules
        
 How to make figures that look right in the paper


        

            The fix for blurry, oversized figures is simple: create the figure at its final size,
            with final font sizes, and save it in a sharp format. Then you never resize it in the
            manuscript. These are the rules, one by one.
        


        


            

                1
                

                    
Make the figure at its final size

                    
Matplotlib's figsize is in inches (1 in = 2.54 cm). Make the figure exactly as wide as it will be printed. Then you insert it at 100% and never drag or stretch it.

                    
                    
    
                        
  • Full text width of a journal page: about figsize=(7, …), which is 17.8 cm.
    • 
                        
  • One column, or one of two figures side by side: figsize=(3.5, …), which is 8.9 cm.
    • 
                        
  • Choose the height freely; about 0.6–0.75 × the width usually looks good.
    • 
                    

                    

                        

                            
ExampleOne columnFull width

                            
                                
Elsevier journals90 mm (3.5 in)190 mm (7.5 in)

                                
Nature journals89 mm (3.5 in)183 mm (7.2 in)

                                
Springer journals84 mm (3.3 in)174 mm (6.9 in)

                                
Thesis in Word, A4 with 2.5 cm margins—16 cm (6.3 in)

                            
                        

                    

                    
These are typical values. Always check the author guidelines of your journal for the exact widths.

                    

                        
                            
                            Set the size in inches or centimetresfigsize=(width, height)
                            
                        
                        

                            
 figure_size.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# figsize is in INCHES (1 inch = 2.54 cm)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))            # full text width  (7 in = 17.8 cm)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 2.6))        # one column       (3.5 in = 8.9 cm)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.8))  # two panels side by side, 3.5 in each

# Think in centimetres? Convert once:
cm = 1 / 2.54
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(17 * cm, 9 * cm))

                        

                    

                

            


            

                2
                

                    
Save at high resolution: 300 dpi or more

                    
dpi = dots (pixels) per inch. The pixel width of a PNG is inches × dpi: a 7-inch figure at 600 dpi is 4200 pixels wide. Use at least 300 dpi, and 600 dpi for line plots with thin lines and small text.

                    
Raising the dpi later in Word does not help: the missing pixels never come back. Choose it when you save.

                

            


            

                3
                

                    
Save as PNG and PDF. Avoid JPG.

                    
                    
    
                        
  • PNG: lossless. Use it for Word and PowerPoint.
    • 
                        
  • PDF: vector. Lines and text are stored as shapes, so they stay sharp at any zoom. Use it for LaTeX and whenever the journal accepts it.
    • 
                        
  • JPG / JPEG is made for photos. Its compression adds specks around lines and text, and they get worse every time the file is saved again.
    • 
                        
  • Some journals ask for TIFF or EPS: Matplotlib can save those too.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Save in the right formatspng at 600 dpi, pdf, and tiff/eps if asked
                            
                        
                        

                            
 save_formats.py

                            
# Raster image (for Word, PowerPoint): at least 300 dpi, 600 for line plots
fig.savefig("figure1.png", dpi=600)

# Vector image (for LaTeX, and many journals): sharp at any zoom, no dpi needed
fig.savefig("figure1.pdf")

# Only if the journal asks for these formats
fig.savefig("figure1.tiff", dpi=600)
fig.savefig("figure1.eps")

# Not for plots: .jpg / .jpeg. Its compression adds grey specks around
# lines and text, and they get worse every time the file is saved again.

                        

                    

                

            


            

                4
                

                    
Remove empty space: use padding

                    
Default figures often have a wide empty border, a title far above the plot, and a colorbar far to the side. That wastes space on the page, and the plot itself ends up small. Use a tidy layout and small padding values.

                    
                    
    
                        
  • layout="constrained" arranges plots, labels and colorbars automatically.
    • 
                        
  • pad= in set_title and colorbar, and labelpad= in axis labels, set each gap.
    • 
                        
  • bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0.03 when saving cuts away the empty border.
    • 
                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Close gaps around title, labels, and colorbarlayout, pad, labelpad, bbox_inches
                            
                        
                        

                            
 padding.py

                            
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 3), layout="constrained")   # tidy spacing

image = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis")
ax.set_title("Sea-surface temperature", pad=6)   # gap: title <-> plot (points)
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)", labelpad=3)      # gap: label <-> tick numbers
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, pad=0.02)             # gap: plot <-> colorbar

fig.savefig("figure1.png", dpi=600,
            bbox_inches="tight",                 # cut away the empty border
            pad_inches=0.03)                     # keep only a thin margin

                        

                    

                

            


            

                5
                

                    
Do not let the colorbar be bigger than the plot

                    
A map that is wider than it is tall leaves a colorbar sticking out above and below it. It looks careless and wastes height. Make the colorbar exactly as tall as the map.

                    
                    

                        
                            
                            A colorbar exactly as tall as the plotmake_axes_locatable, or shrink
                            
                        
                        

                            
 colorbar_height.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.axes_grid1 import make_axes_locatable

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 2.6))
image = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")

# A colorbar axes glued to the right side of the map, exactly as tall as it
cax = make_axes_locatable(ax).append_axes("right", size="4%", pad=0.08)
fig.colorbar(image, cax=cax, label="SST (°C)")

# Simpler option for most plots: constrained layout + shrink
# fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 2.6), layout="constrained")
# fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)

                        

                    

                

            


            

                6
                

                    
Use font sizes that match the manuscript

                    
Manuscript text is usually 10–12 pt. Text in figures should be a little smaller than the body text, and never smaller than about 7 pt at printed size.

                    

                        

                            
Text in the figureOne figure in a row (7 in)Two figures in a row (3.5 in each)

                            
                                
Axis labels10–11 pt9–10 pt

                                
Title (if used)10–11 pt10 pt

                                
Tick numbers9–10 pt8–9 pt

                                
Legend9 pt8–9 pt

                            
                        

                    

                    

                        
                            
                            Set all font sizes onceplt.rcParams.update
                            
                        
                        

                            
 font_sizes.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,           # default for all text
    "axes.labelsize": 10,      # axis labels
    "axes.titlesize": 11,      # title
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,      # tick numbers
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,      # legend
})

                        

                    

                

            


            

                7
                

                    
Two figures in a row: keep fonts the same size as the text

                    
When each panel is made at 3.5 in, the point sizes you set are the sizes readers see. You may go one point smaller if a panel is crowded.

                    
The real mistake is making a figure at 7 in and then shrinking it to half the width in Word or LaTeX: every font becomes half its size.

                    
                

            


            

                8
                

                    
Use the same font as your manuscript

                    
A figure in Arial inside a paper set in Times New Roman looks pasted in. Use the font of the manuscript, and a matching font for maths.

                    

                        
                            
                            Times New Roman, Arial, or LaTeX fontsfont.family and mathtext.fontset
                            
                        
                        

                            
 font_family.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Manuscript in Times New Roman (Word templates of many journals)
plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "Times New Roman",
                     "mathtext.fontset": "stix"})     # maths that matches Times

# Manuscript in Arial / Helvetica
plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "Arial",
                     "mathtext.fontset": "dejavusans"})

# LaTeX manuscript (Computer Modern), only if LaTeX is installed:
# plt.rcParams.update({"text.usetex": True, "font.family": "serif"})

                        
    
                            
  • If Python says "findfont: Font family not found", the font is not installed (common on Linux). Install it, or use "serif" / "sans-serif".
    • 
                        

                        

                    

                

            


        


        
 More points worth adding


        


            

                9
                

                    
Read the journal's author guidelines first

                    
They list the exact figure widths, accepted formats (often TIFF, EPS, or PDF), the minimum font size and line width, and the maximum file size. Five minutes of reading saves a resubmission.

                

            


            

                10
                

                    
Embed the fonts in your PDF

                    
Some journals reject PDFs whose fonts are not embedded. With font type 42, Matplotlib embeds the real font, and the text stays editable.

                    

                        
                            
                            Embed fontspdf.fonttype = 42
                            
                        
                        

                            
 embed_fonts.py

                            
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams["pdf.fonttype"] = 42    # embed real fonts in PDF (journals accept them,
plt.rcParams["ps.fonttype"] = 42     # and text stays editable in Illustrator/Inkscape)

                        

                    

                

            


            

                11
                

                    
Insert the figure at 100%

                    
Because the figure already has its final size, insert it without resizing. In Word, check Format Picture → Size → Scale = 100%. In LaTeX, leave out width=.

                    

                        
                            
                            Insert a PDF figure in LaTeX at its real size\includegraphics without width
                            
                        
                        

                            
 manuscript.tex

                            
% LaTeX: the PDF was already made at full text width (7 in)
\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics{figure1.pdf}    % no width= or scale=: it is used at 100%
    \caption{Daily mean temperature at Taipei and Tainan, January 2026.}
\end{figure}

                        

                    

                

            


            

                12
                

                    
Make lines and markers thick enough

                    
Hairlines disappear in print. Use lines of 1–1.5 pt (never below 0.5 pt) and markers of 3–5 pt. Axis lines of 0.8 pt look clean.

                

            


            

                13
                

                    
Let the caption be the title

                    
Most journals put the description in the caption under the figure, not in a title inside it. Use panel labels (a), (b) instead, and keep titles for slides and posters.

                

            


            

                14
                

                    
Keep PDFs small when you plot many points

                    
A vector PDF stores every single point. With huge scatter plots or dense maps, rasterize only the data and keep the text as vectors.

                    

                        
                            
                            Rasterize only the pointsrasterized=True
                            
                        
                        

                            
 rasterize_points.py

                            
# A PDF with 100 000 scatter points is huge and slow to open.
# rasterized=True turns only the points into a picture inside the PDF;
# axes, labels and text stay sharp vector graphics.
ax.scatter(x, y, s=2, rasterized=True)
fig.savefig("figure1.pdf", dpi=600)     # dpi is used for the rasterized part

                        

                    

                

            


            

                15
                

                    
Check it the way a reader will

                    
Open the saved file at 100% zoom, or print the page, before you submit. Check that every label is readable, the colours work in greyscale, and all figures in the paper look the same.

                

            


        

    


    

        
 Put it all together: a template for every paper figure


        

            This script follows all the rules above: two panels side by side at 3.5 in each (7 in in total),
            Times New Roman, the font sizes from the table, panel labels, a colorbar that fits, no empty border,
            and PNG + PDF files at 600 dpi.
        


                    

                    

                        
                            
                            The complete templateCopy it, then replace the data and labels with your own
                            
                        
                        

                            
 paper_figure_template.py

                            
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ---- 1. One style for every figure of the paper ----
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "Times New Roman",   # same font as the manuscript
    "mathtext.fontset": "stix",
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "axes.linewidth": 0.8,
    "lines.linewidth": 1.4,
    "pdf.fonttype": 42,                 # embed fonts in the PDF
    "savefig.dpi": 600,                 # high resolution PNG
    "savefig.bbox": "tight",            # no empty border ...
    "savefig.pad_inches": 0.03,         # ... only a thin margin
})

# ---- 2. Example data ----
days = np.arange(1, 32)
taipei = 16 + 3 * np.sin(days / 5) + 0.4 * np.cos(days * 1.7)
tainan = 19 + 2.5 * np.sin(days / 5 + 0.6) + 0.4 * np.sin(days * 1.3)
lon, lat = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(118, 124, 60), np.linspace(20, 27, 70))
sst = 29 - 0.8 * (lat - 20) + 0.6 * np.sin(lon * 1.5)

# ---- 3. Two panels side by side: 3.5 in each = 7 in = full text width ----
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.8), layout="constrained")

ax1.plot(days, taipei, "o-", markersize=3, label="Taipei")
ax1.plot(days, tainan, "s--", markersize=3, label="Tainan")
ax1.set_xlabel("Day of January 2026")
ax1.set_ylabel("Mean temperature (°C)")
ax1.legend(frameon=False)

image = ax2.imshow(sst, origin="lower", extent=[118, 124, 20, 27], cmap="viridis")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax2, shrink=0.95, pad=0.02, label="SST (°C)")
ax2.set_xlabel("Longitude (°E)")
ax2.set_ylabel("Latitude (°N)")

for ax, letter in zip((ax1, ax2), "ab"):        # panel labels instead of titles
    ax.text(0, 1.03, f"({letter})", transform=ax.transAxes,
            fontweight="bold", va="bottom")

# ---- 4. Save: PNG for Word, PDF for LaTeX. Never JPG. ----
fig.savefig("figure1.png")
fig.savefig("figure1.pdf")
plt.show()

                        
    
                            
  • The saved figure1.png is 7 in × 600 dpi ≈ 4200 pixels wide: sharp in Word at 100%.
    • 
                            
  • figure1.pdf is a vector file: use it in LaTeX with \includegraphics{figure1.pdf}.
    • 
                            
  • Put the rcParams block in its own file (for example paper_style.py) and import it in every script, so all figures match.
    • 
                        

                        

                    

    


    

        
 Publication figure checklist


        

            
Clear title
Describe the figure accurately.

            
Axis labels
Include variables and units.

            
Readable fonts
Keep text large enough after printing.

            
Good colours
Use clear, colour-blind-friendly contrast.

            
Legend
Explain multiple lines or groups.

            
High resolution
Save at 300 dpi or higher.

        

    


    

        
 Set a consistent style


        
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "Arial",      # the font of your manuscript
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "axes.linewidth": 0.8
})

    


    

        
 Example of a polished figure


        
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5))    # full text width: inserted at 100%

plt.plot(
    days,
    temperature,
    color="#0072B2",
    linewidth=1.5,
    marker="o",
    markersize=4,
    label="Observed temperature"
)

plt.xlabel("Day")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.title("Daily Sea-Surface Temperature")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
plt.legend(frameon=False)

plt.tight_layout()

plt.savefig("figure_temperature.png", dpi=600, bbox_inches="tight")   # for Word
plt.savefig("figure_temperature.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")            # for LaTeX

plt.show()

            Questions That May Come to Your Mind
        


        

            
                Should I save figures as PNG, PDF, or SVG?
            

            

                PDF, SVG, or EPS (vector formats) stay sharp at any size and are best for line plots. Use PNG or TIFF at 300–600 dpi for images and maps with many points. Check what the journal asks for.
            


        

        

            
                What does dpi mean?
            

            

                Dots per inch. A 3-inch-wide figure saved at 300 dpi becomes 900 pixels wide. dpi only affects raster formats like PNG and TIFF. Vector PDFs have no fixed resolution.
            


        

        

            
                Arial gives a "font not found" warning. What should I do?
            

            

                The font is not installed where Matplotlib can see it (common on Linux). Use "DejaVu Sans" or "sans-serif", or install the font and clear Matplotlib's font cache.
            


        

        

            
                Why do my labels get cut off in the saved file?
            

            

                Use bbox_inches="tight" in savefig, or call fig.tight_layout() before saving. Both make room for labels outside the axes.
            


        

        

            
                How large should text be in the final figure?
            

            

                Usually 7–10 pt at the printed size. Make the figure at its real size (for example 8.5 cm wide) so the font size you set is what readers see.
            


        

        

            
                Is it honest to change the axis range?
            

            

                Choosing a range that shows your data clearly is fine. Cutting an axis to make a tiny difference look dramatic is not, especially for bar charts. Comparable panels should use the same scale.
            


        

        

            
                How do I check whether my colours work for colour-blind readers?
            

            

                Use the Okabe–Ito colours shown above or the viridis family, and test your image with a colour-blindness simulator such as Coblis. Different line styles or markers add extra safety.
            


        

        

            
                How do I keep all figures in my thesis consistent?
            

            

                Put your rcParams settings in one style file (for example thesis.mplstyle) and load it with plt.style.use("thesis.mplstyle") at the start of every script.
